title: Revolutionizing the tomato cultivation: advances and frontiers in virus-resistant tomato breeding.
authors: Khaskheli, Maqsood Ahmed; Raza, Ali; Jueping, Song; Hassan, Muhammad Ahmad; Janiad, Sara; Sabir, Sumera; Khaskheli, Raheel Ahmed; Khan, Muhammad Aakif; Zeb, Aqib; Hayyat, Qaisar; Wang, Yong
abstract: Plant viruses are major pathogens that significantly reduce the quality and yield of tomato crops. The most influential viruses belong to the genera Crinivirus, Begomovirus, Tobamovirus, and Potyvirus. Tomato breeders have successfully incorporated virus-resistance genes, such as Ty, Sw, Tm, and Pot 1, from wild germplasms into cultivated varieties. However, the challenge remains that most resistance genes confer only qualitative resistance, making them vulnerable to new viruses, recombination, and mixed infections. To our knowledge, this review is the first to systematically compare the synergy and complementarity among three antiviral breeding strategies-conventional R-gene pyramiding (e.g. Ty, Sw, Tm), RNA interference (RNAi)-based transgenics, and CRISPR/Cas genome editing-in tomato. We also innovatively incorporate the emerging genus Amalgavirus into the antiviral framework and propose targeted countermeasures against its escape mechanisms, including synthetic NLR decoys and Cas13-mediated transcriptional degradation. Using the three breeding methodologies, we concluded by outlining the difficulties and offering recommendations for future improvements in tomato antiviral breeding.

title: Bacterial competence and genetic diversity: Implications for the design of diagnostics and vaccines.
authors: Eba, Wondimagegn Wolde
abstract: Bacterial competence and genetic diversity are key determinants of microbial evolution, directly influencing pathogen adaptability, diagnostic reliability, and vaccine effectiveness. Natural transformation, together with horizontal gene transfer and homologous recombination, enables rapid genomic remodeling, facilitating the acquisition of antimicrobial resistance, modification of diagnostic targets, and generation of antigenic variants. These processes are particularly prominent in naturally competent and highly recombining pathogens, where population structures range from clonal to panmictic, shaping responses to selective pressures such as antibiotic use and immunization. This review synthesizes current understanding of the mechanisms governing bacterial competence and their role in generating genomic diversity, with emphasis on implications for diagnostics and vaccine design. Case studies-including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Helicobacter pylori-illustrate how recombination-driven diversification contributes to serotype replacement, diagnostic escape, and variable vaccine performance. Emerging approaches, including pan-genomic target selection, high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR-based diagnostics, and next-generation vaccine platforms, offer strategies to address these challenges but remain constrained by genomic variability and limited global surveillance. We argue that integrating evolutionary dynamics into diagnostic and vaccine development is essential for sustaining effectiveness. Continuous genomic monitoring and adaptive design frameworks will be critical to anticipate and mitigate competence-driven bacterial evolution in clinical and public health settings.

title: Stable truncating mutations in plakophilin-2 induce arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy-like phenotypes in adult zebrafish.
authors: Liu, Yuting; Niu, Yujuan; Jiang, Yajie; Ma, Taiwei; Yang, Peng; Ma, Wenyu; Liu, Shuai; Xu, Yuehang; Xin, Hui; Zhang, Hong; Wu, Chuanhong; Li, Zhiqiang; Sun, Yuanchao; Ding, Yonghe
abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) is an inherited cardiac disorder characterized by arrhythmias and fibrofatty myocardial remodeling, often leading to heart failure and sudden cardiac death. Mutations in plakophilin-2 (PKP2) represent the most prevalent genetic cause of ACM. Here, we establish zebrafish (Danio rerio) as a complementary vertebrate model for PKP2 mutation-based ACM. Comparative single-cell RNA-seq analyses revealed distinct cardiac expression patterns of PKP2 and its homologs across species. Using CRISPR-Cas9, we generated two truncating mutations in zebrafish pkp2, resulting in frameshifts and premature terminations (p.Glu250Glyfs *17 and p.Glu31Glyfs *72, respectively). Mutant zebrafish exhibited impaired cardiac contractility, arrhythmias, lipid accumulation on the ventricular surface, ultrastructural abnormalities of intercalated discs, and increased susceptibility to swimming exercise-induced sudden death. Transcriptomic analyses identified transcriptional alterations in genes involved in muscle contraction and lipid metabolism. Together, these data establish zebrafish as a useful complementary vertebrate model for studying PKP2-based ACM and gene-environment interactions underlying disease progression.

title: Genome-wide CRISPRa screens identify modulators of CAR T survival across diverse tumor cytokine milieus.
authors: Curtis, Benjamin C; Spurrell, Cailyn H; Flint, Lindsay; Lande, Aalton M; Leonardi, Marissa; Rosser, James M; Parker, Tavie; Chai, Tiffanie; Valdez, Ardizon; Toumi, Ryma; Murren, Nat; Fitzgerald, Michael; Martinez-Reyes, Jasmin; Watt, Finn; Saxby, Christopher P; Summers, Corinne; Gwiazda, Kamila S; Jensen, Michael C V; Oda, Shannon K
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has revolutionized the treatment of B cell malignancies, and extending this success to other cancers remains an urgent clinical objective. CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) is a gene nomination platform with the potential to direct next-generation cell product development, but genome-wide surveys using this technology in primary T cells have been limited by prohibitive cell requirements and short-lived activity. Here, we describe a CAR-restricted T cell expansion platform generating yields of CRISPRa-CAR T cells far exceeding those required for genome-scale screening ( approximately 10(9)). CRISPRa activity is sustained by incorporating divergent, duplicate elongation factor 1alpha core/human T cell leukemia virus hybrid promoters and by delivering guide RNAs late by lentiviral transduction to avoid losing perturbations that compromise early T cell activation or expansion. Manufactured CRISPRa-CAR T cells maintain potent on-target gene overexpression (>85% target(+)) across varied cell subsets, including those associated with T cell exhaustion, and over extended culture periods. When applied to survival-based genome-wide screens, CRISPRa-CAR T cell pools nominate endogenous genes that enhance CAR T cell persistence across varied cytokine levels in the presence of tumor (e.g., IRF4, GFI1, and GSE1). In a proof-of-concept study, we find that the survival effect of GSE1 can be preserved using a clinically relevant transgene overexpression strategy. More broadly, this screening framework establishes a foundation for systematic identification and downstream validation of genes that enhance cellular therapies.

title: Kat6a functions to protect lower jaw patterning during cellular stress.
authors: Eberhart, Johann; Ghosal, Ritika; Swartz, Mary; Liu, Joanna; Patel, Anushree
abstract: Phenotypic outcomes of most birth defects involve complex multifactorial interactions. In humans, heterozygosity for KAT6A or MEF2C causes highly variable syndromes1,2. These syndromes overlap phenotypically with Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS)2,3,4, with defects to the pharyngeal arches-derived craniofacial skeleton. In zebrafish, we demonstrate that cellular stressors, like ethanol, induce ventral patterning defects specifically in the first pharyngeal arch in kat6a mutants and heterozygotes and result in lower jaw defects. This is striking as anteroposterior and dorsoventral patterning of pharyngeal arches are typically independent. Kat6a regulates hox gene expression for anteroposterior patterning. Bmp/Edn1 signaling and their targets, like dlx genes and hand2, regulate dorsoventral patterning. In exposed kat6a mutants and heterozygotes, Bmp/Edn1 signaling remains intact. However, exposure causes a first arch specific loss of ventral specifiers in mutants and heterozygotes. The overall phenotype resembles loss of mef2ca, which governs dorsoventral patterning independent of Bmp/Edn1. We find that mef2ca is selectively lost in the first pharyngeal arch of exposed kat6a mutants and heterozygotes. CRISPR knockdown of mef2ca phenocopies the effect of exposure in kat6a mutants and heterozygotes. Tissue mosaics confirmed that first arch neural crest specifically require kat6a. Thus, multifactorial interactions reveal an unknown link between pharyngeal arch anteroposterior and dorsoventral patterning.

title: High-throughput identification of chromatin-opening transcription factors.
authors: Keith, Aidan; Jain, Shruti; Daza, Riza M; Qiu, Chengxiang; Germain, Pierre-Luc; Shendure, Jay; Domcke, Silvia
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Cell fate transitions involve major changes to the chromatin landscape, some of which are thought to deepen the basin around a newly adopted cell state, stabilizing gene expression programs that might otherwise be transient. Transcription factors (TFs) are central to this process, binding a subset of their genome-wide motif occurrences to create accessible regions that can act as cell type-specific enhancers. However, apart from a few well-studied cases, it is not clear which of the  approximately 1,600 mammalian TFs, when newly expressed, can directly or indirectly initiate newly accessible sites, nor why only some motif occurrences gain accessibility. Here, we applied pooled CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) to upregulate endogenous TFs to physiological levels in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs). After screening guides targeting 240 developmental TFs for transcriptional response, we selected 60 and jointly profiled gene expression and chromatin accessibility in  approximately 140,000 single cells. Some TFs ( e.g. Cdx2 , Sox10 ) appeared to initiate new accessibility on their own, predominantly at distal sites that are closed in mESCs but coincide with cell type-specific enhancers later in development. Others appeared to partner with "co-TFs", either by leveraging preexisting mESC heterogeneity ( e.g.  upward arrow Grhl1 in Tfap2c + mESCs --> opening of sites bearing motifs for both), or by hierarchical activation ( e.g.  upward arrow Sox7 -->  upward arrow Gata6 --> opening of sites bearing either or both motifs). Such dependencies shape which sites are used and which fates are reachable, and may explain the differential behavior of TFs with nearly identical consensus motifs. Thus, the capacity of a newly expressed TF to open chromatin strongly depends on the cell type, cell state and gene regulatory network it lands in. Charting these dependencies will inform how cell fate transitions are initiated in development, homeostasis and disease, and how to engineer them in silico, in vitro and in vivo .

title: SLC25A28 is a synthetic lethal vulnerability in nucleotide excision repair-deficient cancers.
authors: Yang, Nan; Hoeg, Lisa; Bai, Xuechun; Gao, Sizhi; de Stanchina, Elisa; Solit, David; Topka, Sabine; Belhadj, Sami; Carrot-Zhang, Jian; Iyer, Gopa; Durocher, Daniel; Mouw, Kent W; Joseph, Vijai; Offit, Kenneth; Lipkin, Steven
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Approximately 10% of bladder, upper urinary tract, and endometrial cancers harbor deleterious somatic alterations in nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway genes. Although platinum-based chemotherapy is the standard treatment for NER-deficient tumors, its utility is limited by nephrotoxicity, motivating alternative strategies that avoid direct DNA targeting. Here, we employed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen to identify synthetic lethal vulnerabilities in NER-deficient cancer cells. An ERCC4 -null RT112/84 bladder cancer cell line was generated and validated by Sanger sequencing and Western blotting, and functional NER deficiency was confirmed using a host cell reactivation assay. Parallel screens in ERCC4 -deficient and isogenic wild-type cells. nominated SLC25A28 as the top-ranked synthetic lethal candidate in ERCC4 -deficient cells, an interaction further supported by DepMap dependency. Clonogenic assays confirmed that loss of SLC25A28 selectively impaired cell viability in cells deficient for ERCC2 , ERCC3 , ERCC4 , or ERCC5 and inducible knockout selectively suppressed ERCC4 -deficient xenograft growth in-viv o. Mechanistically, RNA sequencing followed by gene set enrichment analysis revealed enrichment of oxidative stress-related pathways, including cellular responses to reactive oxygen species (ROS) and DNA damage signatures, upon SLC25A28 loss. These transcriptional changes are consistent with increased oxidative stress and DNA damage, placing heightened demand on NER-mediated repair. Direct measurement confirmed increased intracellular ROS. Collectively, our nominates SLC25A28 as a previously unrecognized synthetic lethal vulnerability in NER-deficient cancers and implicate mitochondrial iron homeostasis as a candidate metabolic dependency that may be targeted independently of platinum-based chemotherapy. SIGNIFICANCE: This study identifies SLC25A28 as a synthetic lethal vulnerability in nucleotide excision repair-deficient cancers, linking mitochondrial iron homeostasis and oxidative stress to selective DNA damage intolerance and therapeutic opportunity.

title: Niche-dependent epistasis within the cancer genome shapes metastatic fitness.
authors: Liu, Xiyu; He, Le; Zhao, Min; Golomb, Samantha M; Ma, Wei; Yang, Xinrui; Aleksandrovic, Emilija; Borges, Hazel M; Dean, Kevin M; Wang, Lei; Hon, Gary C; Gan, Dailin; Zhu, Hao; Li, Jun; Xu, Lin; Zhang, Siyuan
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Epistasis, the genetic interaction between loci, directs non-additive genotype-to-phenotype outcomes. Within a multicellular organism, how the tissue niche (E) shapes gene-by-gene epistasis (GxG) and its phenotypic consequences remains poorly studied. Using tumor lung metastasis as an experimental model, we mapped GxGxE through combinatorial CRISPR perturbation coupled with depletion of defined host myeloid populations in mice. The metastatic niche first selects disseminated tumor cells on GxG epistatic fitness, then drives transcriptome convergence regardless of genotype. Removing anatomically distinct myeloid populations reshaped the metastatic epistasis landscape despite identical tumor genotypes. Gene-by-gene-by-environment epistasis therefore operates at the organismal level, with interaction magnitude and sign set by niche cells. Beyond metastasis, our data suggest that the tissue niche conditions how genetic interactions translate into divergent phenotypes.

title: p38alpha MAPK integrates opposing oncogenic APC/beta-catenin/TCF and GUCY2C tumor-suppressor axes in colorectal cancer.
authors: Entezari, Ariana A; Caspi, Adi; Alvarez, Jasmine R; Evans, Andrew E; Rappaport, Jeffrey A; Kuret, Thomas J M; Doermann, Allison S; Mitra, Ramkrishna; Snook, Adam E; Waldman, Scott A
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sporadic colorectal cancers (CRCs) form following initiating APC mutations, inducing constitutive beta-catenin/TCF signaling. Similarly, the guanylyl cyclase C (GUCY2C) tumor suppressor axis is universally silenced in CRC. While the GUCY2C receptor is retained, loss of its paracrine hormones guanylin (GUCA2A) and uroguanylin (GUCA2B) is among the earliest events in transformation. Mutant APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling driving CRC transcriptionally silences GUCY2C hormone expression while suppressing that oncogenic pathway reconstitutes hormone production opposing tumorigenesis. p38alpha opposes tumor initiation, and its loss promotes transformation in chemical and genetic mouse models of CRC. In healthy intestine, p38alpha supports a gradient of epithelial differentiation along the crypt-surface axis. Here, we reveal that p38alpha links regulation of oncogenic APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling and GUCY2C hormone expression. METHODS: Regulation of p38alpha by APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling was defined in four genetically engineered human CRC cell lines with conditional oncogenic APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling and healthy human colon organoids. Expression of p38alpha was eliminated from conditional human CRC cell lines by pharmacological inhibition, RNA knockdown, and CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Transcriptomic analysis of these cells by RNA sequencing defined the set of genes regulated by APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling controlled through p38alpha. RESULTS: In CRC cell lines, APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling suppressed p38alpha phosphorylation and activity, whereas inhibition of APC/beta-catenin/TCF restored p38alpha signaling. In the absence of APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling, inhibiting p38alpha repressed GUCY2C hormone expression. Inhibiting APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling enriched phosphorylated p38alpha at the GUCA2A promoter. In that context, analysis of the CPTAC proteomic database revealed that phosphorylation of p38alpha and its upstream kinases MKK3 and MKK4 was reduced in human CRC. Finally, transcriptomic analysis revealed that p38alpha is a critical signaling node controlling the expression of a substantial subset of APC/beta-catenin/TCF-regulated genes in human CRC cells and patient tumors. CONCLUSIONS: APC/beta-catenin/TCF signaling inhibits p38alpha phosphorylation and transcriptional activity, suppressing GUCA2A and GUCA2B expression and functionally silencing the retained GUCY2C receptor. These findings identify p38alpha as a signaling intermediary integrating oncogenic APC/beta-catenin/TCF activity to extinction of the GUCY2C tumor-suppressor axis and reveal a broader p38alpha-dependent component of the APC/beta-catenin/TCF-regulated transcriptome.

title: tRNA-derived second messengers confer bacterial immunity.
authors: Valentin-Alvarado, Luis E; Yoon, Peter H; Lopez, Santiago C; Shulgina, Yekaterina; Langeberg, Conner; Armbruster, Emily; Ur-Rehman, Muhammad Moez; Loi, Kenneth; Taveneau, Cyntia; Esain-Garcia, Isabel; Koka, Mert; Zhang, Zeyuan Terry; Kashin, Dmitry; Schwede, Frank; Burgio, Gaetan; O'Connell, Mitchell R; Doherty, Erin E; Cate, Jamie H D; Knott, Gavin J; Doudna, Jennifer A
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Bacterial small-molecule messengers that function in diverse immune signaling pathways have been thought to derive strictly from biosynthesis using nucleotide and cofactor substrates. Here we report a nuclease-driven immune signaling pathway in which tRNA cleavage generates a specific small molecule that triggers cell death in response to RNA-guided transcript recognition in prokaryotes. We identify a class of type VI-B CRISPR systems in which the RNA-guided nuclease Cas13 and its accessory transmembrane protein, 2TMbeta, are co-encoded in an operon and are jointly required for bacteriophage defense. Upon target RNA recognition, Cas13 activates 2TMbeta by producing mono- and dinucleotide messengers bearing 2',3'-cyclic uridine phosphate ends by tRNA cleavage. Activated 2TMbeta destroys infected cells by forming a multimeric complex that disrupts cell membranes to mediate cell death. These findings demonstrate RNA-programmed tRNA cleavage for second-messenger biogenesis, revealing a new logic for prokaryotic immune signaling.

title: Epigenome Alterations and 3D Chromatin Architecture Remodeling in Inflammatory Macrophage Activation under Diabetic Conditions.
authors: Reddy, Marpadga A; Bhattacharya, Supriyo; Tanwar, Vinay Singh; Malek, Vajir; Chen, Zhuo; Zhang, Lingxiao; Lanting, Linda; Wu, Xiwei; Grant, Maria B; Tompkins, Joshua; Chen, Zhen Bouman; Natarajan, Rama
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Aberrant monocyte/macrophage activation in diabetes drives chronic inflammation and diabetic complications. Although epigenetic mechanisms are implicated in these processes, the contribution of three-dimensional (3D) chromatin reorganization remains unclear. Here, we use integrated multi-omics approaches to profile gene expression, chromatin accessibility and 3D chromatin architecture in human CD14(+) monocyte-derived macrophages exposed to high glucose and TNF-alpha (HT), mimicking the diabetic milieu. HT induces inflammatory transcription programs that recapitulate those observed in diabetes and dynamically remodel chromatin accessibility, enhancer-promoter interactions, and topologically associated domains. Inflammatory genes exhibit increased chromatin accessibility, whereas cell cycle and metabolic genes display reduced accessibility and weakened enhancer-promoter interactions. These architectural changes promote the convergence of lineage-determining and signal-dependent transcription factors at enhancer-promoter loops, generating distinct regulatory hubs that orchestrate pro-inflammatory responses. Similar enhancer-promoter interactions are observed in peripheral blood derived monocytes from individuals with diabetes. Furthermore, perturbing chromatin interactions via CRISPR interference targeting HT-induced enhancers suppresses nearby CCL2 and other chemokine genes. Collectively, this first comprehensive enhancer connectome map of macrophages under diabetic conditions advances the field by revealing extensive disease-associated rewiring of the 3D epigenome, highlighting chromatin architecture and epigenetic mechanisms as potential therapeutic target for diabetes-associated inflammation. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT: In diabetes, high glucose (Glc) and inflammatory cytokines remodel macrophage 3D chromatin architecture and enhancer connectomes, altering enhancer-promoter interactions, facilitating the convergence of lineage-specific and signal-dependent transcription factors (such as NF-kappaB) that regulate inflammatory factors associated with macrophage activation. This can promote chronic inflammation and accelerate diabetic complications. Targeted enhancer editing strategies could enable new epigenetic therapies to mitigate chronic inflammatory diabetes complications.

title: A new mouse model for a high-risk AMD variant, ARMS2 (A69S).
authors: Gogna, Navdeep; Collin, Gayle B; Hyde, Lillian F; Stone, Lisa; Pandey, Ravi; Kennedy, Victoria E; Krebs, Mark P; Naggert, Juergen K; Nishina, Patsy M
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults. The highest genetic risk for AMD maps to Chromosome 10q26. However, due to strong linkage disequilibrium between two genes, ARMS2 and HTRA1 located in this region, it has been difficult to determine whether one or both genes contribute to the AMD-disease risk. Functional studies of ARMS2 have been hampered due to the lack of animal models, as orthologs are only found in the higher primates and the gene is absent in rodents. To model ARMS2 biology in vivo , we used CRISPR-Cas9 to insert the complete human ARMS2 gene carrying the A69S risk variant (rs10490924), into a region of homology between humans and mice, on mouse Chromosome 7, 3.5 kb upstream of Htra1 , preserving its native promoter, spacing, and orientation. We also generated a mouse model bearing its wild-type counterpart ARMS2 (A69) ( ARMS2 (WT) ). RNA analysis revealed tissue- and cell-type-specific patterns of ARMS2 expression with enrichment in neural tissues, testis, and eye, and within the eye, in retinal horizontal cells and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). ARMS2 expression was consistent with human expression data and unaltered by the A69S mutation. By 12 months of age, ARMS2 (A69S) mice developed AMD-relevant phenotypes including increased fundus spots, A69S-specific thinning of the outer nuclear layer, and reduced scotopic ERG amplitudes. Transcriptomic profiling of postnatal day 14 retina and RPE-enriched fractions revealed reduced mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation genes, corroborated by reduced retinal mtDNA copy number and lower maximal respiration, alongside preliminary results that suggest sphingolipid remodeling in the RPE. This humanized model links the ARMS2 A69S variant to mitochondrial dysfunction and provides an in vivo platform for defining AMD mechanisms and testing therapies.

title: Establishment and characterization of LNCaP-TR-BoM, a bone metastasis-derived prostate cancer cell line with an intermediate AR-attenuated phenotype.
authors: Chao, Adrian; Lu, Xin
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: BACKGROUND: Progression of prostate cancer under androgen receptor (AR) pathway-targeted therapy spans a phenotypic spectrum, from tumors that sustain AR pathway output to tumors that become independent of AR signaling. Experimental models that occupy the intermediate portion of this spectrum, in which AR is still expressed but pathway output is reduced, are comparatively scarce. METHODS: LNCaP cells expressing a triple-modality reporter (LNCaP-TR) were injected into nude mice by the intracardiac route, and a bone lesion that arose in the middle spine of one animal was recovered and propagated as LNCaP-TR-BoM. The subline and its parental line were compared by two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture assays, RNA-seq, qRT-PCR, and immunoblotting. AR pathway output was assessed using KLK3 expression under AR antagonist treatment. Public prostate cancer datasets provided clinical context. A CRISPR-Cas9 EPHA3 -edited derivative was evaluated in aggregation and spheroid assays. RESULTS: Relative to parental LNCaP-TR, LNCaP-TR-BoM formed more numerous and larger cell aggregates in monolayer culture and larger, less circular spheroids in both suspension and Matrigel three-dimensional culture. AR mRNA was modestly reduced and AR protein remained readily detectable, whereas KLK3 mRNA and protein were reduced disproportionately more than those of AR. Residual KLK3 expression remained suppressible by AR inhibitors enzalutamide and darolutamide. Transcriptome-based pseudotime placed LNCaP-TR-BoM between the parental line and the androgen-refractory LNCaP-RF variant. Subsequent differential gene expression (DGE) and pathway enrichment analysis revealed that LNCaP-TR-BoM exhibits transcriptomic rewiring concordant with that of clinical mCRPC, thus evidencing LNCaP-TR-BoM as a potentially clinically relevant model cell line. Finally, EPHA3 showed the largest fold change among the most significant differentially expressed genes in LNCaP-TR-BoM compared with the parental line. Therefore, EPHA3 was explored to demonstrate the utility of the LNCaP-TR-BoM cell line as a discovery system for genes that potentially drive the malignancy of bone-metastatic prostate cancer at the intermediate AR-attenuated progression stage. An EPHA3 -silenced derivative of LNCaP-TR-BoM lacking detectable EPHA3 protein formed smaller aggregates and smaller, more circular spheroids, suggesting EPHA3 may play a role in driving the malignancy of AR-intermediate bone-metastatic prostate cancer. This finding provides support for the potential utility of the LNCaP-TR-BoM cell line as a discovery system for genes relevant to driving AR-intermediate bone-metastatic prostate cancer. CONCLUSIONS: LNCaP-TR-BoM is a bone lesion-derived prostate cancer cell line in which AR expression is retained but AR pathway output is attenuated, accompanied by an mCRPC-concordant transcriptomic shift and altered multicellular organization. It provides a paired discovery system for candidate genes such as EPHA3 .

title: Generation of Functional Gene Knockout Melanoma Cell Lines by CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing.
authors: Hargadon, Kristian M; Bushhouse, David Z; Johnson, Coleman E; Willams, Corey J
abstract: Recent advances in the treatment of metastatic melanoma have emerged only from advances in our understanding of melanoma development and progression at the cellular and molecular level. Despite the impact that such advances have made on the clinical management of this cancer over the last decade, additional insights into factors that promote melanoma progression and therapeutic resistance are needed to combat this disease. CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology is a powerful tool for studying gene function in a timely and cost-effective manner, enabling the manipulation of specific DNA sequences via a targeted approach. Herein, we describe a protocol for generating functional gene knockouts in melanoma cell lines by CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, and we present an example application of this protocol for the successful knockout of the Foxc2 transcription factor-encoding gene in the B16-F1 murine melanoma cell line.

title: CAR-NK cell immunotherapy: a comprehensive review of engineering platforms, clinical applications in hematological and solid tumors.
authors: Awadallah, Salma Mohamed; Elmesalamy, NourEldin; Bahr, Ahmed Reda; Atef, Basant; Afroz, Eeman; Hill, Hank C
journal: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-beta, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.

title: Gene Therapy for Inherited Platelet Disorders: From Proof of Concept to Clinical Translation.
authors: Ojeda-Walzuk, Paula M; Marin-Quilez, Ana; Torres, Raul; Rivera, Jose
abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.

title: A DNA-free CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein electroporation protocol for efficient knockout generation in cardiac and skeletal muscle cell lines.
authors: Nami, Babak; Xiao, Yuhe; Kaur, Gurpreet; Kolla, Harish Babu; Vesuna, Aryan; Finnigan, Ethan; Vivek, Aparna; Jose, Anu; Kumari, Simran; Kienesberger, Petra C; Pulinilkunnil, Thomas
abstract: BACKGROUND: Efficient, reproducible gene knockout in cardiomyocyte-related cell models is critical for cardiovascular research but remains challenging because of cell-type-specific sensitivity to genome-editing workflows. METHODS: We developed an optimized CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing protocol using electroporation of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes to generate knockout lines in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. We also provide practical guidance for gRNA design, genotyping, and clonal line generation. Using human AC16 cardiomyocyte-like cells and rodent muscle-derived cell lines (C2C12, L6, and H9C2), we optimized electroporation conditions to maximize editing efficiency while maintaining viability. RESULTS: SpCas9-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) RNPs targeting the lipid-trafficking regulator SAR1B/Sar1b produced high-frequency frameshift indels and marked loss of target protein expression in all models. A composite knockout score that combines editing efficiency and cell survival identified optimal electroporation settings of 1400 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for AC16 cells, and 1500 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for C2C12, L6, and H9C2 cells. CONCLUSIONS: This protocol combines rational sgRNA design, chemically modified sgRNAs for efficient RNP assembly, and standardized genotyping to improve reproducibility. The framework is transferable to other cardiomyocyte and muscle-derived cell types and supports both pthe olyclonal and monoclonal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout approaches.

title: Recovery of a CMV-Reactive TCR from a Clinical Virus-Specific T-Cell Product for Generation of a Defined TCR-T Cell Product.
authors: Shachal, Rotem; Lieberman, Amihai; Ben-Haim, Nimrod; Vax, Einav; Berlinsky, Sagi; Teichman, Shlomit; Shemer, Anat; Rosenberg, Michael; Ashwal-Fluss, Reut; Zuckerman, Netta; Pereg, Mor Hava; Teperberg, Michal; Bielorai, Bella; Adam, Etai; Esensten, Jonathan H; Varda-Bloom, Nira; Jacoby, Elad; Hendel, Ayal; Cafri, Gal
abstract: BACKGROUND: Virus-specific T-cell (VST) therapy is used in the management of viral complications after allogeneic HSCT. Current VST products are polyclonal and heterogeneous. This limits standardization, potency assessment, and precise product characterization. T-cell receptor (TCR)-based engineering may allow antiviral specificity to be captured from donor-derived immunity and redirected into a more defined cellular therapy candidate. OBJECTIVE(S): To identify a functional cytomegalovirus (CMV)-reactive TCR from a donor-derived VST product administered to a patient, generate and characterize a defined anti-CMV TCR-T cell candidate, and assess TRAC knockout as a strategy to support endogenous TCR removal in future allogeneic applications. STUDY DESIGN: A trivalent donor-derived VST product generated against adenovirus, BK polyomavirus, and CMV was administered under compassionate use to a pediatric haploidentical HSCT recipient with post-transplant viremia. Serial post-infusion blood samples were used to assess changes in the peripheral T-cell receptor repertoire over time. The clinical VST product was re-stimulated with the human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-A*02:01-restricted CMV pp65 495-503 epitope. Antigen-responsive CD8(+)4-1BB(+) cultures were used for functional TCR recovery. The selected CMV-reactive TCR was reconstructed with murine constant regions, cloned into an MSGV1 gamma-retroviral vector, and introduced into primary human T cells. Engineered cells were assessed for introduced TCR expression, antigen-specific activation, interferon-gamma (IFNgamma) secretion, HLA-A*02:01-restricted recognition, endogenous TCR expression over time, and generation of a TRAC-disrupted TCR-T cell population. RESULTS: Peripheral TCR repertoire analysis after sequential VST infusions showed temporal changes in dominant circulating TCRbeta clonotypes, with annotation based on overlap with antigen-responsive CD4(+) and CD8(+) reference datasets generated from the clinical VST product. Functional re-stimulation of the VST product with pp65 495-503 enriched antigen-responsive CD8(+)4-1BB(+) cells. From these cultures, a CMV-reactive TCR was recovered and advanced based on reproducible peptide-specific activity. Following reconstruction and retroviral transfer, the selected TCR mediated pp65 495-503-specific activation and IFNgamma secretion in primary T cells. Stimulation with pp65 495-503 induced 35.82% CD3(+)OX40(+)4-1BB(+) cells and approximately 9.8 x 10(3) pg/mL IFNgamma, while responses to non-cognate adenoviral Hexon stimulation remained low. The engineered anti-CMV TCR-T cells showed stronger IFNgamma responses to pp65 495-503 than the parental VST product. Irrelevant TCR controls remained near baseline. Endogenous TCR expression decreased early after TCR transduction alone but recovered by approximately day 14 and persisted through day 35. Following CRISPR/Cas9-mediated TRAC knockout, approximately 70% of cells were within the intended mTCR(+)hTCR(-) population before sorting, and this population was enriched by flow sorting for downstream characterization. CONCLUSION(S): This study demonstrates a clinically grounded workflow for deriving a defined antiviral TCR-T cell candidate from a donor-derived VST product. A functional CMV-reactive TCR was recovered from the clinical VST product and redirected into primary T cells while preserving pp65-specific activity. The recovery of endogenous TCR expression after transduction alone indicates that early downmodulation is not sufficient for durable removal of the native TCR. Incorporating TRAC knockout therefore provides a strategy to generate a more defined engineered T-cell population for future antiviral cellular therapy development.

title: Non-viral delivery and genome editing for CAR-NK engineering in solid tumors: from ex vivo manufacturing to in vivo reprogramming.
authors: Shen, Yidan; Ye, Xiaoye; Shen, Siyuan; Lv, Fei
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered natural killer (NK) cell therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer treatment, offering advantages over CAR-T cells such as a lower risk of cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease and the potential for off-the-shelf manufacturing. Viral vectors have long served as effective tools for CAR-NK engineering, but their dependence on complex manufacturing procedures, considerable production costs, and the potential risks associated with genomic integration has encouraged increasing interest in non-viral alternatives. Recent advances in genetic engineering technologies have facilitated the development of CAR-NK platforms, particularly through non-viral delivery approaches including electroporation, transposon systems and lipid nanoparticles, while CRISPR-based tools enable targeted genome editing. Meanwhile, an increasing number of clinical trials have begun to evaluate the safety and therapeutic potential of CAR-NK cells in both hematological malignancies and solid tumors. However, challenges such as limited NK-cell persistence, antigen heterogeneity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remain. In this review, we summarize recent progress in non-viral CAR-NK engineering strategies, analyze the current landscape of preclinical and clinical trials, and discuss key challenges and future directions for advancing CAR-NK therapy. Collectively, these advances suggest that non-viral engineering technologies may serve as an important technological foundation for next-generation CAR-NK therapies, enabling more flexible ex vivo manufacturing and potentially supporting the future development of in vivo CAR-NK generation strategies for solid tumors.

title: When prevention constrains cure: Institutional lock-in and gene therapy access for beta-thalassemia.
authors: Huang, Qixian
abstract: On 16 November 2023, the United Kingdom Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first CRISPR-based gene therapy for a genetic disease, offering patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) freedom from lifelong monthly transfusions. Yet in China, which carries the world's largest TDT patient population, no patient has received the therapy through the public health system, and the access gap is not explained by price or manufacturing economics alone. This paper argues that prevention-era institutional architecture constrains cure-era access through three lock-in mechanisms: cognitive (the direction of genetic information flow), infrastructural (the spatial distribution of treatment capacity), and fiscal (the structure of payment responsibility). Drawing on a structured comparison of four countries selected to represent distinct institutional pathway types (Cyprus, ecclesiastical-public certification; China, administrative filing; Thailand, public health universal coverage; India, federal fragmentation), the analysis proposes a typology of barrier configurations and illustrates them through four exploratory cases. The administrative-filing pathway is associated with high barriers across information, geographic, and economic dimensions; trust-intention is not assessable on current evidence. The ecclesiastical-public pathway is associated with medium information and low geographic barriers with medium fiscal and low-confidence trust barriers; the universal-coverage pathway provides a balanced platform that remains under-activated for gene therapy; and the federal-fragmented pathway fails the precondition of patient identification. No pathway simultaneously optimizes all four readiness dimensions. Presented as a hypothesis-generating typology rather than a tested diagnostic model, the framework relates pathway type to barrier configuration and offers testable hypotheses for pathway-specific intervention design and for extension to sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and other genetic conditions entering the curative era.

title: A DNAzyme-activated engineered crRNA enables CRISPR-Cas12a biosensing of ALP and S. aureus.
authors: Wang, Xinrui; Shi, Xuening; Zheng, Xiaoxi; Ding, Yukun; Jing, Yixin; Zhang, Jing; Wang, Juan; Li, Hang; Zhao, Chao
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a biosensing is hindered by insufficient sensitivity that necessitates pre-amplification, as well as the limited ability to directly detect non-nucleic-acid targets. Herein, we developed a CRISPR-Cas12a biosensor centered on a DNAzyme-activated engineered crRNA (e-crRNA), enabling Mn(2+)-responsive control over its trans-cleavage activity for nucleic-acid-amplification-free detection. Upon Mn(2+)-dependent activation, the DNAzyme cleaved the e-crRNA to liberate a full-sized crRNA(1) and a split crRNA(2). The combined crRNA(1)/crRNA(2) system enhanced Cas12a trans-cleavage activity, compensating for the activity loss associated with crRNA engineering. Rational design of the split site further improved the signal-to-noise ratio. Moreover, by gating the system activation on Mn(2+), the non-specific activation effects caused by spurious DNA hybridization were mitigated. When coupled with a Mn(2+)-responsive signal conversion strategy, this platform achieved sensitive detection of alkaline phosphatase with the LOD of 0.008 U/L and Staphylococcus aureus with the LOD of 29.76 CFU/mL. This study showcased the innovative use of Mn(2+)-dependent DNAzyme to efficiently activate CRISPR-Cas12a system, establishing a powerful platform for biosensing.

title: Genetic Modification Technologies and Microbial Interventions for Mosquito Control: Recent Advances in Biological Strategies Against Vector-Borne Diseases.
authors: Abbasi, Ebrahim
abstract: BACKGROUND OBJECTIVES: Mosquito-borne diseases continue to pose major global public health challenges, while increasing insecticide resistance and environmental concerns necessitate the development of sustainable alternatives to conventional vector control. This review evaluates recent advances in biological mosquito control, focusing on genetic modification technologies, Wolbachia -based interventions, and entomopathogenic fungi. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. Literature published between 2000 and 2025 was retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Eligible studies investigating mosquito-targeted biological interventions were critically evaluated through qualitative evidence synthesis and methodological quality assessment. RESULTS: The included studies demonstrated variable levels of evidence across intervention types. SIT and selected genetically engineered population-suppression approaches produced substantial reductions in mosquito abundance under field or operational conditions, whereas CRISPR/Cas9 and gene-drive technologies remained supported predominantly by laboratory or contained experimental evidence. Wolbachia population-replacement interventions generated the strongest community-level epidemiological evidence, including reductions in dengue incidence following successful establishment. Entomopathogenic fungi reduced adult mosquito survival mainly under laboratory and semi-field conditions. Across interventions, effectiveness depended on ecological context, operational capacity, surveillance, regulatory requirements, and community engagement. INTERPRETATION CONCLUSION: Biological control technologies provide environmentally sustainable and species-specific alternatives to chemical insecticides. Their successful integration into Integrated Vector Management requires continued ecological monitoring, regulatory oversight, multidisciplinary collaboration, and community engagement to ensure safe and effective large-scale implementation.

title: TaqW-6BL, a novel gene positively regulates grain WE-AX content in wheat.
authors: Li, Qiong; Zeng, Zhankui; Zhao, Yue; Bi, Junge; Yan, Qunxiang; Wang, Chunping
journal: TAG. Theoretical and applied genetics. Theoretische und angewandte Genetik
abstract: The TaqW-6BL gene, which encodes a TAXI-type inhibitor, influences the water-extractable arabinoxylan content in wheat grains. Water-extractable arabinoxylans (WE-AX) are major dietary fiber components and play a crucial role in wheat end-use quality, especially its nutritional quality. In this study, TaqW-6BL was cloned from parental varieties of a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population, in which a missense mutation (+ 296 bp, T/C) was detected and found to cause a methionine (Met) to threonine (Thr) substitution. Overexpression of TaqW-6BL positively regulated grain WE-AX content, thousand kernel weight (TKW) and mean grain perimeter (MP), with increases of 30.80%, 14.59% and 14.53%, respectively. Conversely, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of TaqW-6BL led to significant decreases in WE-AX content, TKW and MP. Cytological observations revealed that the aleurone layer of overexpression lines partially proliferated into two layers, whereas knockout lines showed disordered cell arrangement and abnormal morphology. Subcellular localization analysis confirmed that TaqW-6BL protein localizes in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The relative expression level and WE-AX content of the favorable haplotype (TaqW-6BL(Avocet)) were significantly higher than those of the unfavorable haplotype (TaqW-6BL(Chilero)) at 14 days and 21 days after flowering (DAF) (P < 0.01). Meanwhile, we developed a functional cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS) marker CAPS-6B-296. The wheat varieties with favorable haplotype TaqW-6BL(Avocet) accounted for 68% of 160 wheat varieties. Therefore, our findings provide a valuable gene and a reliable functional marker for nutritional quality breeding in wheat.

title: Establishment and preliminary application of the Mo RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a rapid detection method.
authors: Li, Yongshuai; Wei, Yaya; Chen, Rulong; Wen, Xin; Shi, Huijun; Fu, Qiang; Ma, Xuelian; Li, Na; Chu, Yuefeng; Li, Yang
abstract: Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae (Mo) is a common pathogen prevalent worldwide that causes pneumonia and leads to significant economic losses in sheep farming. Early testing of nasal swabs from diseased sheep in Xinjiang yielded a 51.5% positivity rate, indicating severe infection within the sheep population. Existing detection methods are time-consuming and rely on large-scale equipment, making them unsuitable for frontline clinical testing. Rapid, accurate, and on-site pathogen detection is essential for the early prevention and control of infectious diseases. Conventional nucleic acid detection methods are limited by long reaction duration, sophisticated instruments, and strict operating requirements, which restrict their application in grassroots rapid diagnosis scenarios. Herein, we established a combined Mo-RPA integrated CRISPR/Cas12a detection assay, which realized constant-temperature nucleic acid detection without large-scale laboratory equipment. The entire detection workflow was completed within 30 min under a constant temperature of 37 degrees C. The optimized assay achieved a limit of detection of 10 degrees  copies/muL, with 100% analytical specificity against non-target pathogen strains. In clinical sample verification, the detection consistency between the established method and standard real-time PCR assay reached 100%. The established constant-temperature detection system integrates rapid nucleic acid amplification and CRISPR fluorescent signal output and provides a quantifiable on-site detection scheme for grassroots epidemic surveillance. IMPORTANCE: In this study, we demonstrated a novel RPA-CRISPR-Cas12a-based diagnostic method for Mycoplasma ovipneumoniae (Mo) infection with high sensitivity and specificity. The detection rate reached 51.5% (85/165). Subsequently, an RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a rapid test targeting the 16S rRNA gene of Mo was developed, achieving a detection time of 30 min, 100% specificity, and a sensitivity of 100 copies/muL-10(6) times more sensitive than PCR. During preliminary application, the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a method detected Mo in 84/102 samples (82.35%), representing 1.7 times the detection rate of PCR. Consequently, RPA-Cas12a testing has demonstrated significant potential for routine Mo screening and offers high accessibility for population screening or molecular diagnostics in resource-limited settings.

title: The core interaction network of transcription elongation factors is broadly maintained across diverse bacteria.
authors: Tran, Thao N P; Peterson, Reid E; Jiang, Xiaofang; Sevugan, Swathi A; Ranaweera, Sandeepani; Babitzke, Paul; Fushman, David; Winkler, Wade C
abstract: Bacterial transcription elongation has been investigated most thoroughly for the model bacterium Escherichia coli. The E. coli elongation factor NusG associates through its N-terminal domain with the transcription elongation complex (TEC), while its C-terminal domain forms mutually exclusive interactions with either ribosomal protein S10 or Rho termination factor. The E. coli NusG:S10 complex bridges the TEC with a pioneering ribosome for coupling of transcription and translation. NusG also participates in antitermination complexes (ATC) that inhibit Rho-dependent termination and increase transcription of rRNA operons. A characteristic sequence in the nascent rrn RNA, called boxA, loads E. coli NusB:S10 onto the NusG-bound TEC, leading to the formation of the rrn ATC. However, these findings may not extend to all bacteria. Rho-dependent termination is less important in gram-positive bacteria, including some that do not encode Rho, and transcription and translation remain uncoupled in Bacillus subtilis and many other gram-positive bacteria. It is therefore unclear whether the interaction network for E. coli elongation factors is conserved in these organisms. We identified boxA-like sequences upstream of 16S and 23S genes in Bacillus species and found that they associate directly with NusB. We also found that B. subtilis S10 associates with both NusB and NusG, and that Rho can also associate with NusG. Bioinformatic analyses revealed conservation of interaction interface residues across multiple phyla. Together, these data demonstrate that the core interaction network of bacterial elongation factors is broadly conserved across diverse bacteria, despite differences in how these interactions function in individual species. IMPORTANCE: Escherichia coli is known to use several key elongation factors that promote direct coupling of transcription with translation. These factors also trigger the formation of an antitermination complex that protects the synthesis of ribosomal RNA and CRISPR transcripts from interference by the Rho termination factor. However, Bacillus subtilis is not thought to couple transcription with translation. It is also not known whether B. subtilis needs to suppress Rho, given that its Rho is dispensable. Therefore, we purified B. subtilis elongation factors and mapped their interaction network. Surprisingly, we find that the B. subtilis elongation factors form complexes that closely resemble E. coli counterparts, despite the significant mechanistic differences in how these bacteria control transcription elongation.

title: The Role of METTL3-Mediated m(6)A Methylation in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression and Treatment.
authors: Maduranga, Bala Gamage Nalaka Hasith; Yang, Hee Doo; Lee, Su In; Eun, Jung Woo; Lim, Sun-Young; Kim, Hyung Seok; Jeong, Jee-Yeong
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Emerging evidence has established N(6)-methyladenosine (m(6)A) RNA methylation as a key epitranscriptomic mechanism underlying hepatocarcinogenesis. Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), the catalytic core of the m(6)A methyltransferase complex (MTC), forms a heterodimer with METTL14 and cooperates with auxiliary components of the MTC to deposit m(6)A modifications that modulate mRNA stability, splicing, nuclear export, and translation. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the current understanding of METTL3 biology in HCC, focusing on its structure, assembly within the MTC, regulation of coding and non-coding RNAs, and its roles in driving key oncogenic signaling cascades, such as JAK/STAT3, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/beta-catenin, Hippo/YAP, Notch, Hedgehog, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In addition, we discussed how METTL3 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) by regulating immune responses and metabolic pathways promoting immune evasion and therapy resistance. Therapeutic strategies targeting METTL3-including small-molecule inhibitors, CRISPR-Cas9 approaches, combination immunotherapy, and tumor-selective delivery systems-are discussed together with the challenges that continue to limit clinical translation. Collectively, these findings position METTL3 as a central epitranscriptomic regulator of HCC progression; however, further mechanistic and clinical validation remains necessary to establish its utility as a therapeutic target and prognostic biomarker.

title: Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Inducing Kinase- and Inhibitor of Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Kinase Subunit Beta-Binding Protein Promotes Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy by Regulating Inhibitor of Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Kinase Subunit Beta-Mediated Nuclear Factor Kappa-B Activation.
authors: Xie, Zheng; Zuo, Yingjie; Wang, Mengyao; Zhang, Xin; Zhang, Lirong; Liu, Zixuan; Zhang, Bilong; Su, Zhaohai; Yang, Saichao; Yang, Hailong; Zhang, Jianqing; Ni, Zhonghan; Liu, Hui; Pei, Fang
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is a major risk factor for heart failure. NIBP (NF-kappaB [nuclear factor kappa-B] inducing kinase- and inhibitor of NF-kappaB kinase subunit beta-binding protein) is a key regulator of cytokine-induced NF-kappaB signaling, but its role in cardiac hypertrophy remains unknown. METHODS: We established transverse aortic constriction-induced cardiac hypertrophy in mice and phenylephrine-induced hypertrophy in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes. Genetic interventions included generation of whole-body Nibp knockout mice via CRISPR-Cas9; creation of cardiomyocyte-specific Nibp knockout mice using adeno-associated virus serotype 9-delivered Cre and single-guide RNAs in Rosa26-LSL-Cas9 mice; and cardiac-specific Nibp overexpression via adeno-associated virus serotype 9delivery. In neonatal rat ventricular myocytes, NIBP was knocked down or overexpressed using adenoviruses. Phenotypes were assessed by echocardiography, histology (wheat germ agglutinin, picrosirius redstaining), and molecular analyses. Mechanisms were investigated via RNA-sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and Western blotting for key signaling molecules. RESULTS: NIBP protein was upregulated in hypertrophic hearts and cardiomyocytes. Both Nibp-knockout and cardiomyocyte-specific Nibp knockout attenuated transverse aortic constriction-induced cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibrosis, whereas Nibp overexpression exacerbated these pathologies. Consistently, in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes, NIBP knockdown mitigated, while its overexpression aggravated, phenylephrine-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, NIBP directly interacted with IKKbeta (inhibitor of NF-kappaB kinase subunit beta), enhanced its phosphorylation, and drove hyperactivation of the downstream NF-kappaB pathway. Overexpression of a kinase-dead IKKbeta mutant reversed the hypertrophic effects of NIBP. CONCLUSIONS: NIBP promotes pathological cardiac hypertrophy by activating the IKKbeta/NF-kappaB axis, identifying it as a potential therapeutic target for cardiac remodeling and heart failure.

title: Reconstructing tissue culture to improve Agrobacterium-mediated transformation of maize.
authors: Ono, Seijiro; Ono, Misato; Brettschneider, Reinhold; Sauer, Dagmar; Muller, Katja; Balboni, Martina; van der Heide, Max; Schnittger, Arp
journal: The Plant journal : for cell and molecular biology
abstract: The ability to insert, delete, or modify genetic information is crucial for mechanistic studies and biotechnological applications. However, efficient genetic transformation remains a major bottleneck for research in maize and many other crops. Here, we report an optimized Agrobacterium-mediated transformation platform based on systematic reconstruction of tissue culture handling in the maize inbred line A188. Refinement of callus induction, selection, and regeneration substantially improved recovery of transgenic plantlets. To distinguish independent T-DNA insertion events, we developed TAFLP (T-DNA amplified fragment length polymorphism), a simple and inexpensive assay that amplifies T-DNA flanking sequences and can be performed using standard laboratory equipment. Our enhanced transformation pipeline was also applicable to the inbred line B104 as well as to hygromycin and G418 selection systems, demonstrating broad utility of our method. We validated the platform for CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis and reporter-line generation. Using this approach, we isolated new loss-of-function alleles of the maize-specific MAC1 (MULTIPE ARCHESPORIAL CELLS 1) and F-box protein encoding ACOZ1 (ABNORMAL CHROMOSOME ORGANIZATION IN ZYGOTENE 1), a homolog of the Arabidopsis RMF1/2 (REDUCED MALE FERTILITY 1/2) and rice ZYGO1 (ZYGOTENE 1). The concomitant generation of reporter lines for ACOZ1 and the nuclear lamin-like proteins NCH1 (NMCP/CROWN HOMOLOG1) and NCH2, as well as SUN1 (SUN DOMAIN PROTEIN 1) revealed that the function of this F-box protein class in releasing the somatic constraints of chromosome organization for meiotic recombination is highly conserved in flowering plants.

title: NEAT1 remodeling rewires the MYC degradation pathway.
authors: Jang, Hagoon; Suh, Bo Kyoung; Zhang, Feijie; Lin, Angela; Tan, Mingdian; Liu, Yi; Chua, Mei-Sze; So, Samuel; Kay, Mark A
abstract: MYC is among the most frequently amplified oncogenes in human cancer, yet its intrinsically disordered nature has rendered it refractory to direct pharmacological targeting. Here, we demonstrate that the long noncoding RNA NEAT1_1 functions as a molecular gatekeeper that controls MYC protein stability by regulating its access to the E3 ubiquitin ligase UBR5. We show that NEAT1_1 forms a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex with both MYC and UBR5, and that NEAT1_1 suppression disrupts this interaction, leading to decreased MYC polyubiquitination and enhanced protein stability. To systematically map the regulatory architecture of NEAT1_1 without altering its abundance, we screened 88 antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) mixmers tiling across the transcript. Strikingly, this phenotypic screen identified region-specific mixmers that elicit bidirectional control over MYC, either driving robust MYC destabilization or promoting its stabilization in a strictly expression-independent manner. Mechanistically, MYC-destabilizing mixmers selectively enhance the interaction between MYC and UBR5 to accelerate proteasomal degradation. A focused CRISPR screen targeting the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway independently validated UBR5 as the essential E3 ligase mediating this mixmer-induced turnover. In vivo, our lead mixmer ASO_#24 significantly suppressed tumor growth in MYC-high xenografts, whereas MYC-low tumors remained unaffected. Our findings reveal that the functional output of a scaffold lncRNA is encoded in its sub-domain architecture rather than bulk transcript levels, establishing domain-specific RNA targeting as a tractable strategy to rewire protein turnover pathways for otherwise undruggable oncogenes.

title: From bench to bedside: translational advances, therapeutic targets, and delivery strategies in diabetic retinopathy.
authors: Chen, Haizhi; Chen, Wei
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of preventable blindness in adults of working age. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy is the reference standard for diabetic macular edema (DME), yet in randomized cohorts, approximately 30-40% of DME eyes still show central macular thickening after six months of continuous treatment. In proliferative DR (PDR), the corresponding limitation is recurrence after treatment interruption rather than primary non-response, and these two patterns should not be conflated. This review examines translational research in DR across four domains. First, we review mechanistic work on the neurovascular unit, metabolic memory and its epigenetic substrate, the gut-retina axis, and human platforms including induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived retinal organoids and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) editing. Second, we discuss therapeutic targets beyond VEGF, including the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome and related inflammatory pathways, neuroprotection, complement activation, the angiopoietin-2 (Ang2)/Tie2 axis, and non-coding RNA (ncRNA) networks. Third, in preclinical pharmacology, we regard delivery as the rate-limiting step and analyze in detail why lipid nanoparticle and N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) conjugation strategies, which transformed hepatic RNA interference, have not translated to the retina, and what the terminated bevasiranib, PF-04523655, and iCo-007 programmes imply for trial design. Fourth, clinical translation, including cytokine biomarkers, artificial intelligence (AI)-based screening, combination regimens, and sustained-release implants. Evidence derived from age-related macular degeneration (AMD), including complement inhibition, stem cell transplantation, and photovoltaic implants, is evaluated separately, and its transferability to DR is assessed in light of differences in affected compartment, pathogenic driver, patient age, and expected treatment duration. We conclude that the principal obstacles in DR are no longer mechanistic but concern cell-type-specific delivery, early-phase trial design, and endpoint standardization, and we specify the evidence each candidate class should generate before clinical development proceeds.

title: A zebrafish model of NEXMIF-related encephalopathy identified drivers of hyperlocomotion and provides a scalable platform for drug discovery.
authors: Bernal-Bermudez, Beatriz; Martinez-Morcillo, Francisco J; Fuentes-Martinez, Inmaculada; Martinez-Lopez, Alicia; Cayuela, Maria L; Mulero, Victoriano; Garcia-Moreno, Diana
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
abstract: X-linked Intellectual Disability type 98 (XLID-98) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with a broad phenotypic spectrum caused by pathogenic variants in the neurite extension and migration factor (NEXMIF) gene, formerly known as KIAA2022, KIDLIA, or XPN (OMIM 300524). To investigate the pathogenic mechanisms of XLID-98, a double knock-out zebrafish model (nexmifa/b (-/-)) was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Mutant larvae displayed limited morphological abnormalities, the most notable being an increase in total body length. They also exhibited a significant hyperlocomotor phenotype in the visual-startle OFF assay, which was attenuated by treatment with sodium valproate (VPA) and topiramate, thereby supporting the pharmacological validity of the model. Transcriptomic analysis of larval heads at seven dpf revealed 414 differentially expressed genes enriched in mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling, cell adhesion, and sodium transport pathways. Functional analyses demonstrated that simultaneous CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the upregulated genes entpd3 (ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase 3) and ddx43 (DEAD-box helicase 43) exacerbated the hyperlocomotor phenotype, suggesting that these genes may participate in a compensatory response, whereas reduced kbtbd7 (kelch repeat and BTB domain-containing protein 7) activity may contribute to phenotype severity. A targeted screen of 87 natural compounds identified kahweol acetate, veratridine, and rauwolscine as potent inducers of entpd3. However, despite robust transcriptional activation, rauwolscine failed to improve behavioral outcomes, suggesting that modulation of a single molecular target may be insufficient for phenotypic rescue. Collectively, these findings establish the first zebrafish model of NEXMIF-related encephalopathy, identify entpd3, ddx43, and kbtbd7 as candidate modulators of this behavioral phenotype, and provide a scalable platform for targeted therapeutic discovery in XLID-98.

title: Assessment of the transcriptional and cellular effects of CRISPRa targeting Dopa decarboxylase and GTP cyclohydrolase 1 in HEK293 and SH-SY5Y cellular models of Parkinsonian neurotoxicity.
authors: Bhengu, Siyethaba Zinhle; Singh, Ravesh; Ramsuran, Veron; Msibi, Zama Ndlondlo Princess
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), leading to dopamine deficiency and motor dysfunction. Clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based technologies provide a potential approach for targeted gene modulation, although their effectiveness and safety in cellular models of PD remain to be established. This study investigated the feasibility and transcriptional effects of CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) targeting Dopa decarboxylase (DDC) and GTP cyclohydrolase 1 (GCH1) in human embryonic kidney (HEK293) cells and a 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-induced neurotoxicity model using human neuroblastoma (SH-SY5Y) cells. Parkinsonian-like toxicity was induced in SH-SY5Y cells with 6-OHDA prior to CRISPRa transfection. A vector-free CRISPRa system was used to target DDC and GCH1, with single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) assembled with dCas9-VP64 and MS2-p65-HSF1 (MPH) to form ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes and delivered using Lipofectamine 3000. CRISPRa targeting of DDC was associated with increased DDC expression in SH-SY5Y cells relative to untreated controls at 24 h (p = 0.0496) and 48 h (p = 0.0064). However, expression levels did not differ significantly from those observed in the 6-OHDA-treated PD control group. In contrast, GCH1 expression was not significantly altered following CRISPRa. CRISPRa also had no significant effect on cell viability in HEK293 cells. In SH-SY5Y cells, 6-OHDA significantly reduced cell viability compared with untreated controls (p = 0.0129). Similar reductions were observed in DDC-targeted cells at 24 h (p = 0.0026) and 48 h (p = 0.0017), and in GCH1-targeted cells at 24 h (p = 0.0017) and 48 h (p = 0.0008); however, none of the CRISPRa-treated groups differed significantly from the 6-OHDA-treated PD control. These findings indicate that CRISPRa elicited a modest transcriptional response, characterized by upregulation of DDC without detectable modulation of GCH1, and did not exacerbate 6-OHDA-induced cytotoxicity. Further optimisation, together with protein-level, enzymatic activity, and dopamine measurements, is required to determine whether these transcriptional changes translate into functional effects on dopamine biosynthesis.

title: WasteFams: a database of protein families from global wastewater microbiomes.
authors: Galaras, Alexandros; Chasapi, Iro N; Aplakidou, Eleni; Chasapi, Maria N; Lamari, Efthimia; Diplari, Sophia; Georgakopoulos-Soares, Ilias; Karatzas, Evangelos; Baltoumas, Fotis A; Kyrpides, Nikos C; Pavlopoulos, Georgios A
abstract: Wastewater surveillance has emerged as a critical tool for global epidemiology, yet the functional diversity of wastewater microbiomes remains poorly characterized at the protein level. Here, we present WasteFams, the first comprehensive database dedicated to the systematic exploration of protein families in wastewater metagenomic and metatranscriptomic studies worldwide. Integrating data from 580 metagenomes, 132 metatranscriptomes, and 1709 reference genomes (504 metagenomes, 129 metatranscriptomes, and 1151 reference genomes after filtering), WasteFams catalogs 3887 non-redundant protein families (containing ⪰100 members) derived from over 105 million predicted proteins. Each protein family is enriched with multi-layered annotations, including AlphaFold3 structural predictions, taxonomic classifications, and biome-specific metadata. To further expand their functional annotation, we integrated deep genomic context analysis to link protein families to mobile genetic elements, biosynthetic gene clusters, antibiotic resistance genes, and CRISPR elements. Accessible through the EnvoFams portal, WasteFams provides a user-friendly interface featuring advanced search capabilities, sequence and structural similarity tools, and interactive visualization modules. As global initiatives increasingly leverage wastewater for public health and environmental insights, WasteFams can serve as a critical resource for discovering novel microbial functions, monitoring resistance mechanisms, and exploring the biotechnological potential of secondary metabolites within wastewater-engineered ecosystems.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated editing of SlALS1 enhances fruit sweetness in tomato.
authors: Yang, So Hee; Han, Soon-Ki; Koo, Yeonjong
abstract: Fruit sweetness is a primary determinant of consumer preference and market value in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), yet increasing sugar content without negatively affecting plant performance remains a major challenge in breeding programs. In this study, we targeted Acetolactate synthase 1 (SlALS1), a key enzyme in branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) biosynthesis, to investigate whether modulation of primary metabolism could enhance fruit sugar accumulation. Tomato contains two ALS homologs, SlALS1 and SlALS2. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing, we generated SlALS1 knock-out lines in the Micro-Tom background. Loss of SlALS1 function led to a significant reduction in the levels of valine, leucine, and isoleucine in fruit tissues, confirming disruption of the BCAA biosynthetic pathway. Notably, soluble sugar content was markedly increased in the mutant lines, with glucose and fructose levels elevated by approximately 1.3-fold compared with wild-type fruits, resulting in a significantly higher Brix index. Metabolic profiling indicates that reduced BCAA biosynthesis may influence carbon allocation toward soluble sugar accumulation in fruit tissues, revealing an association between amino acid metabolism and carbohydrate accumulation during fruit development. Our findings demonstrate that precise editing of a central metabolic enzyme can enhance tomato fruit sweetness and suggest that SlALS1 may represent a promising target for genome editing aimed at improving fruit quality traits. However, further evaluation of agronomic traits, including plant growth and fruit yield, will be necessary to assess its potential for practical breeding applications.

title: DeepCNet: A multimodal deep learning model for predicting cell type-specific gene expression and promoter-enhancer interactions from single-cell multiome data.
authors: Chen, Li; Jin, Weijia; Zhao, Fengdi; Ma, Xin; Lu, Qing; Esser, Karyn; Sun, Ramon
abstract: Understanding promoter-enhancer (PE) interactions is essential for elucidating gene regulation mechanisms. Although existing computational methods leverage DNA sequence to predict gene expression, many were developed primarily for bulk-level genomic data and emphasize predictive accuracy rather than regulatory inference. Here, we propose DeepCNet, a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts cell type-specific gene expression and infers cell type-specific PE interactions, enabling the construction of transcription factor gene regulatory networks (TF-GRNs) from single-cell multiome data. Evaluated on two single-cell multiome datasets from blood and brain tissues, DeepCNet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predicting cell type-specific gene expression. Importantly, PE interactions inferred by DeepCNet showed greater concordance with orthogonal chromatin interaction and CRISPR perturbation data than competing approaches. Analysis of cell type-specific GRNs identified TF hubs and highlighted both cell type-specific and shared regulatory programs. DeepCNet further extends to two-condition single-cell multiome studies, enabling the identification of differential PE interactions and characterization of TF-GRN alterations across conditions. As an illustrative application, we applied DeepCNet to single-cell multiome data from one Alzheimer's disease (AD) and one healthy control sample, identifying candidate differential PE interactions at AD risk loci and candidate TF hubs associated with AD-related pathways. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of DeepCNet to characterize transcriptional regulatory programs and cooperative TF interactions underlying cell type- and condition-specific gene expression.

title: Genetic compensation in podocalyxin-like mutants during zebrafish liver development.
authors: Ross, Alexis N; Miscik, Natalie M; Kalasekar, Sharanya Maanasi; Harris, James; Tran, Mimi; Saxena, Aavrati; Baker, Steven Andrew; Evason, Kimberley Jane
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) are critical for normal liver development and regeneration. Podocalyxin-like (podxl) is highly expressed in zebrafish HSCs, but its role in liver development is not known. Here we report that podxl knockdown using CRISPR/Cas9 ("CRISPants") significantly decreased HSC number in zebrafish larvae at different time points and in two independent HSC reporter lines, supporting a role for podxl in HSC development. We generated five podxl mutants, including two mutants lacking the predicted podxl promoter region, and found that none of the mutants recapitulated the knockdown phenotype. Podxl CRISPR/Cas9 injection in mutants lacking the podxl guide RNA cut site did not affect HSC number, supporting the hypothesis that the CRISPant phenotype was specific, requiring intact podxl. Podxl mRNA levels in three podxl mutants were similar to those of wildtype controls. RNA sequencing of podxl mutants and controls showed no significant change in transcript levels of genes with sequence similarity to podxl , but it revealed upregulation of a network of extracellular matrix genes in podxl mutants. These results support a role for podxl in zebrafish liver development and suggest that upregulation of a group of functionally related genes represents the main mechanism of compensation for podxl genomic loss.

title: Antibody-dependent priming of spontaneous germinal centers by autoreactive B cells.
authors: Kim, Danny; Chiang, Kristy; Largent, Andrea D; Pitner, Ragan A; Ponnan, Sivasankaran Munusamy; McKinney, Brock J; James, Richard G; Rawlings, David J; Jackson, Shaun W
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Autoreactive germinal centers (GCs) are central to autoimmune pathogenesis, yet the mechanisms by which single autoreactive B cell clones prime systemic autoimmunity remain unclear. Using the 564Igi mixed chimera model, we demonstrate that autoreactive 564Igi B cells break tolerance in wild-type B cells through an unexpected mechanism independent of cognate T cell interactions. While B cell-intrinsic TLR7 signaling was essential for spontaneous GC formation, deletion of MHC class II, CD40, or CD80/86 on GC-priming 564Igi B cells failed to prevent GCs. Instead, CRISPR-mediated deletion of Prdm1 (encoding BLIMP-1) in 564Igi B cells ablated spontaneous GCs, implicating autoantibody production as the primary driver. These findings reveal that autoantibodies can initiate feed-forward mechanisms that propagate systemic autoimmunity, independent of B cell-intrinsic antigen presentation.

title: Rewiring of Integrin Signaling and Cell-cycle Deregulation Drive SMARCB1-Deficient Epithelioid Sarcoma.
authors: Miyamoto, Ryo; Park, Jiyeon; Dwosh, Gabrielle H; Zuco, Valentina; Pasquali, Sandro; Dickson, Brendan C; Kirsch, David G
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Epithelioid sarcoma (EPS) is an aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma characterized by loss of the chromatin-remodeling subunit SMARCB1. The oncogenic programs driving EPS remain poorly understood. Through CRISPR loss-of-function screens, we identified conserved dependencies on integrin signaling components and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). Genetic disruption of integrin subunit alpha V (ITGAV)-centered signaling impaired epithelioid cluster formation and reduced MYC expression. SMARCB1 re-expression phenocopied these effects and revealed that SMARCB1 loss selectively represses context-dependent integrin subunits while preserving an ITGAV-centered pro-survival axis, associated with altered BAF complex occupancy. Analysis of EPS cell lines and primary tumors revealed frequent genetic or epigenetic inactivation of CDKN2A/p16, indicating that loss of cell-cycle control is a key cooperating event in EPS development and providing a mechanistic rationale for targeting CDK4/6. Together, these findings establish integrin-driven oncogenic signaling coupled with disruption of cell-cycle control as a central oncogenic program in EPS and identify actionable therapeutic vulnerabilities.

title: Identification of genetic variants in Pfs25 and functional evaluation in mosquito infection.
