Long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), which lacks an open reading frame and is thereby often refractory to Cas9-mediated indel production, can be successfully knocked down by Cas13 systems. DeepCas13, a deep learning-based model, was developed to predict Cas13d on-target activity for RNA interference with high accuracy. Here, we describe detailed protocols about sgRNA design and experimental procedures for the lentiviral vector-based CRISPR-Cas13 system to knock down individual lncRNAs. Our protocol can be naturally extended to knockdown other types of coding and noncoding RNAs, including messenger RNA (mRNA) circular RNA (circRNA).

title: Role of Chromatin-Associated RNAs in Eye Physiology and Pathology.
authors: Savickyte, Ieva; Lapinaite, Audrone
abstract: Noncoding RNAs, including long noncoding RNAs, enhancer RNAs, circular RNAs, and small nuclear and nucleolar RNAs, represent a major, yet still largely uncharacterized, regulatory layer in the eye. A subset of these molecules, chromatin-associated RNAs (caRNAs), physically interacts with DNA and nuclear protein complexes to influence genome organization, transcriptional output, and stress responses. Although caRNAs have emerged as essential regulators of chromatin topology and gene expression in diverse tissues, their identity, dynamics, and mechanisms in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remain elusive. Recent high-resolution genomic studies, disease transcriptomes, and mechanistic studies implicate dysregulated caRNAs in age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy, yet causal chromatin-level functions have rarely been demonstrated. In this review, we summarize current understanding of ncRNA-mediated regulation in vision, highlight emerging evidence for caRNA involvement in retinal development, photoreceptor and RPE specialization, and disease-associated epigenetic remodeling, and outline major mechanistic gaps that must be addressed. We then survey the rapidly expanding CRISPR toolbox, including base and prime editors, CRISPRi/a, Cas13 knockdown and editing platforms, and RNA-recruitment and spatial repositioning systems, that now enable targeted perturbation of both caRNA genomic loci and transcripts. These technologies provide the first practical route to move beyond correlative RNA-chromatin maps toward the mechanistic dissection of how caRNAs organize regulatory hubs, modulate enhancer-promoter communication, and shape long-range genome interactions in the eye. As the catalog of pathogenic noncoding variants grows, the ability to decode and engineer caRNA networks will be central to future precision therapeutic strategies for ocular disorders.

title: High efficient production of adenine in Bacillus subtilis with novel metabolic engineering strategies.
authors: Han, Shuang; Shen, Peijie; Ren, Huijun; Xu, Jiangli; Chen, Feng; Huang, Jun; Zhou, Min; Xu, Zhinan
abstract: Adenine, serves as a crucial precursor for nucleic acid drugs and food additives, currently suffered from limited availability since its high production costs associated with expensive precursors and enzyme preparations. Here, we developed an effective strategy for high-yield adenine production using Bacillus subtilis as the host. Beginning with an adenosine-producing strain, we first knocked-out the apt and adeC genes, which were involved in product degradation pathways, and deleted the purR gene to alleviate the feedback inhibition on purine operon through CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Then, we overexpressed the nucleoside hydrolase RihC, PRPP amidotransferase PurF, and ribokinase RbsK to enhance the de novo adenine biosynthesis and enable the recycling of D-ribose. The production of adenine reached 18 g/L after the fed-batch fermentation, and the titer continued to reach 78 g/L when adenosine was added as the substrate subsequently, revealing the significant catalytic role of RihC produced during the fermentation. This work innovatively integrated de novo biosynthesis and enzymatic conversion strategies to achieve high yield adenine production in Bacillus subtilis, demonstrating a promising scalable process for industrial adenine manufacturing.

title: Genomic characterization of Fusobacterium necrophorum subsp. necrophorum strain JKSFn-26 associated with severe ovine footrot in Kashmir, India.
authors: Farooq, S; Bhat, M A; Hassan, M N; Hussain, M I; Dar, H M
abstract: BACKGROUND: Fusobacterium necrophorum is an important anaerobic bacterium associated with the progression and severity of ovine footrot. However, genomic information on footrot associated isolates, particularly those recovered from severe lesions, remains limited. Here, we report the genomic characterization of F. necrophorum subsp. necrophorum strain JKSFn-26, isolated from a severe ovine footrot lesion in Kashmir, India. METHODS: The isolate was characterized phenotypically and assigned to the previously identified JKS-F3 leukotoxin (lktA) variant by partial gene sequence analysis. Whole genome sequencing was performed using the Illumina HiSeq platform. The draft genome was subjected to annotation, phylogenomic analysis, and in silico screening for virulence associated genes, toxin-related determinants, antimicrobial resistance associated genes, and adaptive defense elements. RESULTS: JKSFn-26 belonged to the JKS-F3 lktA variant previously associated with severe ovine footrot in Kashmir, and the analyzed lktA gene fragment showed 100% nucleotide identity with the reported JKS-F3 sequence. The draft genome was 2.23 Mb with a G + C content of 34.37% and contained 2,048 predicted coding sequences, 45 tRNAs, five rRNAs, four annotated non-coding RNAs, one tmRNA, two CRISPR arrays, and ten pseudogenes. Phylogenomic analysis placed JKSFn-26 within the F. necrophorum subsp. necrophorum clade. The genome contained the lktBAC locus and predicted virulence associated determinants related to hemolytic activity, adhesion, iron acquisition, and outer membrane proteins. Multiple toxin-antitoxin modules and putative antimicrobial resistance associated determinants were also identified. The deduced LktA amino acid sequence showed 98.0% identity to the corresponding leukotoxin A sequence of Fusobacterium necrophorum subsp. necrophorum strain ATCC 25286 . CONCLUSIONS: This study provides genomic information on a JKS-F3 lktA variant associated with severe ovine footrot in Kashmir and expands genomic resources for F. necrophorum.

title: Antigen-independent BCR signals limit differentiation and survival of IgM antibody-secreting cells.
authors: Zhang, Ting-Ting; Camp, Nathan; Asher, Gregory D; Romani, Ameena; McKinney, Brock; Chen, Yu; Knebusch, Parker; Rawlings, David J; James, Richard G
abstract: IgM contributes to early and durable humoral immunity, yet the mechanisms governing human IgM plasma cell (PC) maturation and persistence remain unknown. Here, using an ex vivo human B cell system, we found that IgM B cell receptor (BCR) signaling restricts IgM antibody-secreting cell (ASC) differentiation and survival. Using CRISPR-mediated gene disruption and pharmacologic inhibition, we show that surface BCR and its proximal signaling components, particularly SYK, suppressed induction of IRF4 and PRDM1, thereby restraining PC differentiation. Concurrently, ligand-independent BCR signaling increased basal calcium flux and apoptosis in IgM plasmablasts. Inhibition of BCR-proximal signaling also increased PC numbers and persistence after in vivo engraftment. Leveraging this mechanistic insight, we demonstrated that SYK KO in engineered PCs (ePCs) significantly improved output and in vivo durability of IgM-cetuximab-secreting ePCs. Together, these findings reveal IgM-BCR signaling as a previously unrecognized negative regulator of human IgM PC differentiation and survival and show that inhibition of BCR-proximal pathways can improve IgM-based cellular immunotherapies.

title: The evolving landscape of fungal keratitis: from emerging pathogens to precision diagnostics and novel therapeutics.
authors: Das, Sourav; Jain, Mansi; Khapuinamai, Agimanailiu; Joseph, Joveeta
abstract: Fungal keratitis (FK) remains a major cause of vision-threatening corneal infection, especially in tropical and subtropical regions, with an expanding epidemiological spectrum driven by environmental, climatic, occupational and host-related factors. Fusarium and Aspergillus were the most common pathogens reported. Greater etiological diversity is reflected by increasing recognition of dematiaceous fungi, uncommon molds, and cryptic species. The literature search was performed by searching bibliographic databases (PubMed and Google Scholar), covering publications from January 2000 to August 2026. Additional relevant studies were identified by screening the reference lists of key publications. This review provides an overview of the current state of FK including changing epidemiology, established diagnostic approaches, emerging technologies, and evolving therapeutic approaches. Conventional microscopy and culture remain central to diagnosis, with molecular methods, sequencing, MALDI-TOF and noninvasive imaging offering advantages in sensitivity, speed and species-level identification. Novel diagnostic methods such as CRISPR-based tests, genome sequencing, artificial intelligence, biosensors and point-of-care diagnostics may provide rapid and accessible precision diagnosis. Therapeutic challenges include poor corneal drug penetration, antifungal resistance and prolonged treatment. Hence, the exploration of new antifungals, nanotechnology-based delivery systems, photoactivated therapies and antimicrobial peptides. These advances support a transition to integrated, rapid and precision-based management of FK collectively.

title: NEK kinase TcRDK2 controls differentiation, host cell infection, and remodeling of the translation initiation machinery in Trypanosoma cruzi.
authors: Roson, Juliana N; Huckleberry, Jessica; Lander, Noelia; Chiurillo, Miguel A
abstract: Trypanosoma cruzi, the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, alternates between replicative epimastigotes and amastigotes and non-dividing, mammal-infective metacyclic and bloodstream trypomastigotes. Protein phosphorylation is a major regulatory mechanism in trypanosomatids, whose kinomes reveal an expanded family of NIMA-related kinases (NEKs). Here, we investigated the role of T. cruzi RDK2 (repressor of differentiation kinase 2), a conserved NEK that carries a C-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain. Endogenous gene tagging showed that TcRDK2 is expressed in all major life cycle stages and displays a cytoplasmic distribution. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of TcRDK2 did not markedly alter epimastigote growth in rich medium but caused a significant accumulation of cells with abnormal nucleus/kinetoplast configurations, consistent with defects in kinetoplast segregation and cytokinesis; TcRDK2-null parasites also showed reduced in vitro metacyclogenesis and failed to establish efficient infections in human fibroblasts. To probe gain-of-function effects, we generated tetracycline-inducible overexpression lines for full-length TcRDK2 (RDK2(WT)), a PH-deleted variant (RDK2(DeltaPH)), and a catalytically dead mutant (RDK2(K70A)). Overexpression of RDK2(WT) or RDK2(DeltaPH) decreased epimastigote growth, enhanced metacyclogenesis, and strongly impaired host cell invasion and intracellular amastigote proliferation, with more pronounced phenotypes for RDK2(DeltaPH), suggesting that the PH domain normally restrains TcRDK2 activity in vivo. Phosphoproteomic profiling of RDK2(WT)-overexpressing epimastigotes revealed broad phosphoproteome remodeling associated with TcRDK2 upregulation, including changes affecting proteins linked to translation initiation and the cytoskeleton. Together, these findings support a role for TcRDK2 as a NEK kinase in kinetoplast replication/segregation, metacyclogenesis, and host cell infection in T. cruzi and highlight TcRDK2 as a promising kinetoplastid-specific therapeutic target for Chagas disease. IMPORTANCE: Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, remains a major health problem with limited treatment options. To persist in both insect vectors and mammalian hosts, the parasite must precisely coordinate cell division, differentiation into infectious forms, and survival inside host cells. Protein kinases are central regulators of these processes and attractive drug targets, yet many remain poorly understood in T. cruzi. In this study, we investigate RDK2, a member of the NIMA-related kinase family. Using gene knockout, inducible overexpression, and global analysis of phosphorylated proteins, we show that RDK2 is required for accurate segregation of mitochondrial DNA, efficient formation of infective insect stage forms, and successful infection and replication in human cells. These findings identify RDK2 as a key regulator that links parasite cell division to infectivity and highlight it as a promising, parasite-specific candidate for future drug development against Chagas disease.

title: A comprehensive HA-tagged PRC1 toolkit enables standardized chromatin profiling and proteomic analysis in Drosophila melanogaster.
authors: Fritsch, Lauriane; Loubiere, Vincent; Donjon, Axelle; Morales-Sanfrutos, Julia; Sabido, Eduard; Martinez, Anne-Marie; Schuettengruber, Bernd; Cavalli, Giacomo
abstract: Polycomb group (PcG) proteins are evolutionarily conserved epigenetic regulators that maintain transcriptional states during development and are frequently dysregulated in disease. Here, we generated a comprehensive collection of endogenously HA-tagged alleles for the core components of Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1) and additional chromatin regulators in Drosophila melanogaster using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome engineering. We show that endogenous HA tagging preserves protein expression, chromatin localization, and genome-wide binding profiles, enabling direct comparison using a common antibody to analyze distinct PcG subunits. Proteomic analyses recovered known components of canonical and non-canonical PRC1 and Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) complexes and identified additional PcG-associated factors. Notably, multiple components of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) were detected as PcG interactors, and genetic analyses confirmed a functional interaction between them. This resource provides a platform for standardized analysis of Polycomb function and chromatin regulation that can easily be extended to other chromatin regulatory complexes and applied across different developmental stages.

title: The deficiency of htr6 gene results in aberrant brain development and epileptiform discharges in zebrafish larvae.
authors: Chu, Hongyuan; Wang, Hao; Wen, Sijia; Li, Renqiuguo; Zhang, Junjiao; Zhang, Fan; Luo, Huaxia; Wu, Ye; Wang, Jingmin; Gao, Kai; Jiang, Yuwu
abstract: BACKGROUND: The 5-Hydroxytryptamine Receptor 6 (HTR6) is a G protein-coupled receptor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders and epilepsy. Our previous studies identified a somatic HTR6 mutation in brain surgical specimens from patients with focal cortical dysplasia type II, suggesting its potential involvement in disease pathogenesis. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the functional role of the htr6 in zebrafish, focusing on its impact on neurodevelopment and seizure susceptibility. METHODS: A F0 mosaic htr6 crispant zebrafish model was generated using CRISPR/Cas9 and validated by sequencing and TIDE analysis. Morphological and central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities were assessed at 5 days post-fertilization (dpf) by bright-field and Tg (HuC: eGFP) fluorescence imaging. Survival was monitored to 21 dpf. Locomotor behavior was evaluated using DanioVision, and epileptiform activity was examined by local field potential recording. Human HTR6 mRNA rescue experiments, transcriptome sequencing, and qPCR validation were also performed. RESULTS: Deficiency of htr6 resulted in significant reductions in interocular and central nervous system areas. In addition, F0 mosaic htr6 crispant showed significantly reduced survival compared with Cas9 controls. While locomotor activity was markedly unaffected, electrophysiological recordings revealed epileptiform events in 9 of 24 F0 mosaic htr6 crispant but none in the Cas9 controls. Co-injection of human HTR6 mRNA rescued both neurodevelopmental abnormalities and epileptiform activity. Transcriptome analysis identified 402 differentially expressed genes, including the upregulation of 355 and the downregulation of 47 genes, suggesting profound neuronal impacts from htr6 deficiency. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis linked these changes to ABC transporters and metabolic pathways, demonstrating the significance of htr6 in maintaining neuronal health. CONCLUSION: Deficiency of htr6 in zebrafish results in abnormal brain development and epileptiform activity, underscoring its critical role in neurodevelopment and neuronal excitability. These findings suggest the importance of HTR6 in neurodevelopment and epilepsy, providing a foundation for further research on therapeutic strategies targeting HTR6-related pathways in neurological disorders.

title: Aquaporins in Brain Tumor-Related Edema: A Narrative Review.
authors: Al-Nuaimy, Yusor; Baloi, Denise; Rawson, Clayton; Kim, Jerick; Karsy, Michael; Pahlevani, Mehrdad
abstract: BACKGROUND: Brain tumor-related edema is a major contributor to morbidity in patients with intracranial neoplasms, arising from interactions between blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction, tumor biology, and dysregulated water transport. Aquaporins (AQPs), and particularly AQP4, are central to cerebral water homeostasis, and alterations in their expression and spatial polarization within and around brain tumors influence both cytotoxic and vasogenic edema. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on AQP biology in the tumor-bearing brain and critically appraises the translational maturity of AQP-directed therapy. SUMMARY: AQP4 is the predominant central nervous system AQP, concentrated at astrocytic end-feet and essential for water flux across the BBB and along glymphatic pathways. In high-grade gliomas, AQP4 is upregulated and loses perivascular polarity, a pattern that accompanies extensive vasogenic edema, impaired perivascular clearance, and enhanced tumor cell invasion. Low-grade gliomas and meningiomas show more restricted or vascular-predominant AQP expression, including AQP1 in meningioma vasculature, and comparatively less peritumoral edema. Experimental work demonstrates a bidirectional, context-dependent role for AQP4: it promotes astrocytic swelling when the BBB is intact, yet facilitates reabsorption of extracellular fluid once the barrier is disrupted. This duality has not been resolved in human tumor tissue and constrains any single-direction therapeutic strategy. Candidate interventions, including small-molecule inhibitors (AER-270/AER-271), monoclonal antibodies, SUR1-TRPM4 modulation, RNA interference, and CRISPR/Cas9-based editing, have shown activity in rodent injury models but have not been evaluated in brain tumor populations. KEY MESSAGES: (1) AQP4 is not uniformly pro-edematous; its net effect depends on BBB integrity, edema phase, and preservation of perivascular polarity, so undifferentiated inhibition risks impairing fluid clearance in precisely the tumors that most need it. (2) The evidence base remains dominated by rodent injury models and small immunohistochemical series rather than human tumor tissue, and no AQP-targeted agent has entered a brain tumor trial. (3) Meaningful progress will require human-tissue studies that quantify AQP4 polarity rather than total expression, prospective imaging biomarkers such as diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space capable of stratifying patients before treatment, and astrocyte-targeted, temporally controlled gene-editing approaches rather than constitutive gene deletion.

title: Quercetin upregulates TLE4 to block the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway and inhibit cell migration and invasion of cervical cancer cells.
authors: Mai, Yirui; Ju, Keyi; Yang, Yongkang; Wang, Weijing; Zhang, Ting; Wang, Jiake; Wang, Yu; Gao, Weihua; Li, Tuanwang; Gong, Beier; Li, Yuanyuan
abstract: METHODS: Using established TLE4-overexpression and CRISPR-Cas9-knockout cervical cancer cell lines and nude mouse tumorigenesis models, we verified the biological function and regulatory mechanism of TLE4 in cervical cancer. RESULTS: Quercetin treatment upregulated the expression of TLE4 in HeLa cells. Compared with normal cervical tissues from clinical specimens, the expression of TLE4 in the nucleus of cervical cancer tissues was significantly downregulated. Transwell assays showed that the migration and invasion of C-33A TLE4-overexpression cells were significantly suppressed, accompanied by an upregulation of the expression of E-cadherin and a downregulation of the expression of N-cadherin, Vimentin, and Snail. Conversely, the migration and invasion of Ca Ski TLE4-knockout cells were significantly enhanced, and the expressions of these EMT-related markers showed the opposite trend. Meanwhile, the in vivo xenograft experiment revealed that the Ca Ski TLE4-knockout group exhibited faster tumor growth compared with the wild-type group. Furthermore, we examined the role of TLE4 in the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway. In C-33A TLE4-overexpression cells, beta-catenin, TCF-1, TCF-4, CyclinD1, c-Myc, and MMP-7 were decreased, p-beta-catenin expression was increased, whereas in Ca Ski TLE4-knockout cells, the expression trends of these factors were opposite. After treating TLE4-knockout Ca Ski cells with quercetin, the enhanced migration and invasion capabilities induced by TLE4 knockout were effectively reversed. CONCLUSION: Quercetin targets and upregulates the expression of TLE4, which inhibits the migration and invasion of cervical cancer cells by blocking the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway, thereby providing theoretical and experimental evidence for quercetin therapy in cervical cancer.

title: Artificial intelligence and biotechnology for smart storage: Quality and safety perspectives in horticultural produce.
authors: Sui, Yuan; Zhao, Yu; Chen, Wenxuan; Duan, Bin; Wang, Zhenshuo; Chen, Zhuo
abstract: Addressing the global challenge of postharvest losses in horticultural produce requires the continuous development of innovative strategies that integrate cutting-edge technology with fundamental biological knowledge. This review explores the synergy between artificial intelligence (AI), biotechnology, and traditional postharvest management strategies to improve the quality, safety, and shelf-life of fruits and vegetables (F&V). We examine the physiological and molecular mechanisms driving postharvest deterioration, including respiration, senescence, and host-pathogen interactions, while evaluating how AI-driven tools are advancing quality monitoring, predictive analytics, and supply chain optimization. Furthermore, we assess the potential of advanced biotechnological interventions, such as CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing and RNA interference techniques, to extend shelf-life and enhance the disease resistance in horticultural crops. By evaluating recent progress in these domains, we present integrated strategies that combine biological insight with digital transformation for sustainable postharvest management. The effective implementation of these approaches holds considerable potential to reduce F&V waste, enhance food security, and create horticultural supply chains that are more resilient to ever growing global production and evolving environmental challenges.

title: Recent advances in CRISPR technologies for biomedical applications and disease treatment.
authors: Wu, Xue; Kou, Xiaorong; Bai, Liping; Liu, Chao; Wu, Qinjie; Zhang, Ming; Wang, Ning; Gong, Changyang
abstract: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), a precise genome-editing platform, has revolutionized genetic engineering. The highly selective and programmable characteristics of CRISPR have enabled its broad application. Recent advances in CRISPR biotechnology have promoted its widespread use in various biomedical fields, such as CRISPR screening. Ongoing preclinical and clinical trials will help determine the full capabilities of CRISPR in disease therapy. The efficacy of CRISPR-based applications is fundamentally dependent on optimized delivery strategies. Multiple approaches for delivering the CRISPR components have been investigated, primarily relying on physical, viral and non-viral delivery methods. Each method has specific strengths and limitations. Notably, non-viral delivery systems hold significant promise for CRISPR applications, offering distinct advantages such as transient expression, low immunogenicity, and fewer size constraints for cargo delivery. Various biomaterials demonstrate strong potential for delivering CRISPR components to achieve gene editing, including inorganic nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, lipid nanoparticles, metal-organic frameworks, DNA origami, and virus-like particles. Therefore, this review provides an overview of recent research on the molecular principles of CRISPR and its biomedical applications. Recent advances in CRISPR-based treatments and their delivery vectors are also reviewed. Finally, the challenges faced by CRISPR technology are discussed.

title: Variable alterations in frequencies of CRISPR/Cas9-induced nucleotide deletion and insertion in transgenic maize callus tissues exposed to chromatin modifiers.
authors: Nagy, Bettina; Jameel, Aysha; Horvath, Gabor V; Torok, Katalin; Ayaydin, Ferhan; Laszlo, Nikolett; Dondapati, Divya Teja; Morocz, Sandor; Zombori, Zoltan; Ferenc, Gyorgyi; Dudits, Denes
abstract: Given the growing emphasis on the efficient application of CRISPR/Cas9 in plant genome editing, there is a need for methodologies that enhance targeted mutagenesis efficiency. In the present study, we utilized stable transgenic maize callus tissues harboring active CRISPR/Cas9 vector systems targeting either the abnormal cytokinin response 1 (ARE1) gene or the potassium channel gene (KAT2). The presented DNA sequencing data indicate that the KAT2-targeting vector, which utilizes a 3'-end truncated guide RNA, retained mutagenic activity, albeit at a notably low frequency. We quantified mutagenic events following exposure to elevated temperatures (37  degrees C for 48 h) and various chromatin-modifying compounds, including sodium butyrate (NaBt), nicotinamide (NA), and 5-azacytidine (AZA). High-temperature treatment alone increased the frequency of nucleotide deletions (5.8-fold relative to the untreated samples) in the ARE1 target gene. Conversely, in the KAT2 gene, both deletions and insertions were stimulated (6.4 and 6.2-fold, respectively). As a novel approach, we evaluated the mutagenic efficacy of chromatin-modifying compounds administered in conjunction with heat treatment. The combined application of NaBt and AZA with elevated temperature was particularly effective in increasing insertion frequencies; in the ARE1 (with NaBt + heat: 17.3-fold) and KAT2 (with AZA + heat: 21.4-fold) genes. Cell cycle analysis of suspension-cultured cells revealed that chromatin-modifying treatments altered cell cycle progression, evidenced by an accumulation of cells in the G2 phase and a significant reduction in the number of mitotic cells. Subsequent DNA sequencing demonstrated a differential increase in the induction of deletions and insertions, alongside an expansion of the deleted regions.

title: Generation and Validation of a GnRH-iCreERT2-tdTomato Mouse Line for Genetic Manipulation in GnRH Neurons.
authors: Dong, Shuhua; Han, Zi'ang; He, Yuanyuan; Wang, Ze; Qi, Dashi; Feng, Weijun
abstract: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons play a key role in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. We generated a new GnRH-P2A-iCreERT2-P2A-tdTomato (hereafter referred to as the GnRH-CT-tdT line) knock-in mouse line utilizing CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Characterization analysis of this line revealed that tdTomato expression precisely recapitulates endogenous GnRH expression and iCreERT2 recombines in GnRH neurons with excellent specificity and sensitivity. Therefore, this newly constructed GnRH-CT-tdT mouse line provides a useful tool to perform genetic manipulation in GnRH neurons. As a proof-of-principle, we used this line to investigate the role of Chd7 (Chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 7), a gene with its loss-of-function associated with isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone deficiency (IGD). Surprisingly, ablation of Chd7 in GnRH neurons does not affect the number of GnRH neurons, pubertal onset, and reproductive organ morphology. Therefore, Chd7 is dispensable in GnRH neurons after they have initiated GnRH expression. In summary, the GnRH-CT-tdT mouse line is a valuable tool to study gene function in GnRH neurons and to dissect the pathogenesis of IGD.

title: Research progress in gene editing of Brassicaceae crops.
authors: Wang, Xiaolong; Shangguan, Bingbing; Zhang, Yanwen; Su, Tongbing; Ji, Jialei; Zhao, Jianjun; Zhang, Changwei; Li, Ying; Hou, Xilin; Liu, Tongkun
abstract: Brassicaceae crops are globally important economic plants, whose yield and quality directly affect the supply of edible oil and vegetables. Most of these crops are polyploids with complex genomes and numerous homoeologous gene copies, which demand high efficiency and specificity from gene editing tools, while providing ideal models for studying the rules of polyploid genome editing. Traditional breeding methods, such as crossbreeding and mutation breeding, are constrained by long cycles, low efficiency, and poor specificity, making them insufficient for precise genetic improvement. Gene editing technologies, characterized by precision, efficiency, and targeting specific genomic loci, are core tools for crop breeding. Among these, ZFNs and TALENs rely on protein-DNA recognition and are complicated and costly to design; CRISPR-Cas, which achieves precise recognition through base pairing between guide RNA and target DNA, is simple, efficient, and the most widely used editing tool. Base and prime editors enable single-nucleotide substitutions or small fragment insertions without generating double-strand breaks, making them suitable for directed modification of point mutations. This review summarizes the progress of gene editing in Brassicaceae for bolting/flowering, plant architecture, nutritional quality, tolerance to abiotic stresses (temperature, salinity, drought, heavy metals), and resistance to biotic stresses (diseases, pests). We analyze challenges, including off-target effects, difficulties in polyploid genome editing, and imperfect genetic transformation systems, and discuss future directions integrating gene editing with multi-omics and artificial intelligence. This review aims to provide a theoretical basis and technical support for precise molecular breeding of Brassicaceae crops.

title: Modulation of the sensitivity to ruxolitinib-mediated JAK2 inhibition by mutationally activated SHP2 exhibits cell context dependency in pre-clinical models of myeloproliferative neoplasms.
authors: Rowsell, Tegan M; Pandey, Garima; Mazzacurati, Lucia; Amin, Narmin E; Reuther, Gary W
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Classic Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are hematopoietic stem cell cancers that result in aberrant trilineage myeloid cell proliferation, bone marrow fibrosis, and increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia. MPNs are driven by deregulated activity of the JAK2 kinase, induced by mutations in the JAK2, CALR, and MPL genes, but approved JAK2 inhibitors primarily offer palliative effects, not remission. Cell models that demonstrate MPN oncogene driven JAK2 activity requisite for cell proliferation are important research tools for the development of anti-JAK2 and anti-JAK2 signaling therapeutics for MPN. SET2 and UKE1 cells are two such cell lines, as they express JAK2-V617F, one of the major driving mutations of MPN, and require signaling by JAK2 for their growth and viability. These cell lines are AML cell lines that were derived from patients with a previous diagnosis of MPN before they developed AML. Our previous studies demonstrated that the SHP2 phosphatase may be a therapeutic target for MPNs, and here we report our identification and characterization of an activating point mutation of SHP2 (encoded by the PTPN11 gene), SHP2-F71L, in UKE1 cells. Given SHP2 functions downstream of JAK2 and mediates JAK2 activation of RAS, we set out to determine the effect of mutational activation of SHP2 on the sensitivity of MPN model cells to JAK2 inhibition. We used CRISPR-Cas9 to edit this mutation in UKE1 cells back to wildtype such that these cells only express wildtype SHP2. These cells exhibited enhanced sensitivity to SHP2 inhibition and, notably, enhanced sensitivity to the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib. This altered sensitivity was reverted by exogenous expression of SHP2-F71L but not SHP2-WT, indicating expression of an activated SHP2 may alter sensitivity to JAK2 inhibition in MPN model cells. We further explored this by genetically editing SET2 cells to express SHP2-F71L but observed no change in SHP2 inhibitor or JAK2 inhibitor sensitivity in cells with a SHP2-F71L encoding allele of PTPN11. Using the cytokine dependent BaF3 cell line where deregulation of JAK2 signaling by expression of JAK2-V617F induces cytokine independent transformation that remains dependent on this JAK2 signaling, we observed no effect of the expression of an activated SHP2 mutant on the sensitivity of the growth and viability of these cells to ruxolitinib. Recent studies have demonstrated activation of RAS signaling can antagonize JAK2 inhibition in pre-clinical MPN models, and the presence of RAS pathway mutations associates with patients whose disease advances on ruxolitinib therapy. Such mutations include activating mutations in PTPN11, as SHP2 is an upstream activator of RAS signaling. Our results suggest that activating PTPN11 mutations have the potential to desensitize the effects of JAK2 inhibition therapy in patients undergoing therapy and may be dependent on unknown cell and molecular profile contexts.

title: Glycogen synthase AfGsy2 regulates mycelial growth, stress response, predatory activity, and chlamydospore development in the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans.
authors: Shi, Qianfei; Zhang, Yu; Mo, Minghe; Li, Guohong
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Glycogen is a universal carbon and energy reserve that plays crucial roles in fungal stress adaptation, cellular homeostasis, and predatory activity. However, the role of glycogen metabolism in nematode-trapping fungi has largely remained unexplored. Here, we performed a systematic functional characterization of AfGsy2, the glycogen synthase-encoding gene in the biocontrol fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans. METHODS: Using a CRISPR-Cas9-mediated deletion mutant, together with overexpression and complementation strains, we investigated the involvement of AfGsy2 in mycelial growth, stress tolerance, trap formation, nematicidal activity against Caenorhabditis elegans, chlamydospore production and germination, and glycogen accumulation. Subcellular localization was examined using an AfGsy2-GFP fusion protein. RESULTS: Deletion of AfGsy2 reduced hyphal growth on both nutrient-rich and nutrient-poor media but enhanced tolerance to osmotic, salt, and oxidative stresses, suggesting that blocked glycogen synthesis may trigger metabolic rerouting toward alternative stress-protective compounds. Notably, the DeltaAfGsy2 mutants exhibited reduced trap production and nematicidal activity against C. elegans, whereas overexpression of AfGsy2 accelerated these processes, suggesting a link between glycogen metabolism and predatory activity. Moreover, AfGsy2 positively regulated chlamydospore production, glycogen accumulation, and chlamydospore germination. AfGsy2-GFP predominantly localized to the vacuoles of chlamydospores, and complementation restored the mutant phenotypes to wild-type levels. DISCUSSION: Collectively, these findings uncover a link between glycogen metabolism and growth, stress resilience, sporulation, and predatory activity in A. flagrans, and establish a molecular foundation for the rational improvement of nematode-trapping fungi. Together, these results identify AfGsy2 as a pleiotropic regulator linking glycogen metabolism to biocontrol-related traits.

title: Temporal organization of leptin signaling reveals distinct regulatory roles for STAT3 and ETV6.
authors: Pathak, Ekta; Bernecker, Miriam; Mallet, Noemi; Konig, Ann-Christin; Gutierrez-Aguilar, Ruth; Mencias, Cristina; Schriever, Sonja C; Pfluger, Paul T
abstract: Leptin regulates energy homeostasis through activation of its long-form receptor (LepRb), primarily via JAK2-dependent phosphorylation of STAT3. However, the temporal organization of leptin-induced transcriptional responses and how parallel signaling pathways contribute to these dynamics remain incompletely understood. Here, we established a LepRb-expressing hypothalamic cellular model to investigate the temporal architecture of leptin-induced transcription factors and pathways identified by transcriptome and proteome profiling at baseline (0 min), early (30 min), and late (180 min) time points. Overall changes in acute leptin stimulation were primarily reflected at the level of transcriptional and regulatory reprogramming. Proteomic remodeling mirrored the transcriptome but appeared smaller, likely due to assay insensitivity and slower dynamics of protein regulation, making the transcriptome the more informative kinetic readout. Structured transcriptional dynamics included the rapid activation of stress- and inflammatory-associated genes followed by sustained cytokine and interferon signaling modules. Transcription factor regulon and pathway activity inference identified coordinated activation of STAT, NF-kappaB, and MAPK-associated regulatory programs underlying these expression trajectories. CRISPR-Cas9-based deletion of Stat3 markedly altered basal transcriptional states and attenuated leptin-induced gene expression while revealing activation of alternative signaling pathways. In contrast, CRISPR-Cas9-based deletion of the ETS transcriptional repressor Etv6 strongly affected baseline transcription but had minimal impact on leptin-induced regulatory dynamics. Together, these findings reveal a temporally organized regulatory architecture in which STAT3 governs stimulus-responsive transcriptional dynamics, whereas ETV6 primarily modulates baseline transcriptional states.

title: Accurate prediction of CRISPR editing outcomes in somatic cell lines and zygotes with few-shot learning with inDecay.
authors: Zheng, Weizhong; Yu, Lu; Wu, Chao; Cao, Shaoxian; Zhao, Mengying; Wang, Guoliang; So, Kam Ho; Song, Jun; Cheng, Chen; Ho, Joshua W K; Liu, Xueqin; Wu, Meng; Liu, Zhonghua; Wang, Huili; Liu, Pentao; Lan, Guocheng; Huang, Yuanhua
abstract: Prediction of CRISPR/Cas outcomes remains unsatisfactory in embryos due to distinct DNA repair preferences and the lack of large-scale embryo editing profiles. We introduce inDecay, a flexible system for predicting the proportion of CRISPR-induced indels from the target sequence. Owing to its parameter-efficient and cell-type-aware design, inDecay performs well in both in-sample training and out-of-sample fine-tuning. Starting with cross-cell-line predictions, we observed that inDecay maintains high accuracy in mouse zygote editing and in goat, cattle and porcine embryos. inDecay may accelerate mouse model generation, livestock embryonic editing, and gene therapy applications.

title: A phage DUF669 protein mediates post-cleavage DNA repair against host CRISPR immunity.
authors: Zhu, Heng; Dai, Shengkun; Deng, Hewen; Hou, Shifeng; Li, Yuelong; Tan, Xin; Jia, Ning; Li, Nan; Ma, Yingfei
abstract: Phages have evolved various anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins or RNA-based anti-CRISPR (Racr) to evade host CRISPR immunity by direct interference. However, whether other counter-CRISPR mechanisms exist remains unexplored. Here, we report a phage-encoded two-protein system, termed Healer, which neutralizes CRISPR immunity via a post-cleavage DNA repair mechanism. This phage replication-associated system comprises two proteins: Gp63 (a DUF669 domain-containing protein), and Gp64 (an AAA domain-containing protein). Mechanistic investigations elucidate that Gp63 acts as a rapid-response effector of CRISPR-induced DNA breaks. After Gp63 binds ssDNA, it promotes Gp64-mediated homologous recombination, which repairs CRISPR-generated phage DNA breaks and supports phage viability. Notably, co-expression of the Healer system with Cas9/Cas12 in E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and A. baumannii demonstrated high phage genome-editing efficiency. Collectively, our findings reveal an important anti-CRISPR complementary strategy, providing a promising tool for genome engineering.

title: EpOME functionally antagonises prostaglandin signalling in Spodoptera exigua via a specific GPCR conserved across metazoans.
authors: Shahmohammadi, Niayesh; Khan, Falguni; Jang, Haneol; Kim, Il-Hwan; Lee, Donghee; Wallen, Joseph; Choi, Hyeok Jin; Jeong, Jin Boo; Vik, Anders; Kim, Yonggyun
abstract: The eicosanoid PGE(2) upregulates intracellular Ca(2)(+)/cAMP levels and induces a cellular immune response, whereas EpOME inhibits PGE(2) activity in insects. However, the molecular interactions between the two antagonistic ligands remain largely unexplored. Here we identify nine homologs of vertebrate C18-oxylipin-associating GPCRs among the GPCRs of Spodoptera exigua (SeGPCRs). Functional homology is validated through RNA interference screening, followed by heterologous expressions in both directions between insect and human cell lines. A deletion mutant of SeGPCR48, generated via CRISPR/Cas9, loses responsiveness to EpOME, which is confirmed functionally and by differential gene expression analysis following RNA-seq. In silico binding assay indicate high binding affinity of EpOME to SeGPCR48, which is supported by experimental follow-up, involving ligand-binding functional assays and point mutagenesis of two residues in the binding pocket. In congruence with the in vitro experiments, the EpOME-SeGPCR48 ligand-receptor pair showed marked inhibitory activity against PGE(2)-mediated immunity. Collectively, this study identifies an insect EpOME receptor within an orphan GPCR subfamily that is phylogenetically conserved across metazoans.

title: Loss-of-function variants in CFAP57, SEPTIN4, SPEM2, and CFAP46 cause asthenoteratozoospermia.
authors: Nawaz, Shoaib; Kitakaze, Hiroaki; Abdulla, Maha A; Khan, Nida; Miyata, Haruhiko; Djekidel, Mohamed Nadhir; Ata, Manar; Kaneda, Yuki; Khan, Hammal; Khan, Ihsan; Esteves, Maria; Devadoss Gandhi, Geethanjali; Choucair, Fadi; Hussain, Shabir; Aliyev, Elbay; Hatanaka, Yuki; Kujime, Yuma; Tsujimura, Go; Imanaka, Takahiro; Kuribayashi, Sohei; Ueda, Norichika; Arafa, Mohamed M; Elbardisi, Haitham T; Takezawa, Kentaro; Fukuhara, Shinichiro; Nonomura, Norio; Sathappan, Abbirami; Salhab, Abdul Rahman; Awwad, Johnny; Ullah, Imran; Fakhro, Khalid; Ikawa, Masahito; Avella, Matteo A
abstract: STUDY QUESTION: What are the genetic causes of asthenoteratozoospermia in consanguineous families, and what is the specific role of cilia- and flagella-associated proteins (CFAP) 46 in mammalian spermiogenesis? SUMMARY ANSWER: CFAP46 is a central apparatus protein essential for sperm flagellar assembly and head remodeling. WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY: Asthenoteratozoospermia is a genetically heterogeneous condition characterized by reduced sperm motility and abnormal morphology. While several CFAPs are known to support axonemal organization, the functional role of CFAP46 in mammals remained uncharacterized prior to this study. STUDY DESIGN, SIZE, DURATION: We performed whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing on 13 consanguineous families affected by primary male infertility. Functional validation was conducted using three CRISPR/Cas9-engineered mouse models: a null allele, a FLAG-tagged knock-in, and a humanized patient-specific nonsense allele. PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING, METHODS: Genomic DNA from affected individuals and fertile relatives was analyzed by NGS and validated via Sanger sequencing. Mouse phenotypes were characterized through sperm analysis, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy. Protein interactions were identified via immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry. Additionally, a gene-level burden analysis was applied to unresolved cases across 345 spermiogenesis-associated genes. MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE: We identified homozygous loss-of-function variants in CFAP46, CFAP57, SEPTIN4, and SPEM2 segregating with infertility. Cfap46-deficient males were infertile due to significantly decreased sperm count, motility, and severe axonemal disruptions. CFAP46 was found to form an in vivo complex with CFAP54, CFAP74, and CFAP221. In families without a monogenic cause, affected individuals harbored a significantly higher burden of rare deleterious variants (4-16 genes) compared to fertile controls. LARGE SCALE DATA: Large-scale datasets and scripts are available via GitHub (https://github.com/sirusb/Nawaz_et_al_scripts). LIMITATIONS, REASONS FOR CAUTION: While functional mouse data strongly supports the identified variants, the rare-variant burden analysis identifies associations that require further functional validation to confirm specific oligogenic interactions. WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS: This study establishes CFAP46 as a regulator of mammalian spermiogenesis and suggests that, beyond monogenic defects, aggregated rare-variant burden may also contribute to male infertility. These findings refine the genetic basis of asthenoteratozoospermia, supporting precise molecular diagnosis, individualized prognostic counseling, and informed use of assisted reproduction (e.g. ICSI) in affected couples. FUNDING: This work was supported by Sidra Medicine grant SDR400185 (to M.A.A.), the FERTILITY-IQ Study and Qatar National Research Fund (QNRF) grant NPRP12S-0318-190394 (to M.A.A. and K.F.), the Qatar Research, Development and Innovation (QRDI) grant GSRA12-I-0311-250014 (to M.A.Abd.), the Quaid-i-Azam University Research Project (URF-QAU) 2020-21 (to I.U.), Japan Society for the Promotion of Science KAKENHI grants JP24K12461 (to H.K.), JP23K18328 (to H.M.), and JP21H05033 and JP23K20043 (to M.I.), Japan Agency for Medical Research and Development (AMED) grants JP23jf0126001 and JP26gn0110011 (to M.I.), and JSRM Ferting Grant 2025 (to H.K.). Open access funding was provided by the Qatar National Library. DISCLOSURES: The authors declare no competing interests.

title: Astrocytic Cystine/Glutamate Antiporters Promote Diabetic Encephalopathy via the Induction of Glutamate Excitotoxicity.
authors: Chiang, Jung-Ying; Wang, Hwai-Lee; Huang, Yen-Chih; Wang, Chi-Chung; Wei, Sung-Tai; Hsieh, Chia-Hung
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cystine/glutamate antiporter (xCT) imports extracellular cystine in exchange for intracellular glutamate. Although it plays an essential role in diabetes-associated processes such as impaired wound healing, its contribution to diabetic encephalopathy (DE) remains unclear. METHODS: Wild-type and xCT-deficient (xCT-/-) mice were subjected to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) induction using a highfat diet combined with streptozotocin. xCT expression and activity in the brain were evaluated through quantitative polymerase chain reaction, Western blotting, immunofluorescence, chloride-dependent [14C]-L-cystine uptake, and measurements of extracellular glutamate. An adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 approach was employed to generate region-specific, cell type-restricted xCT knockout animals. Neuronal injury and cognitive function were evaluated via in vivo propidium iodide (PI) and neuronal nuclei antigen (NeuN) double staining, the Y-maze spontaneous alternation test, the Morris water maze test, and the object location test. RESULTS: xCT deficiency protected mice from T2DM-induced DE. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia upregulated xCT expression via activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), thereby enhancing xCT function in hippocampal astrocytes. This maladaptive increase promoted excessive extracellular glutamate, neuronal loss, and cognitive impairment. Both astrocyte-specific deletion of xCT and pharmacological inhibition of xCT ameliorated these deficits. CONCLUSION: These findings identify astrocytic xCT as a key driver of diabetes-induced glutamate excitotoxicity and DE progression, underscoring its potential as a therapeutic target.

title: Generation of a ror2-EGFP transgenic Xenopus line for tracking Ror2-expressing cells during limb and intestinal development.
authors: Shibata, Yuki; Fujimoto, Kenta; Machida-Sano, Ikuko; Hasebe, Takashi
abstract: During Xenopus metamorphosis, thyroid hormone (TH) induces extensive remodeling of the intestine including the development of adult epithelial stem cells (ASCs). Ror2 (receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor 2), a receptor involved in non-canonical Wnt signaling, is expressed in a limited population of larval epithelial cells that undergo dedifferentiation into ASCs. To examine when and how the fate of Ror2-expressing larval epithelial cells is specified toward the ASC lineage, we successfully generated a new transgenic Xenopus expressing EGFP under the control of the ror2 promoter (Ror2-EGFP Tg) to visualize Ror2-expressing cells. This was achieved using the recently developed NEXTrans method, a CRISPR-Cas9-based targeted transgenesis system for Xenopus laevis. We found that 19.4% (13/67) of F0 tadpoles expressed DsRed1, a transgenic marker, in one or both eyes. Efficient germline transmission (approximately 30%-70%) was achieved in F1 Tg tadpoles. Interestingly, strong EGFP signals were observed in the limb buds and were subsequently detected in Col2A1-positive chondrocytes at stage 54, when all five toes had developed in the hindlimb. Co-expression of endogenous ror2 and transgene-derived EGFP was confirmed in the hindlimb buds by hybridization chain reaction (HCR). This co-expression was also confirmed in the intestinal epithelium as early as premetamorphic stage 54. This new transgenic line provides a valuable tool for tracking Ror2-expressing cells during limb development and intestinal stem cell formation in Xenopus.

title: The conserved function of bHLH121 and overexpression of N-terminal bHLH121 fragment suppresses iron deficiency response in Arabidopsis.
authors: Zhou, Peijun; Liu, Chuanfa; Pan, Yilin; Fei, Yuchen; Shen, Renfang; Wang, Ruonan; Lan, Ping
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: Iron (Fe) homeostasis is fundamental to plant growth and development and is centrally regulated by a well-conserved network of basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors. In Arabidopsis thaliana, bHLH121 regulates the expression of FER-like iron deficiency-induced transcription factor (FIT) and clade Ib bHLH38/39/100/101 genes, among others. However, its functional conservation remains unexplored, and some contradictory results have been reported regarding the effects of bHLH121 overexpression. Here, we investigated the evolutionary conservation of bHLH121 through complementary tests in the Arabidopsis bhlh121 mutant created by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. We also investigated the effects of ectopically expressing full-length, N-terminal, and C-terminal fragments of bHLH121 on plant responses to Fe deficiency in Arabidopsis. Transgenic plants overexpressing the full-length bHLH121 driven by the cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter (bHLH121 ox) resulted in shorter roots and more severe leaf chlorosis compared to wild-type plants under Fe-limiting conditions. Moreover, overexpression of the N-terminal fragment (N121 ox) rendered plants highly sensitive to Fe deficiency, whereas overexpression of the C-terminal fragment (C121 ox) did not. Consistent with the phenotypic observations, N121 ox plants accumulated lower Fe content, and the ferric chelate reductase activity was significantly reduced. In N121 ox plants, the induction of key Fe regulatory genes, especially FIT, was significantly inhibited under Fe deficiency. Confocal imaging showed that both N121-GFP and C121-GFP fusion proteins could localize to the nucleus. Electrophoretic mobility shift assay showed that both full-length bHLH121 and N121 could effectively bind the probes derived from the promoter of FIT. The present work reveals a conserved function of bHLH121 in Fe homeostasis across several dicot species and demonstrates that overexpression of N121 potently suppresses Fe deficiency responses in Arabidopsis.

title: A phage-encoded small RNA that mimics chimeric guide to inhibit CRISPR-Cas9.
authors: Chen, Ying; Zhao, Peng; Guo, Chenmin; Chen, Dandan; Yun, Caihong; Chen, Jiyun; Liu, Liang
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 relies on a dual CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) guide, yet whether RNA-based anti-CRISPRs exist for this system has remained unknown. Here, we identify a phage-encoded small non-coding RNA, rAcrIIA1, that adopts an unexpected chimeric crRNA-tracrRNA architecture, faithfully recapitulating the entire single-guide RNA (sgRNA) of Cas9. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Cas9-rAcrIIA1 binary complex and the Cas9-rAcrIIA1-DNA ternary complex reveal that rAcrIIA1 engages Cas9 nearly identically to the native sgRNA, competitively blocking crRNA and tracrRNA loading and thereby abolishing DNA interference. Strikingly, beyond its natural inhibitory function, rAcrIIA1 is fully reprogrammable: with variable guide sequences, it directs Cas9 for sequence-specific DNA cleavage with efficiency comparable to the canonical sgRNA, and it activates trans-cleavage more potently. Thus, rAcrIIA1 provides an experimentally validated, mechanistically resolved RNA-based inhibitor of CRISPR-Cas9, reveals a distinct anti-CRISPR mechanism through complete sgRNA mimicry, and serves as a versatile bifunctional scaffold for genome editing and diagnostics.

title: Single-strand break repair pathway disruption impacts radiosensitivity to both low- and high-LET radiation.
authors: Gardner, Lydia L; Guerra Liberal, Francisco D C; Thompson, Shannon J; Chevalier, Francois; Butterworth, Karl T; McMahon, Stephen J
abstract: Differences in individual radiosensitivity are not currently reflected in radiotherapy treatment planning, and identifying genetic drivers of this variation is a key step in personalising future treatments. While the role of DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair in radiosensitivity is well-studied, the impacts of single-strand break (SSB) repair defects are relatively unexplored. Through targeted SSB repair gene knockout, we show that disrupted SSB repair increases radiosensitivity, with stronger effects for high Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation. Mechanistic studies identified both an increase in DSB production at low LETs, due to delayed SSB repair, and higher levels of unrepaired complex damage at high LETs. This altered sensitivity is also reflected by differences in disease-specific survival for patients with SSB repair gene alterations in a retrospective pan-cancer clinical analysis. SSB repair pathway disruption may therefore be clinically relevant and important to consider for radiotherapy personalisation, particularly for high-LET radiation treatments.

title: Complete genome and phenotypic characterization of Zobellella denitrificans MW1 reveal carbon source preferences and a phosphate-associated shift in polyhydroxybutyrate accumulation.
authors: Guzik, Maciej; Prajsnar, Justyna; Faruga, Anna; Cichon, Ewelina; Kluza, Anna; Szeligowski, Adam; Trzaskowska, Wanda; Kaminski, Arkadiusz; Aleksic, Ivana; Nikodinovic-Runic, Jasmina; Mozejko-Ciesielska, Justyna
abstract: Zobellella denitrificans MW1 is a halotolerant, facultatively anaerobic bacterium with high poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (PHB) productivity that lacked a complete genome sequence. Here we report its first complete circular genome (4.10 Mb, 63.6% GC), obtained by hybrid Illumina-Nanopore assembly, with multi-scale cultivation data. The genome encodes a conserved phaCAB operon, multiple sucrose uptake and catabolic systems, and a canonical Pho regulon with polyphosphate metabolism genes (ppk, ppx). Ten CRISPR arrays, an intact prophage and no acquired multidrug resistance determinants were identified. Carbohydrate utilization was broad yet selective: sucrose, glucose and fructose supported the highest biomass, sucrose yielding up to 76% PHB of cell dry weight (CDW) in flasks; sucrose-rich beet molasses sustained PHB accumulation in flasks and 5 L bioreactors. In single, non-replicated fed-batch runs, a high-phosphate process reached 23 g L(-)(1) CDW with minimal PHB, whereas a low-phosphate process reached 53 g L(-)(1) CDW with 78% PHB. Because each regime was run once, these data are observations rather than a statistically supported comparison. They suggest that phosphate availability may be an important variable governing the growth-versus-storage balance, and that sucrose-rich industrial side-streams can be converted into PHB. The genomic co-occurrence of the Pho regulon, polyphosphate metabolism and phaCAB offers a hypothesis that remains to be tested by expression, enzyme-activity and targeted genetic experiments. Overall, MW1 is established as a genomically resolved platform for PHB production from low-cost, sucrose-rich feedstocks under saline conditions.

title: Reinforcement of Solid Lipid Nanoparticles for Targeted PD-L1 Downregulation in Breast Cancer.
authors: Onan, Deniz; Ozder, Melike; Erel-Akbaba, Gulsah; Cakiroglu, Ece; Senturk, Serif; Kantarci, Ayse Gulten; Akbaba, Hasan
abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype characterized by the absence of targetable receptors and limited therapeutic options. Its inherently low immunogenicity necessitates strategies to enhance its susceptibility to immune attack. This study aimed to enhance the antitumor immune response by inducing downregulation of the programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), thereby increasing cancer cell recognition and activating tumor-specific immunity. To this end, a targeted solid lipid nanoparticle (tSLN) system was developed for the precise delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids to achieve functional PD-L1 downregulation. The SLN formulation comprised a cetyl palmitate core stabilized with cationic and PEGylated lipids. Functionalization with the tumor-penetrating peptide iRGD yielded tSLN, which demonstrated good colloidal stability, serum protection of the CRISPR cargo, and minimal cytotoxicity. In vitro studies in two breast cancer subtypes, the luminal MCF-7 and the triple-negative 4T1 line, confirmed greater transfection efficiency and PD-L1 knockdown by tSLN:Crispr/PD-L1 relative to non-targeted controls. In an orthotopic 4T1 mouse model, systemic administration of tSLN:Crispr/PD-L1 significantly inhibited tumor growth and metastasis while enhancing T cell infiltration, and was more effective than standard chemotherapy (paclitaxel) in this model. The targeted approach also exhibited a favorable short-term safety profile, with no organ toxicity detected over the treatment period. These findings underscore the potential of SLN-mediated CRISPR delivery as an immunomodulatory strategy for breast cancer, and particularly for TNBC.

title: Genetic Biosensors for High-Throughput Biomedical Applications: Challenges and Advances.
authors: Ahvaraki, Akram; Teimouri, Mobina; Shirvani-Farsani, Zeinab; Omidfar, Kobra
abstract: Genetic biosensors represent a particularly promising class of bioengineered instruments designed to enable accurate, real-time monitoring of cellular and molecular processes, with especially strong relevance to high-throughput biomedical workflows. In this review, we provide a systematic, clearly structured overview of the field, covering the fundamental design principles that form the basis of today's platforms. We focus in particular on DNA-based, RNA-based, and CRISPR-based architectures while also examining engineered synthetic biology circuitry, and we place these foundational concepts in the context of more recent advances. These developments encompass improved sensitivity, increased scalability, and broader functionality for multiplexed detection. Beyond summarizing technological progress, we critically evaluate challenges that remain deeply embedded at both technical and biological levels, including limitations driven by signal-to-noise ratio constraints, practical difficulties in delivering probes into cells, and relatively restricted dynamic ranges. Taken together, these issues continue to hinder widespread, routine clinical adoption. Importantly, rather than presenting the topic only as a catalog of improvements, we argue for a unifying framework: the convergence of artificial intelligence and synthetic biology is actively reshaping biosensor engineering, moving it away from a largely empirical, trial-and-error approach toward a more reliable, data-driven discipline. To convert this conceptual shift into tangible outcomes, we also outline a practical implementation framework aimed at reducing the distance between research activities and real-world deployment. This framework emphasizes the need for scalable manufacturing processes, robust and reproducible clinical validation, and regulatory pathways capable of evolving as new evidence emerges. An integrated strategy of this kind is therefore essential for fully realizing the potential of real-time, multichannel biosensing platforms in both complex clinical diagnostics and point-of-care environments.

title: KATNAL2 dysfunction impairs microtubule dynamics and contributes to syndromic neurodevelopmental disease.
authors: Sonmezler, Ece; Hiz Kurul, Semra; Erez, Ozlem; Ekinci, Burcu; Yaras, Tutku; Binokay, Leman; Karakulah, Gokhan; Lochmuller, Hanns; Horvath, Rita; Yaramis, Ahmet; Cakan-Akdogan, Gulcin; Oktay, Yavuz
abstract: Katanins are microtubule-severing ATPases. Dysfunction of katanin subunits has been implicated in impaired neurogenesis, morphogenesis, and neuronal migration. Although heterozygous variants in KATNAL2 (katanin-like 2), a known autism-spectrum disorder (ASD) risk gene, have been reported in patients with ASD or other neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a homozygous missense variant in KATNAL2 (NM_001387690.1:c.1390T>C; p.(Ser464Pro)) in a pediatric patient presenting with severe global developmental delay, intellectual disability, infantile-onset epilepsy, and autistic features, extending the phenotypic spectrum beyond prior autism-focused associations. To elucidate the cellular mechanisms underlying KATNAL2 dysfunction, we established induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patient fibroblasts and differentiated them into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) for quantitative immunofluorescence analyses of microtubule organization, microtubule regulatory proteins, and transcriptome profiling. In parallel, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants and assessed body patterning and axonal projections using the transgenic nbt:dsRed line. Patient iPSC-derived NPCs showed impaired interphase microtubule network organization with increased angular standard deviation in directionality and mitotic/cytokinetic abnormalities, including abnormal positioning of the microtubule-rich cytokinetic midbody region. In vivo, CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants showed abnormal body patterning together with disorganized motor neuron and posterior lateral line nerve axonal projections. Together, these findings support KATNAL2 as a regulator of microtubule network organization and mitotic progression in human NPCs. Our data from patient-derived NPCs and a zebrafish model provide functional evidence linking the p.(Ser464Pro) variant to an expanded syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype.

title: Cas9 nickase-mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington's disease mouse model.
authors: Murillo, Alvaro; Alpaugh, Melanie; Peter Durairaj, Ruban Rex; Randall, Emma L; Larin, Meghan; Heraty, Laura; Aston, Alys N; Taylor, Alysha S; Monteys, Alex Mas; Stoberl, Nina; Heuchan, Aeverie E R; Aeschlimann, Pascale; Fears, Kyle; Landles, Christian; Osborne, Georgina F; Mangin, Antoine; Bhattacharyya, Soumyasree; Metzakopian, Emmanouil; Allen, Nicholas D; Puymirat, Jack; Bates, Gillian P; Davidson, Beverly L; Cicchetti, Francesca; Lelos, Mariah J; Dion, Vincent
abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington's disease (HD) patient-derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient-derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non-cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

title: Endogenous Protein Tagging in Postmitotic Neurons via Lentiviral and Adeno-associated Virus Delivery.
authors: Benedetti, Lorena; Yi, Hyun Ah; Wang, Lihua; Lippincott-Schwartz, Jennifer
abstract: This protocol describes a method for endogenous protein tagging in postmitotic primary neurons using homology-independent targeted integration (HITI), a CRISPR/Cas9-based approach that exploits non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Unlike homology-directed repair (HDR), HITI does not require cell division, making it uniquely suited for postmitotic neurons. SpCas9 is delivered by a replication-incompetent simian immunodeficiency lentiviral vector (pLenti SIV), while the sgRNA, donor tag cassette, and a fluorescent plasma membrane marker are co-packaged in a single AAV vector. The two vectors are co-delivered at DIV5, and endogenous tagging is assessed at DIV15-23. The workflow is illustrated using Junctophilin-3 (JPH3) tagged with mEmerald at its endogenous locus. Airyscan microscopy imaging of endogenously tagged JPH3 at native expression levels revealed its localization at endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane (ER-PM) contact sites and uncovered a periodic distribution of ER-PM junctions along the dendritic arbor, enabling identification of a previously unrecognized ladder-like organization of the ER in neuronal dendrites. Genomic integration of the tag is validated at both 5' and 3' junctions by next-generation sequencing. The protocol can be adapted to other neuronal proteins by redesigning the guide RNA and donor sequence, and supports fluorescent proteins as well as epitope and self-labeling tags. The plasma membrane marker can also be replaced with other fluorescent reporters or markers for intracellular organelles to assess infection efficiency and verify subcellular localization of the protein of interest. The full workflow takes 5-6 weeks. (c) 2026 The Author(s). Current Protocols published by Wiley Periodicals LLC. Protocols included in this article: Basic Protocol 1: sgRNA design and HITI donor vector cloning Basic Protocol 2: Primary rat neuron culture and viral co-transduction Basic Protocol 3: Live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged proteins Support Protocol 1: Production of lentiviral and AAV particles Support Protocol 2: Validation of knock-in by next-generation sequencing (NGS).

title: Dysregulation of macrophage colony stimulating factor in Paget's disease of bone.
authors: Azfer, Asim; Berg, Kathryn; Johnson, Katya; Thomson, Pippa; Wilson, James F; Wani, Sachin; Tang, Jonathan C Y; Albagha, Omar M E; Ralston, Stuart H
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine if common genetic variants at the chromosome 1p13 locus which predisposes to Paget's Disease of Bone (PDB) regulate Macrophage Colony stimulating factor (M-CSF) expression in bone cells and to determine if there is dysregulation of M-CSF in patients with PDB. METHODS: The regions surrounding single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) previously associated with PDB at a genome wide significant level were deleted in clones of MG63 osteoblast-like cells using CRISPR/Cas and levels of M-CSF mRNA and protein were evaluated in cells with and without deletions. Serum M-CSF was measured by ELISA in PDB and controls and values in patients were related to clinical features of PDB and biochemical markers of bone remodelling. RESULTS: Deletion of the region surrounding rs484959 increased expression of M-CSF mRNA by 1.31 fold [95%,1.04-1.58], p = 0.026 and M-CSF protein by 1.91 fold [1.25-2.57], p = 0.013, compared with control cells. Serum M-CSF was significantly elevated in PDB versus controls (mean +/- SD = 781.7 +/- 678 vs. 541 +/- 491 pg/mL, p < 0.001). Furthermore, M-CSF levels were associated with number of affected bones (p = 0.029), bodily pain assessed by SF-36 (p = 0.026) and biochemical markers of bone turnover. CONCLUSION: The rs484959 SNP is a regulatory variant which modulates M-CSF mRNA and protein expression in osteoblasts. Serum M-CSF is increased in PDB, is associated with pain, disease extent and biochemical markers of bone remodelling. This suggest that there is dysregulation of M-CSF in PDB and that this cytokine may play a role in pathogenesis of the disease.

title: Genomic Exploration of CRISPR-Cas Systems in Raoultella species: Diversity and Architecture.
authors: Abuden, Ahmed Velit; Colak, Cigdem Yilmaz
abstract: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein (CRISPR-Cas) systems are adaptive immune mechanisms that protect bacteria against invading mobile genetic elements. They can influence horizontal gene transfer, phage resistance, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics. Although these systems have been investigated in several Klebsiella species, information on historically defined Raoultella species remains limited. In this study, 103 complete genomes representing Raoultella species, currently placed within the broader Klebsiella lineage, were analyzed to characterize the distribution, architecture, and diversity of CRISPR-Cas systems. CRISPR-Cas loci were identified using CRISPRCasFinder and CRISPRone, followed by subtype classification, direct repeat and leader sequence analyses, spacer matching, Cas1-based phylogenetic analysis, and AMR determinant screening. Complete CRISPR-Cas systems were detected in 23 genomes, predominantly in R. ornithinolytica strains. All complete systems were chromosomally located, whereas plasmid-associated orphan CRISPR arrays were observed in selected R. ornithinolytica strains. Two major architectures were identified, with Type I-E being dominant and Type I-F restricted to fewer strains. Direct repeat analysis revealed six consensus sequences, while leader regions displayed conserved AT-rich motifs and strain-specific divergence. Spacer analyses suggested historical interactions with phages and plasmids, particularly mobile genetic elements associated with Klebsiella and other Enterobacteriaceae. Cas1 phylogeny showed subtype-dependent clustering, indicating that CRISPR-Cas evolution does not strictly follow core genome phylogeny. The coexistence of predicted CRISPR-Cas loci and AMR determinants indicates that the presence of these loci does not necessarily preclude the carriage of resistance determinants. Overall, this study expands current knowledge of CRISPR-Cas diversity among the analyzed Raoultella genomes and provides a genomic framework for future functional studies.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of FERMT3 reveals kindlin-3-independent neutrophil activity in LAD-III.
authors: Webbers, Steven D S; Rojas-Rodriguez, Felipe; Gankema, Angela A F; Khan, Imran; Geissler, Judy; Tool, Anton T J; Ollinger, Rupert; van Bruggen, Robin; van Dam, Teunis J P; Fagerholm, Suzanna C; Moser, Markus; Kuijpers, Taco W
abstract: Mutations in human FERMT3 (encoding kindlin-3 protein) impair beta2 integrin activity in neutrophils from patients with leukocyte adhesion deficiency III (LAD-III). Yet kindlin-3's contribution to neutrophil integrin affinity regulation and function remains unclear. Using CD34+ human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) differentiated into neutrophils, we investigated how CRISPR/Cas9-mediated kindlin-3 deletion affects neutrophil characteristics. CRISPR/Cas9 targeting FERMT3 resulted in an  approximately 80-bp deletion within exon 2, impairing protein production. FERMT3 KO neutrophils retained normal in vitro development and phenotype with similar surface marker expression, nuclear morphology, and expansion potential compared with untreated cultured neutrophils. Loss of kindlin-3 abolished zymosan-induced NADPH oxidase activity, recapitulating the ROS production defect of LAD-III neutrophils. However, although basal adhesion was reduced, stimulus-induced integrin activity remained largely intact. FERMT3 KO neutrophils retained fMLP-driven chemotaxis while showing impaired migration in response to C5a. Together, these findings show that disruption of kindlin-3 largely recapitulates the LAD-III phenotype while exerting some effector functions upon stimulation without intact kindlin-3.

title: Long Non-Coding RNAs: Key Regulators of Economic Traits in Livestock From Mechanisms to Breeding Applications.
authors: Khani, Keyvan; Harkinezhad, Mohammad Taher; Sepehri, Rahimeh
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as critical regulators of economically important traits in livestock, including growth, reproduction, disease resistance and product quality. Unlike protein-coding genes, lncRNAs orchestrate gene expression at epigenetic, transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels, acting as molecular switches, scaffolds, decoys, and competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs). This review synthesises current knowledge on key lncRNA mechanisms such as ceRNA networks, liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and RNA-targeting clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR-Cas13) screening alongside trait-specific case studies in muscle hypertrophy (Callipyge locus), embryonic development (lnc_2217 in goats) and fecundity (ceRNA networks in sheep and chickens). We highlight the integration of lncRNAs with Genome Wide Association Studies (GWAS) data, where over 90% of trait-associated variants reside in non-coding regions, and propose a practical roadmap for functional validation and incorporation of lncRNAs into genomic selection and breeding programs. Harnessing lncRNA biology supported by recent functional annotation of animal genomes (FAANG) epigenomic maps and CRISPR-Cas13 applications in livestock, researchers will accelerate genetic gain in growth rate, marbling score, litter size and disease resilience, marking a paradigm shift toward precision livestock breeding.

title: Microneedle-Assisted CRISPR Biosensing Platform for Presymptomatic Detection of Plant Diseases.
authors: Cao, Chulin; Jiang, Dong; Zhang, Xuemei; Pal, Tathagata; Liu, Zilong; Hadlock, Thomas; Neice, Jacob; Lu, Chang; Sun, Wujin; Vinatzer, Boris; Li, Song; Chen, Juhong
abstract: Presymptomatic diagnosis of tomato bacterial speck caused by Pseudomonas syringae requires rapid sample preparation and specific molecular readout. Although existing methods offer high reliability, their requirement for destructive sampling and centralized laboratory infrastructure severely limits their suitability for monitoring of plant diseases. We address this gap with a microneedle-assisted CRISPR platform that integrates on-leaf sample extraction with pathogen-specific detection. A hydrophilic and swelling polyvinyl alcohol microneedle patch mechanically bypasses the cuticle to extract pathogen-associated nucleic acids from the plant apoplast within minutes, and a CRISPR-based fluorescence assay reports the presence of plant pathogens with high detection specificity. The platform can detect unamplified pure target DNA at 0.16 nM, and as few as 103 copies following PCR preamplification. For bacterial suspensions, this platform can achieve a limit of detection at a concentration of 104 CFU/mL without amplification and 103 CFU/mL with PCR within 2 h. In inoculated plants, the platform reliably achieved presymptomatic detection of P. syringaeon day 3 postinoculation, preceding macroscopic necrotic specks by 24 h. These results establish a rapid and minimally invasive sampling-to-molecular biosensing pipeline that significantly accelerates conventional diagnostic turnaround and provides a versatile foundation for presymptomatic plant disease surveillance.

title: A role for eIF5A in translational control of stress-inducible proteins in multiple myeloma cell lines.
authors: Both, Demi; Derks, Ingrid A M; Vanleyssem, Raphael; Leclercq, Marine; El Hachem, Najla; Close, Pierre; Eldering, Eric; Haselager, Marco Vincent
abstract: Impaired protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) causes ER stress and activates the unfolded protein response (UPR), which can induce apoptosis during prolonged ER stress. ER stress is therapeutically targeted in plasma cell malignancies, such as multiple myeloma (MM), but these treatments remain noncurative, and UPR signaling in B-cell malignancies is incompletely understood. A targeted CRISPR-Cas9 screen in RPMI-8226 cells exposed to thapsigargin identified known ER stress regulators (XBP1, IRE1, and calreticulin) and the translation factor eIF5A (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5A), whose role in ER stress remains unclear. Competition assays showed that eIF5A depletion is detrimental under basal conditions but confers a proliferation advantage during thapsigargin treatment. Inducible EIF5A knockouts confirmed reduced sensitivity specifically to thapsigargin, loss of eIF5A had no or sensitizing effects on cell death induced by other ER stress drugs. Polysome profiling revealed that not general translation, but the translation of specific mRNA transcripts coding for UPR components and apoptotic proteins was affected by eIF5A depletion. Correspondingly, EIF5A KO cells showed reduced thapsigargin-induced UPR activation. In conclusion, these findings indicate that loss of eIF5A alters the stress response in MM cells.

title: Synthetic Biology Toolbox for Lactiplantibacillus plantarum: Engineering Next-Generation Probiotic Cell Factories.
authors: Su, Peiyun; Ma, Yulin; Nie, Qian; Yang, Tingxing; Wei, Tao
abstract: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum has emerged as a promising synthetic biology chassis owing to its food-grade safety, probiotic properties, and adaptability to the gastrointestinal tract.
