Its engineering potential has expanded rapidly in live biotherapeutics, functional foods, biosensors, and animal health. However, its broader application is still limited by the lack of standardized genetic parts, versatile engineering tools, and industrially compatible chassis. This review summarizes recent advances in the synthetic biology toolbox of L. plantarum, including expression elements, genome engineering strategies, and representative applications. Particular emphasis is placed on the development of genetic components, conventional and CRISPR-based engineering technologies, and their applications in medicine, food biotechnology, biosensing, and animal nutrition. Current challenges and future opportunities, including standardized genetic parts, precision genome engineering, AI-assisted strain design, and high-performance chassis development, are also discussed. This review provides a comprehensive framework for developing next-generation programmable probiotic cell factories based on L. plantarum.

title: Arbovirus diagnostics: from conventional methods to emerging technologies-a chikungunya virus-centric review.
authors: Zhu, Yongqing; Li, Jiaxuan; Mao, Haiyan; Chen, Keda; Li, Jianhua
abstract: Arboviruses remain an important global health concern because of their expanding distribution, diverse transmission patterns, and the challenges associated with accurate and timely diagnosis. This review is centered on Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) as a representative model, focusing on diagnostic strategies across different stages of infection and the key diagnostic pitfalls that affect CHIKV detection in co-circulation settings. In this review, we summarize current laboratory-based approaches for CHIKV detection and differential diagnosis, including virus isolation, antigen detection, nucleic acid amplification and serological assays, with discussion of their applications, strengths and limitations. We further review recent developments in emerging diagnostic technologies, including next-generation sequencing, CRISPR-based detection methods, aptamer-based recognition systems, biosensors, and point-of-care testing platforms, highlighting their potential advantages and current limitations. Comparative examples involving dengue virus (DENV) and Zika virus (ZIKV) are discussed specifically to illustrate cross-reactivity and misclassification risks relevant to CHIKV diagnosis. Particular attention is given to persistent issues affecting diagnostic accuracy and practical implementation, including serological cross-reactivity among co-circulating arboviruses and the challenges of translating advanced technologies into accessible tools for field and resource-limited settings. Overall, this review summarizes progress in CHIKV-relevant diagnostics and outlines future opportunities for developing more reliable, rapid, and widely applicable detection strategies.

title: Drosophila Appl loss disrupts proteins in mitochondrial oxidative and glycosylation pathways conserved in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Smith, Zachary M; Vonhoff, Fernando J
abstract: The physiological functions of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) remain unclear due to genetic redundancy and complex phenotypes. For decades, Drosophila amyloid precursor protein-like (Appl) research has relied on Appl (d), a presumed null allele generated by irradiation. Here, we show that Appl (d) contains complex chromosomal rearrangements and background mutations confounding the interpretation of gene function. To address this, we created a precise CRISPR toolkit, including a clean null and a reporter allele. Deep proteomic profiling reveals that true Appl loss affects proteins associated with N-linked glycosylation, mitochondrial, and metabolic functions in a distinct signature from the background of Appl (d). This conserved metabolic signature mirrors alterations in human patients and mouse Alzheimer's models and is associated with disrupted sleep and locomotion in flies. Our findings correct the genetic understanding of Appl, establishing it as a conserved regulator of metabolic balance essential for neuronal function.

title: Targeted protein degradation via chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-mediated antigen endocytosis in T cells.
authors: Wang, Youguang; He, Zihao; Yin, Na; Peng, Min
abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) holds significant therapeutic potential over conventional biologics. However, existing platforms are constrained by their reliance on host protein degradation machinery and limited durability, rendering them inadequate for chronic diseases requiring sustained treatment. Here, we constructed a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) incorporating the TNFR1 ectodomain as the antigen-binding domain (TNFR1T cells) and used CRISPR-mediated knockout of BCOR and ZC3H12A to generate persistent TNFR1T(IF) cells. TNF binding, endocytosis, and degradation were assessed in vitro by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence. Immunocompetent syngeneic, Tnf (-/-), and hTNF-tg rheumatoid arthritis (RA) mice (n = 4-9) were used in vivo to evaluate engraftment, persistence, and disease severity (clinical scoring and grip strength), with adalimumab (Humira, 1 or 10 mg/kg) as a comparator. Safety was assessed by intravenous Listeria monocytogenes challenge (1 x 10(4) colony-forming units [CFU], n = 6) and Thy1.1-based depletion (0.25 mg, n = 3). We found that TNFR1T cells specifically bound, endocytosed, and degraded soluble TNF in vitro. Without lymphodepletion preconditioning, TNFR1T(IF) cells expanded and persisted for one year in immunocompetent mice. A single infusion into hTNF-tg mice reduced serum hTNF to near wild-type levels, preventing and treating all stages of RA with superior efficacy and durability than the repeated high-dose adalimumab. Antibacterial defense remained uncompromised, and anti-Thy1.1 antibody efficiently eliminated TNFR1T(IF) cells in vivo. This approach extends CAR-T cell targeting from cellular antigens to soluble extracellular proteins, establishing a host-machinery-independent, durable cellular-TPD platform for chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Golgi-derived COPI vesicles fuel the biogenesis of coronavirus replication organelles.
authors: Wang, Zhaohuan; Su, Xinyue; Gong, Kaoyi; Yang, Zixiao; Liu, Shu-Rui; Zheng, Bi-Rong; Shi, Keda; Ye, Yu; Zhou, Xinrong; Pan, Jian; Guo, Deyin; Hou, Panpan; Li, Chun-Mei
abstract: Positive-strand RNA viruses remodel host endomembranes to form replication organelles (ROs). However, the membrane sources for coronavirus double-membrane vesicle (DMV) biogenesis remain unclear. Here, we used proteomic, genetic, pharmacological, and imaging approaches to identify the central membrane supply route for DMV formation. APEX2-based proximity proteomics first identified candidate pathways, followed by functional validation using siRNA knockdown, CRISPR/Cas9 editing, and Golgicide A (GCA) inhibition. DMV formation and viral RNA synthesis were assessed by electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, and qRT-PCR. Golgi-DMV association was analyzed by sucrose gradient fractionation and confocal imaging. In vivo relevance was evaluated in C57BL/6J mice infected with mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) and treated with GCA (intraperitoneal, 50 mg/kg; n = 4-5 per group). We showed that coronaviruses hijack the host GBF1-ARF1-COPI machinery to redirect Golgi-derived membranes to viral replication sites for DMV formation and expansion. Disruption of this pathway markedly impairs viral RNA synthesis, DMV biogenesis, and replication of multiple coronaviruses, including severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Pharmacological inhibition of Golgi-specific Brefeldin A-resistance factor 1 (GBF1) suppressed viral replication and pathology in vivo. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized Golgi-derived membrane supply route for coronavirus ROs and highlight the GBF1-ARF1-COPI pathway as a potential host-directed target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapies.

title: CRISPR Technology Applied to the Analysis of Antibiotic Resistance Genes in the Environment.
authors: Yan, Jiayin; Yuan, Xiaoxian; Zhu, Zijun; Li, Zhuang; Wu, Minghuo; Liu, Jing; Zhu, Lizhong; Feng, Wei
abstract: Environmental transmission of antibiotic resistance poses a risk to human health. Understanding the behavior and health risks of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in the environment requires accurate nucleic acid analyses. Technical challenges remain in the sequencing of ARGs in low abundance relative to total environmental DNA and in on-site analysis. CRISPR technology has been applied to the characterization and monitoring of ARGs in various environmental media. For sequencing of ARGs, CRISPR technology has enabled the enrichment of ARGs present in the environment at a very low abundance. Using CRISPR/Cas9 systems with a pool of guide RNAs (gRNAs) could simultaneously enrich a large panel of ARGs in one environmental sample before sequencing for good coverage and reading depth. CRISPR/Cas9 also enabled targeted long-read sequencing for understanding the genetic context of low-abundance ARGs. CRISPR-based rapid detection has the potential for on-site analysis. Current applications include the analysis of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) and ARGs in the air and the urban water cycle. CRISPR technology is also useful for differentiating single-nucleotide mutations between antibiotic-susceptible and -resistant variants. Rapid detection of antibiotics together with ARGs is also possible with the use of aptamers that specifically bind to antibiotics.

title: Prospects for improvement of coffee quality and stress resilience using genomic and genetic resources.
authors: Rajkumar, Mohan Singh; Laughlin, David A; Echeverria-Beirute, Fabian; Norton, Roger D; Mandadi, Kranthi K
abstract: Coffee is one of the most widely traded and highly valuable commodities, known for its pleasant flavor, unique aroma, and caffeine's stimulatory effect. Beyond their sensory perceptions, coffee beans are rich in several bioactive compounds and biomolecules beneficial to human health. Only two species, Coffea arabica and Coffea canephora, account for nearly all the world's coffee production, owing to their high quality and commercial value. Despite low variability and narrow genetic diversity, coffee plant genomic resources are underrepresented. Recent advancements in high-throughput sequencing technologies and reduced costs have enabled the development of various crop genomic resources, including coffee. In this review, we systematically cataloged the genetic and genomic resources available to the coffee research community, including reference genomes, DNA polymorphisms, transcriptomes, and non-coding regulatory transcripts. Furthermore, we highlighted promising candidate genes that may have functional roles in improving coffee quality, yield, and stress resilience. These resources provide an excellent knowledge base for studying genetic factors influencing coffee quality and agronomic traits, and for developing new breeding and CRISPR-based biotechnological strategies for coffee improvement.

title: Context-dependent oxytocin receptor signaling: from molecular architecture to transcript-level receptor engineering.
authors: Jurek, Benjamin; Winter, Julia J; Quintana, Daniel S
abstract: The oxytocin receptor (OXTR) is a G protein-coupled receptor that integrates neuroendocrine release, cellular signaling, and behavioral effects across species. Despite extensive research, the mechanistic basis underlying variability in oxytocin's effects remains incompletely understood. This review synthesizes recent advances in OXTR biology and focuses on three biological sources of signaling heterogeneity: variation in receptor sequence and structure, epigenetic and cell-state-dependent regulation, and temporal patterns of receptor activation. It examines targeted manipulation of receptor transcripts as an experimental strategy for testing intracellular mechanisms with behavioral outcomes. Mechanistic studies show that subtle structural changes, including single nucleotide polymorphisms, can bias intracellular signaling toward distinct pathways. Chronic receptor activation induces transcriptional and post-transcriptional reprogramming that can invert behavioral outcomes relative to acute stimulation. Intracellular signaling converges on core pathways, including Ca(2+)-dependent cascades, MAPK signaling, and transcriptional regulators such as CREB and MEF2A, which together shape gene expression, protein synthesis, and cellular morphology. Human studies reveal substantial variability in oxytocin effects, consistent with context-dependent signaling and limited control over intracellular pathways. These observations illustrate the challenge of linking receptor-level processes to behavioral phenotypes and underscore the importance of mechanistic approaches to OXTR signaling. Within this framework, GapmeR-mediated manipulation of OXTR transcripts and CRISPR-based genetic or epigenetic approaches are discussed as preclinical research strategies for testing receptor-level mechanisms. These strategies complement classical biased-ligand-pharmacology and support a model in which OXTR functions as a context-sensitive signaling hub, determined by receptor structure, activation history, and intracellular state.

title: Precision Editing of Cyclophilin A Generates Cyclosporine and Voclosporin Resistant Cellular Therapies.
authors: Wobma, Holly; Calderon, Francesca Alvarez; Dong, Jiayi; Omdahl, Kayleigh; Rui, Xianliang; Palato, Elisa J Rojas; Bermea, Rene S; Albanese, Alexandre; Wachter, Franziska; Winschel, Marlana; Michaelis, Katherine A; Burns, William A; Selig, Gillian; Cagnin, Lorenzo; Tkachev, Victor; Prockop, Susan E; Nigrovic, Peter A; Blazar, Bruce R; Gerdemann, Ulrike; Kean, Leslie S
abstract: Recipients of allogeneic transplants or patients with autoimmune disease require immune suppression, often with calcineurin inhibitors. There is an expanding repertoire of immune effector cell therapies, including CD19 CAR-T cells and viral-specific T cells, deployed in these patients; however, ongoing calcineurin inhibition may be detrimental to cell therapy function. We developed a CRISPR/Cas9-based approach to engineer dual cyclosporine/voclosporin resistant cell therapies by targeting PPIA (encoding cyclophilin A), a critical binding partner for both drugs. Because Cyclophilin A has homeostatic functions in T cells, a complete knock-out is detrimental to cell viability. We thus targeted its C-terminus, disrupting drug binding while leaving the majority of the protein intact. C-terminal editing was stable throughout expansion and preserved Cyclophilin A expression. Edited CD19 CAR-T cells retained effector function in the presence of cyclosporine and voclosporin, including proliferation, cytokine production, and target cell killing, resulting in improved survival in murine models of CD19+ leukemia. Edited CMV-specific T cells also demonstrated preserved antigen-specific proliferation and cytokine production in the presence of these drugs. C-terminal editing of Cyclophilin A offers a promising avenue for developing next-generation cell therapies for patients receiving calcineurin inhibitors.

title: Resistance mechanisms and translational bottlenecks in CAR-T cell therapy for pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia: a perspective.
authors: Xu, JiLi; Sui, Lili; Yang, Wenzhe; Xu, Li; Shan, Mingliang
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable remission rates exceeding 80% in relapsed/refractory pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), yet 40-50% of patients eventually relapse within the first year. This therapeutic ceiling is not a single failure mode but the convergence of at least four interrelated layers: loss of CAR-T persistence, antigen escape driven by CD19 splicing variants and lineage switch, CAR-T cell-intrinsic exhaustion from chronic tonic signaling, and an immunosuppressive bone marrow microenvironment that actively extinguishes effector function. Our systematic analysis of 226 pediatric-eligible CAR-T trials shows that 95.6% are Phase I-II, 3.5% (8/226) are registered as Phase III/IV, and 58 of 102 completed trials (56.9%) had no outcome recorded in the source database. In this Perspective, we synthesize the molecular mechanisms of CAR-T resistance, contextualize them within the current clinical trial landscape, and critically evaluate emerging engineering strategies-from dual-targeting and armored CAR architectures to CRISPR-edited allogeneic products and in vivo mRNA delivery. We argue that progress depends on both smarter receptor design and structural reforms in trial design, outcome transparency and global collaboration.

title: Parkinson's disease LRRK2 mutations dysregulate iron homeostasis and promote oxidative stress and ferroptosis in human neurons and astrocytes.
authors: Mamais, Adamantios; Batchelor, Richard D Jr; Chairmandurai, Aravindraja; Ladd, Thomas B; Shute, Austin J; Subrahmanian, Nitya; Maio, Nunziata; Vulpe, Christopher D; LaVoie, Matthew J
abstract: BACKGROUND: Iron accumulation is a hallmark of sporadic and familial Parkinson's disease (PD) and correlates with clinical motor symptom severity. The biochemical mechanisms driving iron dyshomeostasis in PD brain and whether these are early or late events in the neurodegenerative process remain unknown. Nigral iron levels in LRRK2-PD patients have been reported to be even higher than in idiopathic PD, and greater in non-manifesting LRRK2 carriers than controls, suggesting that iron accumulation precedes clinical onset in LRRK2-associated PD. However, the cells affected and mechanisms governing iron dyshomeostasis in PD remain unclear. METHODS: Here, we investigated multiple independent measures of iron homeostasis in human iPSCs and iPSC-derived models, including glutamatergic and dopaminergic neurons, and astrocytes, carrying pathogenic LRRK2 mutations. High-content and super-resolution microscopy of iron-specific probes and ICP-MS were used to determine iron content and distribution across different cell types and LRRK2 genotypes. Upstream effectors and downstream consequences of iron dyshomeostasis, including oxidative stress and ferroptosis-related phenotypes were also examined. RESULTS: Pathogenic heterozygous LRRK2 mutations were associated with altered iron homeostasis across multiple human cell models. Lysosomal ferrous iron was consistently elevated across iPSC-derived glutamatergic neurons, dopaminergic neurons, and astrocytes carrying LRRK2 mutations and these phenotypes were reduced by varying degrees following treatment with the selective LRRK2 inhibitor, MLi-2. Importantly, we show that lipid peroxidation and ROS levels are elevated in isogenic LRRK2 mutant neurons, while iron chelation or MLi-2 reduced LRRK2-dependent ROS damage. In addition, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of Rab8a produced overlapping iron-related phenotypes, while exogenous Rab8a expression normalized lysosomal iron levels in R1441C LRRK2 iPSCs, supporting a contributory role for Rab8a-dependent trafficking in these effects. CONCLUSIONS: Together, our findings show that pathogenic LRRK2 mutations converge on disrupted iron homeostasis across multiple human neural cell types, including dopaminergic neurons, and support a link between LRRK2 signaling, lysosomal iron dysregulation and ferroptosis-related stress.

title: Metabolic plasticity underlies ferroptosis resistance driven by mutant p53 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
authors: Celesia, Adriana; Piccoli, Filippo; Wang, Tian; Hu, Yushu; Danzi, Federica; Aparo, Antonino; Cisterna, Barbara; Pacchiana, Raffaella; Poles, Maria; Scupoli, Maria Teresa; Luchini, Claudio; Ugel, Stefano; Donadelli, Massimo; Fiore, Alessandra
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy characterized by late diagnosis, rapid progression, and resistance to conventional therapies. Mutations in the tumor suppressor gene TP53 are prevalent in this cancer and have been associated with gain-of-function activities that promote tumor survival. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability. However, the influence of mutant p53 on ferroptosis susceptibility remains poorly understood. METHODS: We employed isogenic pancreatic cancer cell models, including CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TP53 Knockout (TP53-KO) and transient overexpression of common mutant TP53 variants, to examine ferroptosis sensitivity. Cell viability, reactive oxygen species accumulation, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial integrity, and metabolic profiling were assessed following treatment with ferroptosis inducers. Transcriptional changes were analysed by RNA sequencing, and functional contributions of glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were evaluated using metabolic flux assays. Pharmacological reactivation of wild-type p53 was tested in combination with ferroptosis inducers in vitro and in orthotopic murine models. RESULTS: Deletion of mutant TP53 sensitized pancreatic cancer cells to ferroptosis, accompanied by increased oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Mutant TP53 expression preserved mitochondrial integrity and sustained bioenergetic flexibility under ferroptotic stress. Transcriptomic analyses revealed a multi-layered adaptive program, including upregulation of antioxidant and metabolic genes, and activation of PI3K-AKT signaling, which is associated to a selective glycolytic shift to maintain ATP levels. Functional modulation confirmed that glucose supplementation enhanced, whereas glycolytic inhibition impaired, survival under ferroptotic conditions in mutant TP53-expressing cells, but not in TP53-KO cells. Pharmacological reactivation of wild-type p53 disrupted this adaptive network, abrogating glycolytic reprogramming and significantly increasing ferroptotic cell death both in vitro and in vivo. CONCLUSIONS: Mutant p53 orchestrates transcriptional and metabolic plasticity that confers ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic cancer. Reactivating wild-type p53 in combination with ferroptosis induction overcomes this resistance, highlighting a therapeutically actionable vulnerability and supporting the development of combinatorial strategies for this aggressive malignancy.

title: Periplocin targets low density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 and protects against osteoarthritis.
authors: Liu, Jincheng; Fu, Qingyang; Li, Chunlin; Gao, Kun; Sun, Mengsi; Xu, Mingyu; Chen, Junfei; Zhai, Xu; Zhang, Wencan; Li, Le; Xu, Wanlong; Liu, Yang; Wu, Xinhui; Si, Haipeng; Wang, Kaidi
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is recognized as the most common chronic joint disease, characterized primarily by the degeneration of articular cartilage. Through screening a natural product library, we identified periplocin as a candidate agent capable of promoting chondrocyte anabolism. Periplocin, a cardiotonic steroid isolated from Periploca forrestii, has been proven to be involved in antiinflammatory responses. However, the role and mechanism of periplocin in OA have not been confirmed. This study aims to explore the biological role and potential of periplocin in chondrocyte metabolism and OA treatment. A drug library was screened to identify candidate components that promote chondrocyte anabolism. In vitro experiments showed that periplocin could promote chondrocyte anabolism, enhance chondrogenic differentiation, and inhibit inflammation-induced chondrocyte catabolism. Using a surgically induced destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) OA mice model, combined with histological staining, micro-computed tomography, and behavioral assessments, we confirmed that periplocin alleviated cartilage degeneration, suppressed osteophyte formation, improved motor function, and relieved OA-related pain in DMM mice. Molecular docking, Drug Affinity Responsive Target Stability (DARTS) assay, Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA), and Molecular dynamic (MD) simulation identified LRP4 as the key target of periplocin, with Asp812 serving as its critical binding site. With the help of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to knock out low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4) in C28I2 and generate chondrocyte-specific Lrp4 knockout mice, the dependence of periplocin-mediated regulation of chondrocyte function on LRP4 was verified. This study not only provides new insights into understanding the chondroprotective effect of periplocin targeting LRP4 and its underlying mechanism but also offers experimental evidence for the use of periplocin as a potential disease-modifying OA drug (DMOAD) in OA treatment.

title: Targeting neuronal FKBP5 attenuates mechanical allodynia by suppressing NF-kappaB-mediated neuroinflammation in an NTG-induced chronic migraine mouse model.
authors: Peng, Cheng; Fan, Tianhua; Zhou, Gang; Zhao, Min; Wang, Tianxiao; Cao, Tingting; Zheng, Jingyuan; Guo, Zijuan; Liang, Guining; Zhang, Zhenchang; Guan, Ji-Song; Wang, Yonggang
journal: The journal of headache and pain
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic migraine (CM) is a debilitating neurological disorder characterized by persistent trigeminovascular sensitization and neuroinflammation. While FK506-binding protein 51 (FKBP5) modulates spinal neuroinflammation in chronic pain, its specific role in trigeminovascular nociceptive processing and CM pathogenesis remains largely unknown. METHODS: We used a nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced CM mouse model. Following RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) of total RNA isolated from trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) tissue lysates, target expression was validated via reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), Western blotting, and immunofluorescence. To establish causality, we used a neuron-specific CRISPR-Cas9 editing system for Fkbp5 knockout within the TNC, alongside pharmacological interventions using the specific FKBP5 antagonist SAFit2 and the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kappaB) inhibitor PDTC. Migraine-like behaviors were evaluated using von Frey filaments, coupled with biochemical analyses of NF-kappaB cascade activation and trigeminovascular neuroinflammation. RESULTS: RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence consistently confirmed a marked upregulation of Fkbp5 mRNA and FKBP5 protein in the TNC of NTG-treated mice, predominantly localized to neurons. Concurrently, significant microglial and astrocytic activation was observed in the TNC. Both neuron-specific Fkbp5 knockout and pharmacological inhibition with SAFit2 significantly attenuated NTG-induced periorbital and hind paw mechanical allodynia. Furthermore, FKBP5 deficiency blunted the NTG-triggered phosphorylation of p65 and IkappaBalpha, effectively suppressing the downstream release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), as well as the upregulation of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and c-Fos. Crucially, targeted blockade of the NF-kappaB cascade with PDTC recapitulated the protective behavioral and biochemical effects of FKBP5 deficiency. CONCLUSIONS: We demonstrate that neuronal FKBP5 is significantly associated with CM pathogenesis. FKBP5 sustains mechanical allodynia by activating the NF-kappaB-mediated neuroinflammatory cascade. Consequently, targeting FKBP5 represents a promising therapeutic strategy for CM.

title: Interacting climatic, environmental, biologic and socio-economic drivers of the global dengue expansion.
authors: Semenza, Jan C
abstract: Dengue is the most rapidly expanding mosquito-borne viral disease worldwide. The worst year on record was 2024, with over 100 countries reporting 14.4 million cases and over 11,000 deaths. Since then, and up to August 2026, another 7.4 million cases and over 5000 deaths have been reported. The region of the Americas was impacted the most, followed by South-East Asia and the Western Pacific. Both the spread of dengue viruses (DENV) and their primary vectors, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, are driven by several factors. Globalization has accelerated vector dispersal, particularly through international trade and transportation networks. The movement of desiccation-resistant eggs in used-vehicle tyres and the inadvertent transport of adult mosquitoes via trucks and passenger vehicles have enabled the establishment of vector populations in previously uncolonized regions. Human mobility and unplanned urbanization further contribute to dengue emergence by introducing DENV into susceptible populations where competent vectors circulate. Climate change has enhanced dengue transmission potential by altering temperature and rainfall patterns that influence mosquito survival, reproduction, biting behaviour and viral replication. Containing or even reversing this global dengue expansion will require a complementary set of interventions that rely on proven and novel control strategies, including sterile insect techniques, Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, virus-resistant mosquito strains through CRISPR-Cas9 gene drive, vaccines, antiviral drug prophylaxis and urban interventions that eliminate Aedes habitats. Building climate-resilient urban environments through sustainable development to minimize the urban heat island effect and advancing climate-informed early warning systems are long-term strategies for effective dengue control.

title: Identification and validation of NCOA5-ZCCHC3/FGF22 axis as a prognostic marker in lung adenocarcinoma migration and invasion.
authors: Yu, Yiran; Jin, Wen; Chaogetu, Erdun; Zhang, Xiaoli; Liu, Xi; Gao, Yahan; Li, Feng; Su, Rila
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), the most common subtype of lung cancer, is associated with substantial global mortality. Nuclear receptor coactivator 5 (NCOA5) has been implicated in several malignancies; however, its functional role and regulatory mechanisms in LUAD remain largely unknown. In this study, NCOA5 expression was evaluated in 94 paired LUAD and adjacent tissues using immunohistochemistry, RT-PCR, and Western blotting. Functional analyses were conducted using shRNA knockdown, CRISPR-mediated knockout, and overexpression models to assess the effects of NCOA5 on LUAD cell proliferation, migration, invasion, apoptosis, cell cycle progression, and organoid formation. Xenograft models were used to validate tumorigenicity in vivo. IP-MS and co-immunoprecipitation identified NCOA5-interacting proteins, while ChIP-seq and dual-luciferase assays interrogated downstream transcriptional regulation. NCOA5 was significantly upregulated in LUAD tissues and associated with advanced stage, poor differentiation, and reduced overall survival, serving as an independent prognostic factor (P < .040). NCOA5 knockdown inhibited LUAD cell proliferation, migration, invasion, induced G0/G1 arrest, promoted apoptosis, reduced organoid formation, and suppressed xenograft growth, whereas NCOA5 overexpression produced the opposite effects. Among 39 candidate interacting proteins identified by IP-MS, ZCCHC3 was validated as a direct NCOA5-binding partner. ZCCHC3 depletion phenocopied NCOA5 loss and reversed NCOA5-induced proliferation, migration, invasion, and colony formation, supporting a functional NCOA5-ZCCHC3 interaction. ChIP-seq analysis identified fibroblast growth factor 22 (FGF22) as a direct transcriptional target of NCOA5. FGF22 was markedly downregulated in LUAD tissues and higher FGF22 expression was associated with improved patient survival. NCOA5 suppressed FGF22 transcription, while NCOA5 inhibition increased FGF22 expression. Functionally, FGF22 knockdown enhanced LUAD aggressiveness, whereas FGF22 restoration abrogated the oncogenic effects of NCOA5 in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify a previously unrecognized NCOA5-ZCCHC3/FGF22 axis that drives LUAD progression and provide new mechanistic insight into the role of NCOA5 in LUAD biology.

title: The application progress of detection technology for Bacillus cereus in food: Challenges, innovations and future prospects.
authors: Zhang, Yuhang; Zhang, Xin; Zheng, Haiying; Wang, Haifeng; Yu, Ming; Jia, Weijuan; Jia, Zelin; Cui, Jiayu; Xiong, Huisheng; Ma, Yujie; Wang, Xueli
abstract: Food safety is a key issue of global public health. As a foodborne pathogen - Bacillus cereus (B. cereus), it is widely distributed in nature and can cause diseases in both humans and animals. The rapid detection of B. cereus is of great significance for the prevention and control of such diseases. This article provides a detailed overview of the development of B. cereus detection techniques in food, transitioning from traditional methods to a series of current technologies such as immunology, molecular biology and MALDI-TOF-MS. The principles, advantages and disadvantages of various detection techniques, as well as their application progress, were outlined. Furthermore, the application and advantages of combining different techniques in the detection of B. cereus in food were demonstrated. The CRISPR/Cas system possesses the characteristics of high specificity, high sensitivity and ease of operation, and shows great potential in the field of foodborne pathogen detection. This article also explains that the combination of CRISPR/Cas technology with RPA, LFA and AI technologies can further enhance the detection rate and accuracy. The aforementioned technology can enable the early detection and prevention of B. cereus in food, ensuring food safety and preventing the outbreak of foodborne diseases. This article has certain reference value in the research on the detection techniques of B. cereus and other foodborne pathogens in food, and provides strong support for safeguarding food safety and maintaining human health.

title: Next-generation CRISPR-based molecular diagnostics for veterinary parasitology: From laboratory innovation to one health surveillance.
authors: Basit, Abdul; Hanif, Muhammad
abstract: Veterinary parasitic diseases remain a major threat to livestock production, companion animal health, wildlife conservation, and public health worldwide. Conventional diagnostic methods, including microscopy, serology, and culture-based techniques, often suffer from limited sensitivity, poor specificity, prolonged turnaround time, and dependence on specialized laboratory facilities. Recent advances in Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-based diagnostics have introduced highly sensitive, rapid, and field-deployable platforms for parasite detection. This review critically summarizes the principles and recent applications of CRISPR/Cas12, Cas13, and emerging Cas14-based diagnostic approaches in veterinary parasitology, covering protozoan, helminthic, and arthropod-borne parasites. It further compares CRISPR platforms and discusses their integration with isothermal amplification, lateral flow assays, fluorescence detection, and portable biosensors to improve diagnostic performance. Moreover, current challenges, including sample preparation, assay standardization, multiplex detection, regulatory approval, and commercialization, are highlighted. Finally, future perspectives on amplification-free CRISPR assays, artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostics, and point-of-care platforms are discussed. By providing a translational perspective from laboratory innovation to field application, this review highlights the potential of CRISPR-based diagnostics to transform veterinary parasite surveillance and disease control.

title: Interbacterial competition triggers stress-induced CRISPR immunity against bacteriophages.
authors: Custodio, Rafael; Martignoni, Maria M; Zhu, Wenlong; Kuske, Rachel; Alseth, Ellinor O; Moura-Alves, Pedro; Brown, Sam P; Westra, Edze R
abstract: Bacteria-phage interactions are often studied in relatively simple experimental systems involving a single bacterial strain infected by a single phage.(1) In natural environments, however, bacteria typically inhabit complex multispecies communities where species compete for limited resources and ecological niches.(2)(,)(3)(,)(4) Recent studies show that the microbial community context can have profound effects on the evolution of phage resistance.(5) For example, Pseudomonas aeruginosa evolves phage resistance primarily through receptor loss when grown in isolation but switches to CRISPR-based immunity in the presence of bacterial competitors.(6)(,)(7) Previous work showed that interspecies competition can favor CRISPR-immune bacteria over surface mutants after phage resistance has evolved.(6) However, it remains unknown whether competition also alters the initial generation of CRISPR immunity by changing CRISPR-Cas expression and spacer acquisition before selection among resistance phenotypes occurs. Here, we show that interbacterial competition can trigger CRISPR-Cas activation and adaptation in P. aeruginosa. When co-cultured with Acinetobacter baumannii, P. aeruginosa exhibited markedly increased expression of CRISPR-Cas genes and a higher frequency of new spacer acquisition, whereas no such induction occurred in monoculture or mixed communities lacking A. baumannii. This upregulation was associated with markers of DNA damage and stress signaling, indicating that competition-induced stress primes the bacterial adaptive immune response. These findings identify interbacterial antagonism as an ecological and physiological trigger for CRISPR activation, linking competitive interactions to enhanced antiphage defense. More broadly, our results suggest that bacteria sense and respond to competitive stress in complex microbial communities by increasing the generation of more adapted genotypes.

title: Evolution of the arbuscular mycorrhizal regulatory network through differential GRAS gene retention and protein interaction in land plants.
authors: Wu, Wen-Shen; Zhao, Peng; Zeng, Zhen; Li, Xiao-Tong; Wu, Ping; Ding, Qian; Feng, Xing-Yu; Zhang, Yan-Mei; Hu, Shuai-Ya; Xue, Jia-Yu; Wang, Qiang; Liu, Yang; Chen, Jian-Qun; Shao, Zhu-Qing
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Plants rely on an ancient genetic "toolkit" to establish arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis (AMS) with fungal partners. However, the symbiotic outcomes vary among AMS hosts, indicating divergence in downstream transcriptional reprogramming after the perception of symbiotic signals. To uncover the cross-species variation of the AMS regulatory network, we traced the evolutionary trajectory of the GRAS gene family, which encodes the major group of transcription factors in AMS regulation. Phylogenetic analysis of the GRAS family across land plants placed known symbiotic GRAS members within 12 anciently diverged lineages, with multiple lineages showing pronounced gene loss in nonmycorrhizal plants. This pattern pointed to three additional GRAS lineages as candidates for AMS regulation. Given that tomato harbors single-copy, AMS-induced genes in these lineages, we selected it for functional validation. CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis, combined with detailed phenotyping of fungal colonization and arbuscule morphology, and transcriptome profiling of mutant roots, confirmed that all three tomato genes are individually required for AMS development, designated Symbiosis-Required GRAS (SRG) 1 to 3. Large-scale phylogenomic analysis and protein interaction assays (by yeast two-hybrid and bimolecular fluorescence complementation) further showed that both the repertoire and interaction networks of symbiotic GRAS members vary among AMS hosts. In summary, together with 12 previously characterized lineages, the three SRGs identified in this study bring the total number of GRAS lineages with known symbiotic members across land plants to fifteen. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the symbiotic GRAS network has been dynamically reshaped by gene loss and rewiring of protein interactions during land plant evolution.

title: Revisiting Ehrlich carcinoma in the era of precision oncology: bridging classical models with modern systems biology.
authors: Manjunath, Varshini; Nayak, Rachana Rajesh; Bhujanga, Ananth Koushik; Ramesh, Arpitha Maraliga; Santhekadur, Prasanna Kumar
abstract: Ehrlich carcinoma (EC) and its ascitic form, Ehrlich ascites carcinoma (EAC), are among the oldest and most widely used experimental tumor models in cancer research. Although they have traditionally been used for anticancer drug screening, their potential to address broader aspects of aggressive tumor biology has received comparatively less attention. EC/EAC exhibits several characteristics associated with advanced malignancy, including rapid tumor growth, angiogenesis, immune dysregulation, metabolic changes, therapeutic resistance, and complex interactions between the tumor and host. These features make EC/EAC a useful complementary model for studying different aspects of tumor progression. However, research using these models has largely focused on transcriptional changes and individual signalling pathways, while post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms remain less explored. In particular, the role of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), a major component of microRNA-mediated gene regulation, is still poorly understood in EC/EAC. In this review, we discuss the major limitations of current EC/EAC research, including the limited use of multi-omics approaches, single-cell and spatial analyses, functional genomics, immune checkpoint profiling, and integrated systems-level studies. We further discuss how incorporating RISC-centered regulatory networks with emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based studies, spatial transcriptomics, and metabolic profiling could provide deeper mechanistic insights and improve the translational value of these models. Bringing together the strengths of this established tumor model with contemporary approaches in cancer biology could help reposition EC/EAC as a relevant and versatile platform for studying tumor progression and therapeutic responses.

title: CCKBR signalling controls human definitive endoderm specification and pancreatic lineage differentiation.
authors: Saber, Lama; Kozawa, Kei; Karampelias, Christos; Jing, Changying; Jaki, Jessica; Akgun Canan, Melis; Sterr, Michael; Rodrigues Pereira, Osvaldo; Czarnecki, Oliver; Korbutt, Gregory S; Pepper, Andrew R; Moya, Noel; Burtscher, Ingo; Lickert, Heiko; Bakhti, Mostafa
abstract: AIMS/HYPOTHESIS: Paracrine signalling by hormone-producing endocrine cells potentially influences pancreatic development, but this feedback regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the roles of gastrin (GAST), cholecystokinin (CCK) and their receptor cholecystokinin B receptor (CCKBR) during human pancreatic development. METHODS: Human iPSCs were differentiated stepwise into definitive endoderm and then the pancreatic endocrine lineage. To assess CCKBR function, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to generate CCKBR-knockout iPSC lines. We profiled transcriptional states by bulk and single-cell RNA-seq with computational analyses, and complemented these with biochemical assays, flow cytometry (FACS) and confocal microscopy. RESULTS: CCKBR expression peaked during definitive endoderm formation and progressively declined during differentiation, remaining detectable in pancreatic progenitors but largely absent from the endocrine lineage. By contrast, GAST and CCK were expressed only transiently during pancreatic progenitor and endocrine lineage formation. Pharmacological activation/inhibition and genetic knockout implicated CCKBR signalling during definitive endoderm formation. Consistently, bulk RNA-seq indicated that CCKBR deletion triggered ectodermal- and mesodermal-associated transcriptional programs and diminished pancreatic lineage specification. During pancreatic induction and lineage formation, sustained CCKBR activation with GAST or CCK attenuated endocrinogenesis and promoted epithelial structure formation. Further analysis revealed the emergence of a pancreatic ductal-like cell formation under prolonged CCKBR stimulation. CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION: This study provides mechanistic evidence that the GAST/CCK-CCKBR axis is functionally important during human endoderm and pancreas development. This pathway is repeatedly required during in vitro pluripotent stem cell differentiation, regulating germ-layer formation as well as ductal vs endocrine fate decisions. These findings support the optimisation of pancreatic differentiation protocols and inform future studies on whether this axis contributes to human pancreas development and disease.

title: Nano Delivery Systems for In Vivo CRISPR/Cas-Based Gene Therapy: From Vectors to Clinical Outcomes.
authors: Chen, Ruhan; Zhou, Haimei; Wu, Qinjie; Gong, Changyang
abstract: As a powerful gene-editing tool, the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas) system features simple construction, precise targeting, and higher editing efficiency, bringing prospects of radical cures for numerous critical illnesses at the genomic level. To date, ex vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies represented by Casgevy have achieved significant clinical advances. Nevertheless, cumbersome operational workflows and prohibitive treatment costs severely hinder their widespread clinical accessibility. In contrast, in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies stand out with convenient administration procedures and reduced overall costs, endowing them with enormous translational potential. Although it holds great promise, the clinical translation of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies remains hampered by a number of factors. Among those multiple obstacles restricting the clinical translation of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies, delivery systems constitute the core bottleneck dominating in vivo editing efficiency and therapeutic potency. Centered on delivery platforms for in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies, this review systematically summarizes prevailing in vivo CRISPR/Cas nano delivery systems, recapitulates relevant preclinical and clinical outcomes, discusses translational hurdles, and prospects the evolution of next-generation delivery systems, aiming to facilitate further development of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies.

title: Multiplexed CRISPRi reveals a transcriptional switch between KLF activators and repressors in the maturing neocortex.
authors: Kirk, Ryan W; Sun, Liwei; Xiao, Ruixuan; Clark, Erin A; Nelson, Sacha B
abstract: A critical phase of mammalian brain development takes place after birth. Neurons of the mouse neocortex undergo dramatic changes in their morphology, physiology, and synaptic connections during the first postnatal month, while properties of immature neurons, such as the capacity for robust axon outgrowth, are lost. The genetic and epigenetic programs controlling prenatal development are well studied, but our understanding of the transcriptional mechanisms that regulate postnatal neuronal maturation is comparatively lacking. By integrating chromatin accessibility and gene expression data from two subtypes of neocortical pyramidal neurons in the neonatal and maturing brain, we predicted a role for the Kruppel-like factor (KLF) family of transcription factors in the developmental regulation of neonatally expressed genes. Using a multiplexed CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown strategy, we found that a shift in expression from KLF activators (Klf6, Klf7) to repressors (Klf9, Klf13) during early postnatal development functions as a transcriptional 'switch' to first activate, then repress a set of shared targets with cytoskeletal functions including Tubb2b and Dpysl3. We demonstrate that this switch is buffered by redundancy between KLF paralogs, which our multiplexed CRISPRi strategy is equipped to overcome and study. Our results indicate that competition between activators and repressors within the KLF family regulates a conserved component of the postnatal maturation program that may underlie the loss of intrinsic axon growth in maturing neurons. This could facilitate the transition from axon growth to synaptic refinement required to stabilize mature circuits.

title: Genome editing beyond transgenes: DNA-free technologies in crop improvement.
authors: Senthilkumar, Roshini; Palaniswamy, Rakshana; Rathnasamy, Sakthi Ambothi; Rajagopalan, Veera Ranjani; Eswaran, Kokiladevi; Sengodan, Radhamani; Govindasamy, Ashok Kumar; Muthurajan, Raveendran; Kanagarajan, Selvaraju; Manickam, Sudha
abstract: Conventional and transgenic approaches to crop improvement are increasingly constrained by biosafety concerns, stringent regulatory frameworks, and limited public acceptance, necessitating new precision breeding methods. DNA-free genome editing using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach has emerged as a transformative approach that enables precise, targeted genetic modifications without the stable integration of a foreign gene (transgene). This strategy transiently introduces CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, or in vitro transcribed mRNA, into plant cells. This review focuses primarily on CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing and its applications in crop improvement. After targeted genome cleavage, the editing elements are rapidly degraded, leaving only the desired genomic modification and resulting in plants indistinguishable from those developed through conventional breeding. To achieve targeted, DNA-free genome editing, researchers have developed numerous molecular platforms and delivery systems, such as protoplast transfection, biolistic bombardment, nanoparticle-based systems, and emerging pollen- and meristem-targeted systems, for major crop species. Researchers have successfully enhanced several notable traits, including disease and pest resistance, nutritional quality, abiotic stress tolerance, and agronomic performance, in cereals, vegetables, oilseeds, and perennial crops. Recent advancements, including base editing, prime editing, and multiplex gene editing, are further expanding the precision, efficiency, and scope of DNA-free genome editing. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing offers a route to crop improvement that avoids stable transgene integration, though its wider deployment depends on progress in regeneration, molecular validation, and regulatory convergence.

title: Paper integrated aptamer-CRISPR sensing enables multiplexed small-molecule sensing in a low-cost device.
authors: Sen, Anindita; Bock, Douglas James; Foster, Tegan; Fleming, Rachel; Hodgkiss, Justin M
abstract: CRISPR/Cas12a-based diagnostics achieved attomolar sensitivity for nucleic acid detection, yet their extension to small-molecule targets remains constrained by the need for solution-phase aptasensor-CRISPR coupling and laboratory infrastructure incompatible with resource-limited settings. Here we report a Paper-integrated Aptamer-Cas12a Sensing platform (PACSense) in which the complete aptasensor-CRISPR/Cas12a signal transduction cascade is air-dried within a paper substrate, enabling a one-pot, amplification-free small-molecule detection workflow that is initiated by sample addition alone. Two orthogonal sensing modalities are demonstrated: first, a signal-OFF bivalent aptamer channel for adenosine 5'-triphosphate (ATP), achieving solution- and paper-phase limits of detection of 336 nM and 446 nM respectively, and second, a signal-ON complementary strand-displacement channel for cocaine, which to our knowledge represents the first coupling of the NC195 aptamer to CRISPR/Cas12a sensing, with solution- and paper-phase LODs of 0.605 microM and 16.15 microM respectively. Both channels are operated simultaneously on a single multiplexed paper chip with a cross-channel geometry that routes sample passively to four spatially distinct reaction zones, enabling independent and simultaneous detection confirmed by fluorescence imaging under a 495 nm blue LED. Air-dried chips retain 76% of initial fluorescence signal after 30 days of ambient storage without cold chain, with a 93% signal retention measured from the functional equilibration baseline. The complete assay workflow is completed within 20 minutes using a reusable sodium acetate hand warmer for incubation and a 3D-printed smartphone-compatible reader, designed to align with ASSURED criteria for point-of-care diagnostics. PACSense establishes paper-integrated aptasensor-CRISPR sensing as a viable route to multiplexed, laboratory-instrument-free small-molecule diagnostics at the point of need.

title: The emerging role of CRISPR-Cas systems in helicobacter pylori and the gut microbiota as regulators of gastrointestinal cancer risk.
authors: Bhatti, Muqadas; Thalib, Husna Irfan; Tayyebah, Ammarah; Zobairi, Aleena; Dahan, Nada; Hassan, Fatma E
abstract: Gastrointestinal cancers contribute to 26% of global cancer incidence and 35% of deaths, with major contributors such as Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection, gut dysbiosis, and lifestyle factors. CRISPR-Cas systems, while best known for their role in bacterial adaptive immunity, also shape bacterial physiology and host-microbe interactions, yet their influence on gastrointestinal carcinogenesis is poorly understood. This review brings together current evidence on the functions of CRISPR-Cas systems in H. pylori and the gut microbiota, highlighting their potential impact on cancer risk, diagnostics, and therapy. Key themes synthesized in this review include their role in bacterial immunity, contributions to microbial imbalance and virulence regulation, and emerging applications in cancer detection, microbiome modulation, and precision oncology. CRISPR profiles are being explored as biomarkers, while engineered systems show promise in targeted editing, phage therapy, and highly sensitive diagnostic platforms such as Cas12a-based assays. Despite this progress, challenges remain, including the risk of off-target effects, technical difficulties in detecting CRISPR signatures within complex microbial communities, and a lack of longitudinal human studies. Overall, CRISPR-Cas systems are emerging as natural regulators of microbial ecology and as engineered tools with potential applications in gastrointestinal cancer research, diagnostics, and precision microbiome interventions.

title: Biofilm-associated genes in Staphylococcus aureus: role in chronic infections and therapeutic challenges.
authors: Azhar, Mohammad Asim; Mir, Tanveer Ahmad; Ahmed, Sana; Assiri, Abdullah M; Broering, Dieter C
abstract: One of the major contributors to persistent healthcare and community-associated infections is S. aureus, which has a remarkable ability to form biofilms that protect it against the host immune system and antimicrobial therapy. In recent years, it has become clear that biofilm development is a highly orchestrated and dynamic process, controlled by complex genetic networks, transcriptional regulators, two-component systems (TCSs), and environmental signals. The present review covers the molecular mechanisms involved in the initiation, maturation, maintenance, and dispersal of biofilms in general, and in particular, the coordinated functions of adhesins, the icaADBC operon, components of the extracellular matrix (ECM), global regulators (agr, sarA, and sigB), and two-component regulatory systems, as well as emerging insights from transcriptomic studies on biofilm adaptation. We then review the roles of these regulatory pathways in metabolic heterogeneity, antibiotic tolerance, immune evasion, and persistence in clinically relevant biofilm-associated infections, including infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, catheter-associated infection, and diabetic foot infection. The review further outlines the latest developments in antibiofilm therapeutics, including matrix-degrading enzymes, quorum-sensing inhibitors, antimicrobial peptides, bacteriophage-based therapeutics, lysins, nitric oxide donors, nanoparticle-assisted therapeutics, and CRISPR-Cas-based antimicrobials. Incorporating molecular regulation into infection-specific pathogenesis and emerging therapeutic strategies, this review offers a new perspective on the biology of S. aureus biofilms and highlights opportunities to develop mechanism-based interventions to combat chronic biofilm-associated infections.

title: The m(6)A regulatory network in plant stress adaptation: from mechanisms to breeding potential.
authors: Zhang, Jun; Jiang, Sainan; Yang, Jie; Zou, Jingjing; Xing, Wen; Li, Zeqing
abstract: N(6)-methyladenosine (m(6)A) is the most abundant internal modification of eukaryotic mRNA and is dynamically regulated by three classes of proteins: writers, erasers, and readers. Writers deposit methylation marks, erasers confer reversibility, and readers translate these signals into specific regulatory outcomes, collectively modulating mRNA stability, translation efficiency, splicing, and polyadenylation, thereby influencing plant stress adaptation. Studies across diverse plant species have revealed both conserved principles and species-specific variations in this regulatory network. Technological advances, such as methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (MeRIP-seq) and nanopore direct RNA sequencing, have enabled transcriptome-wide m(6)A profiling. However, functional validation of m(6)A modification in most crops remains limited to a few model species and controlled environments, and their practical breeding potential requires systematic evaluation. This review systematically summarizes the functions of m(6)A writers, erasers, and readers in crop stress responses, synthesizes the regulatory patterns at the levels of mRNA stability, translation efficiency, and splicing and discusses m(6)A-based breeding strategies and their current bottlenecks, providing a theoretical reference for stress-resilient crop breeding. CRISPR/dCas13-based targeted modification systems, together with methyltransferase overexpression or demethylase knockout strategies, have demonstrated breeding potential in several crops, although field-level validation remains limited. Future research needs to prioritize how the writer-eraser-reader network achieves stress-specific regulation without causing pleiotropic developmental defects, how m(6)A pattern differs between single and combined stresses, and how natural variation in m(6)A regulatory gene can be exploited for breeding. On this basis, establishing causal links between specific m(6)A sites and agronomic phenotypes, while integrating multi-omics approaches and precision editing technologies, will be essential to translate epitranscriptomic knowledge into crop improvement.

title: Molecular mechanisms and application potential of MYC2 transcription factor-mediated plant stress responses.
authors: Yang, Liu-Qing; Shu, Si-Lin; Zhang, Yong-Hao; Huang, Gang
abstract: Plant adaptation to drought, salinity, temperature extremes, pathogens, and herbivorous insects depends on coordinated hormone signalling, transcriptional control, and metabolic reprogramming. The jasmonic acid (JA) pathway is a major regulator of defence and the growth-defence trade-off, and the bHLH transcription factor MYC2 is a central node in JA output. Mechanistically, MYC2 is controlled through demonstrated protein-protein interactions with JAZ repressors, MED25, and selected transcriptional or chromatin regulators; it binds G-box-related cis-elements to regulate specific promoters, whereas many reported links to LOX/AOS, CBF, and antioxidant pathways are transcriptional or pathway-level rather than physical interactions. This integrative narrative review compares MYC2 orthologues across species, distinguishes MYC2-specific functions from those shared with MYC3/MYC4 or other clade IIIe bHLHs, and organises beneficial and detrimental stress phenotypes around pathogen lifestyle, target-gene polarity, tissue and developmental context, paralogue redundancy, and experimental design. We integrate genome-wide DNA-binding, transcriptomic, metabolomic, and protein-level studies, and critically evaluate demonstrated versus prospective applications of CRISPR/Cas genome editing. The synthesis identifies regulatory strategies that may exploit MYC2 networks whilst limiting growth, defence, and quality trade-offs.

title: Saponin conjugation improves p-CRISPR delivery by polyethylenimine modified carbon dots.
authors: Kelkawi, Ali Hamad Abd; Kamrani Mousavi, Seyede Mahtab; Hasanzadeh, Akbar; Saeedi, Sara; Kheiri Yeganeh Azar, Behjat; Kamali, Babak; Hooshmand, Seyyed Emad; Rastgoo Korande, Mohadese; Hamblin, Michael R; Gaaib, Jawdat N; Karimi, Mahdi
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Non-toxic and efficient delivery platforms are important for gene editing applications. In this report, the preparation of saponin-conjugated low molecular weight polyethyleneimine (PEI(1.8kDa)) modified carbon dots (CD-PEI-Sap) is described. METHODS: Polyethyleneimine modified carbon dots (CD-PEI(1.8kDa)), were synthesized by one-step microwave-mediated pyrolysis of citric acid (CA) and PEI(1.8kDa) to produce non-toxic fluorescent particles. When saponin was added at this stage followed by microwave treatment a completely clear solution of CD-PEI-Sap was produced. RESULTS: These 80 nm nanoparticle vectors not only transfected green fluorescent protein plasmid (p-GFP) (3 kb) with 60% expression in human embryonic kidney (HEK 293T) cells, and>60% in hard to transfect human breast adenocarcinoma cells (MCF7), but could also transfect a large clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat plasmid (p-CRISPR) with 5-fold higher efficiency (50%) than the gold standard reagent, branched PEI MWt 25 kDa (PEI(25kDa)). Moreover, the CD-PEI-Sap system produced good transfection with a low concentration of p-CRISPR and in the presence of 30% fetal bovine serum (FBS). CONCLUSION: This system demonstrated efficient transfection and serum resistance, making it a promising tool for future gene editing research.

title: Advancing cardiac xenotransplantation: overcoming challenges and ethical considerations for clinical integration.
authors: Abdelrehim, Ahmed A; Hurst, Daniel J; Gray, W Hampton; Sorabella, Robert; Padilla, Luz A
abstract: Advanced heart failure affects over 6 million adults in the United States alone. Orthotopic heart transplantation remains the definitive treatment, with over 90% one-year survival and meaningful gains in functional status and quality of life. The therapy is, however, constrained by an intractable supply problem. For decades, xenotransplantation (XTx), the transplantation of organs across species, has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, though for most of that time it remained a theoretical aspiration. With the discovery of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, improved immunosuppressive strategies, and refined preclinical models, the field has accelerated at an unprecedented pace. Multi-gene-edited porcine donors have survived for more than 200 days in orthotopic non-human primate models, and two compassionate-use pig-to-human cardiac transplants at the University of Maryland (2022 and 2023) demonstrated some feasibility for clinical cardiac XTx for the first time. In May 2026, the FDA granted clearance under an investigational new drug application to allow the EXPRESS study, the first prospective clinical trial of a gene-edited porcine heart, to proceed. In this perspective, we discuss the ethical, regulatory, and equity considerations that remain as decisive barriers to clinical integration and may shape how this therapy is introduced along the remaining immunologic and virologic challenges. We outline what we regard as the near-term priorities: defining the antibody targets that drive xenograft rejection, standardizing virologic surveillance, candidate selection and outcome benchmarking, and building access patterns with embedded distributive justice from the outset of its implementation.

title: From delivery to integration: CRISPR-mediated large insert gene editing in primary human T cells.
authors: Buttle, Ben; Verdon, Daniel; Sheppard, Hilary M
abstract: Large insert gene editing in ex vivo, primary human T cells represents an important approach for engineering next-generation cellular immunotherapies. While CRISPR-based editing is well-established for small genetic modifications, large insert knock-in remains a technical bottleneck. This review examines current strategies for achieving efficient, precise and safe integration of large genetic elements. We compare delivery methods for CRISPR components, highlighting electroporation of Cas9 ribonucleoproteins as the most efficient but often cytotoxic approach; emerging alternatives such as cell-penetrating peptides and lipid nanoparticles offer improved cell viability at the expense of editing efficiency. The influence of genomic locus selection, guide RNA design and chromatin context on editing outcomes, as well as the role of homology-directed repair (HDR) template design is evaluated. Various template formats-including linear double- and single-stranded DNA, plasmids, circular single-stranded (css) DNA and recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV)-are assessed for their efficiency, toxicity and risk of off-target integration. Where possible, cross-study normalisation is used to enable meaningful comparisons. rAAV templates consistently achieve the highest insertion rates but come with concerns regarding cost, size limitations and insertional mutagenesis, whereas non-viral approaches such as cssDNA templates show promise. Additionally, we review the use of small-molecule modulators to enhance HDR efficiency, noting trade-offs between improved insertion rates and potential genomic instability. Overall, successful large insert editing requires balancing of editing efficiency, cell viability and genomic safety considerations. Continued optimisation of delivery systems, template design and repair pathway modulation will be critical for advancing scalable and clinically viable T-cell therapies.

title: Targeting phenol-soluble modulins: eco-friendly theragnostic strategies against Staphylococcus aureus biofilms.
authors: Chakraborty, Avijit; De, Anuvab; Sharma, Shubham; Prakash Dwivedi, Shashi; Bhattacharya, Debasmita; Lahiri, Dibyajit; Nag, Moupriya; Singh Gill, Harjot; Pandit, Soumya
abstract: The growing resistance to antibiotics by Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a global health threat. Traditional antibiotics act on the viability of bacteria, whereas new ones are now increasingly targeting virulence factors. Phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) are essential virulence factors that play important roles in inflammation, neutrophil lysis, cytotoxicity and biofilm formation. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were used for literature search of articles published between 2010 and 2026. Green-synthesized metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been found to be capable of altering these mechanisms by inducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, membrane damage, and by interfering with the quorum-sensing mechanism of the bacteria, along with inhibiting the Agr system. Optimization of NP-based interventions can be supported by multi-omics approaches such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Other potential methods of targeted PSM pathway and Agr pathway suppression are also available, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and dCas9, but there are delivery difficulties. The potential use of combining nanotechnology, gene editing, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology could allow for development of more advanced anti-virulence strategies against S. aureus infections targeted at PSM.

title: Advancing assisted reproductive technology in Africa: a narrative review on the promising role of molecular biology and molecular techniques.
authors: Kyei, Foster; Napo, Clement; Nabawo, Collins; Asante, Emmanuel Opoku; Nyarko, Benjamin; Adu, Isaac Kofi; Aidoo, Cara Obenewaa; Essien, Victoria; Barnie, Prince Amoah; Ansah, Emmanuel Owusu; Fosu, Kwadwo
abstract: Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) has significantly improved fertility outcomes globally, yet its full potential remains underutilized. In Africa, persistent barriers including high costs, limited access, inadequate infrastructure, lack of awareness, and sociocultural and ethical concerns impedes its utility. This review explores the promising role of molecular biology and advanced molecular techniques in overcoming these challenges and advancing ART on the continent. Techniques such as preimplantation genetic testing (PGT), non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT), and single-cell RNA sequencing offer opportunities to enhance embryo selection, minimize genetic and epigenetic risks, and improve pregnancy success rates. Furthermore, innovations like biomarker discovery, liquid biopsy, and genomic screening can personalize treatment strategies and improve reproductive outcomes. We also provide a narrative on the progress made in expanding ART services, improving affordability through low-cost protocols, and building local expertise through training and collaborations. While challenges persist, especially in regulation and access to ART, the integration of molecular innovations in a phased manner has the potential to transform ART if implemented within appropriate infrastructural, ethical, and policy frameworks. This review underscores the need for sustained investment, policy reform, and interdisciplinary collaboration to bridge existing gaps and ensure that ART technologies are accessible, safe, and effective for all individuals and couples affected by infertility in the region.

title: Efficient genome editing in ASC-derived porcine lung organoids via GFP-guided enrichment.
authors: Jeon, Beom-Jin; Moon, Byeongho; Jang, Hyun-Sung; Kwon, Dong-Hyeok; Jeon, Young-Lim; Eom, Kyeong-Hyeon; Choi, Jae-Yoon; Kim, Young-Chai; Jang, Goo
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adult stem cell-derived organoids are invaluable tools for disease modeling and translational medicine owing to their tissue-specific correspondence. However, their complex three-dimensional structure and low genome-editing efficiency have posed significant challenges for functional genetic studies. To address these limitations, this study aimed to establish porcine lung organoid (PLOs) and to develop a robust, high-efficiency genome-editing platform by leveraging the high physiological and anatomical similarity between pigs and humans. METHODS: PLOs were derived from lung tissues and characterized by immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry analysis. To enhance genome-editing efficiency using CRISPR/Cas9 and prime editing, a GFP-guided enrichment strategy was used by co-targeting a GFP transgene and endogenous loci, followed by the selection of GFP-negative organoids. Clonal expansion from single organoids was performed to generate genetically homogenous lines. Genetic modifications were validated through cDNA sequencing and western blot analysis. Structural integrity was assessed using AlphaFold2 modeling, and functional changes were evaluated using the forskolin-induced swelling assay. RESULTS: The established PLOs exhibited sustained self-renewal capacity and expression of surfactant protein C alongside both proximal epithelial and mesenchymal markers, reflecting a composite lung organoid identity. GFP-guided enrichment significantly enriched edited cells; the mutation ratio in the GFP-negative group was significantly higher than that in the GFP-positive group. This system successfully generated fully gene-edited clones with high genetic homogeneity, and effectively enriched for precisely edited organoids, even when applying complex modalities such as prime editing. CONCLUSIONS: The PLOs and genome-editing platform developed in this study provide a powerful resource for translational medicine. By enabling precise genetic manipulation in a model that closely mimics human lung physiology, this system offers an essential platform for recapitulating human lung pathologies, studying zoonotic infectious diseases, and validating the efficacy of gene therapies.

title: Targeting the mitochondrial complex I subunit NDUFS2 potentiates FLT3 inhibition in acute myeloid leukaemia with FLT3 internal tandem duplication.
authors: Tong, Xiqin; Chen, Guopeng; Pan, Yuzhe; Chen, Yanling; Tan, Yuxin; Jiang, Hongqiang; Wang, Qian; Ma, Linlu; Li, Ruihang; Liang, Yuxing; Liu, Xiaoyan; Zhou, Fuling
abstract: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with FLT3 internal tandem duplication (FLT3-ITD) frequently relapses after FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy, highlighting the need to define mechanisms of drug tolerance. Here, we identify the mitochondrial complex I core subunit NDUFS2 as a determinant of FLT3 TKI tolerance in FLT3-ITD AML. A metabolism-focused CRISPR-Cas9 sensitiser screen, integrated with transcriptomic profiling of gilteritinib-resistant cells and primary samples, identified NDUFS2 as upregulated in acquired resistance and preferentially expressed in FLT3-ITD AML. NDUFS2 knockdown impaired complex I activity, oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, thereby promoting apoptosis and sensitising FLT3-ITD AML cells to gilteritinib. Pharmacologic complex I inhibition with IACS-010759 similarly enhanced gilteritinib activity in FLT3-ITD AML cell lines and primary FLT3-ITD samples, activated AMPK-PERK-ATF4-CHOP stress signalling, promoted apoptosis, and reduced leukaemia burden in a patient-derived xenograft model. Genetic NDUFS2 knockdown also prolonged survival in a xenograft model. A preliminary murine safety assessment showed no overt toxicity under the tested short-term dosing schedule. These findings identify NDUFS2-dependent complex I activity as an adaptive metabolic dependency supporting FLT3 inhibitor tolerance and provide mechanistic insight for further preclinical evaluation.

title: Cryo-Engineered DNA Cryogels with Interconnected Macroporous Architectures for Enhanced Mass Transfer and Ultrasensitive cTnI Detection via an Integrated Microfluidic Platform.
authors: Jiang, Meng; Wang, Bing; Geng, Xinran; Sun, Xinghan; Wang, Jingyi; Xu, Kejia; Li, Nan; Zhao, Jinjin; Jia, Licong; Niu, Lingmei
abstract: Cardiac Troponin I (cTnI) is a definitive clinical biomarker for the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Thus, its rapid and precise quantification is of paramount significance for clinical intervention. DNA hydrogels represent a premier choice for constructing rapid detection platforms due to their excellent target responsiveness. However, the severe mass transfer resistance inherent in the dense nanoscale networks of conventional hydrogels restricts the transport of biological macromolecules and signal probes, thereby limiting detection efficiency and sensitivity. In this study, an intelligent colorimetric sensing platform was developed by coupling a CRISPR-Cas12a system with a cryo-engineered DNA cryogel, integrated with a microfluidic chip and machine learning algorithms. Compared with conventional DNA hydrogels, the cryo-engineered DNA cryogel features an interconnected macroporous architecture that significantly reduces mass transfer resistance, thereby enabling bidirectional transport enhancement of CRISPR-nanozymes and accelerating signal response. Under optimized conditions, coupled with a microfluidic system and machine learning, the sensing platform exhibited a robust linear relationship within the range of 0.003-10.00 ng mL-1, with an ultralow detection limit of 0.011 pg mL-1. This strategy pioneers a novel pathway for rapid home screening of cTnI, establishing a critical paradigm for high-performance sensing platforms through material structural modulation and multidisciplinary integration.

title: The MBW complex regulates floral volatiles in petunia: transcriptional repressor EOBV is a MYB component of the complex.
authors: Skaliter, Oded; Cohen, Raz; Leor-Librach, Ehud; Shor, Ekaterina; Rudich, Ori; Edelbaum, Orit; Shklarman, Elena; Masci, Tania; Vainstein, Alexander
abstract: Anthocyanin biosynthesis in Petunia is regulated by the bHLH AN1 and the WDR protein AN11, which together with interchangeable MYBs form the MYB-bHLH-WDR (MBW) complex. As they share the same biosynthetic pathway, anthocyanins are interlinked with phenylalanine-derived volatiles. However, involvement of the MBW complex in regulating these floral volatiles has not been demonstrated. TRV-based suppression of either AN1 or AN11 led to an increase in volatile emission, indicating that they are involved in negative regulation of this trait. Yeast two-hybrid and in-planta pairwise and three-way protein-interaction assays revealed that EMISSION OF BENZENOIDS V (EOBV) is a component of the MBW complex. Headspace and internal pool analyses of flowers from eobv-knockout lines, generated using a viral-based CRISPR/Cas9 system, revealed that EOBV fine-tunes volatile production: phenylpropenes and vanillin levels increased while those of benzenoids and phenylpropanoid-related compounds decreased. Accordingly, transcript levels of C4H2, directing carbon flux to phenylpropenes and vanillin production, and ADT3 were significantly elevated in eobv-knockout flowers, along with decreases in PAAS and BSMT. Moreover, in-planta promoter activity assays in petunia flowers further demonstrated that C4H2 is negatively transcriptionally regulated by EOBV. In addition to its involvement in volatile production, EOBV is heat-responsive and affects flower development under high-temperature conditions by mitigating the reduction in flower size. EOBV's participation in the MBW complex that regulates volatiles and anthocyanins reveals an intriguing molecular link between these showy traits and flower development.

title: A Novel CCMS Model Reveals a Critical Intronic Sequence in the Snrpb Gene that is Required for Normal Development.
authors: Beauchamp, Marie-Claude; Alam, Sabrina; Moore, Joshua; White, Harriet; Jerome-Majewska, Loydie A
abstract: Pathogenic variants in SNRPB, a common core spliceosomal factor, cause Cerebrocostomandibular Syndrome (CCMS). Most CCMS-associated variants result in increased inclusion of a PTC-containing alternative exon 2 (AE2). Using CRISPR/Cas9 we generated two mutant mice that carried a 46bp or a 61bp deletion upstream of Snrpb AE2. Mice and embryos carrying the 46bp deletion are normal. Whereas heterozygous and homozygous mutant embryos carrying the 61bp deletion (Delta61) exhibited smaller heads, micrognathia, malformations in the bones of the craniofacial region and ribs, and reduced survival, at low penetrance. Embryos homozygous for Delta61 showed a tendency towards increased inclusion of AE2 and reduced levels of Snrpb. In addition, this deletion increased the penetrance and severity of defects in Snrpbncc and Snrpbmes mutant embryos. Our findings indicate that this intronic region is important for SNRPB regulation in mice and should be investigated in CCMS patients that do not carry mutations in SNRPB coding exons.

title: Nucleic acid technologies in crustacean disease management: Diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance.
authors: Dinakarkumar, Yuvaraj; Abdulrajak, Rizwan; Gnanaprasad, Sowmiya; Radhakrishnan, Muthezhilan
abstract: Crustacean aquaculture, particularly shrimp, crab, and lobster production, contributes around US$10 billion annually to the global food supply but remains highly vulnerable to viral and bacterial diseases.
