Pathogens such as White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV), Yellow Head Virus (YHV), Taura Syndrome Virus (TSV), and Vibrio species continue to cause substantial economic losses, and conventional management based on visual inspection, histopathology, and antimicrobial treatment is often slow and insensitive. This review examines how nucleic acid technologies are reshaping diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance in crustacean health management. Molecular diagnostic platforms including PCR, quantitative PCR, reverse transcription PCR, loop mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, and multiplex assays allow rapid, sensitive, and specific detection of pathogens, often before clinical signs appear. RNA interference shows strong therapeutic promise against viral pathogens, with experimental studies reporting 40 to 80% reductions in cumulative mortality, although stability, dosing, delivery, and production cost continue to limit commercial use. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) and Cas (CRISPR-associated) has emerged as a powerful platform for functional genomics, immune gene characterisation, and the future development of disease resistant strains, though application in crustaceans remains largely proof of concept. Environmental DNA and molecular biosurveillance enable early pathogen detection through water and sediment sampling, supporting proactive biosecurity and precision aquaculture. Persistent barriers include scalability, infrastructure gaps in producing regions, regulatory uncertainty, and public acceptance. Future progress will rely on improved delivery systems, expanded crustacean genomic resources, and integration of molecular tools with digital farm management to deliver sustainable disease control.

title: Generation and characterization of a barley strigolactone mutant collection: from plant architecture to drought stress response.
authors: Fontana, Irene M; Buchcik, Weronika; Kumlehn, Jochen; Melzer, Michael; Hensel, Goetz; Daszkowska-Golec, Agata; Marzec, Marek
abstract: Strigolactones (SLs) are known to regulate shoot architecture and to be involved in plant responses to environmental stress, whereas their specific contributions to drought adaptation in barley remain incompletely defined. In this study, we analysed transcriptional, hormonal, and physiological responses to water deficit in barley SL mutants affected in early biosynthesis (Hvd10 and Hvd17), late biosynthesis (Hvmax1a), or signalling (Hvd14). The Hvd10, Hvd17, and Hvd14 mutants exhibited the typical high-tillering phenotype of SL deficiency, whereas Hvmax1a displayed characteristics similar to the wild type (WT), indicating functional differences within the SL biosynthetic pathway. Transcriptome analysis showed a clear overlap in gene expression among the high-tillering SL mutants under both control and drought conditions. We also used computational methods to identify potential transcription factors that might regulate SL-dependent gene expression. A drought experiment showed that SL mutants exhibited reduced biomass, relative water content, and photosynthetic efficiency, with the most pronounced effects observed in the high-tillering lines. Drought also activated the abscisic acid (ABA) pathway in all genotypes, with particularly high accumulation of ABA metabolites in the high-tillering SL mutants. Notably, Hvmax1a resembled the mutant-like metabolic profile, despite maintaining a wild-type-like architecture. Taken together, these results provide new insights into the roles of SL pathway components in drought responses and highlight functional differences among individual genes influencing both plant architecture and stress-related transcriptional programmes. Furthermore, the mutants generated in this study using Cas9-mediated genome editing represent a valuable genetic collection for future research into SL-mediated development and stress responses in barley.

title: Creation of fragrant wheat by targeted mutagenesis of either BADH1 or both BADH1 and BADH2 using CRISPR/Cas9.
authors: Luo, Jinman; Yan, Lei; Li, Jingying; Zhang, Chen; Li, Shaoya; He, Yubing; Guo, Yan; Xia, Lanqin
abstract: Editing TaBADH1 alone or TaBADH1 and TaBADH2 via CRISPR/Cas9 produced fragrant wheat with up to 11.24-fold higher 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline than the wild type without yield penalty, revealing asymmetric functional redundancy between these two genes and providing elite germplasm for wheat quality improvement.

title: Patient-Derived Organoids in Functional Precision Oncology: Tumor Modeling, Drug-Response Prediction, and Clinical Translation.
authors: Jabri, Abdullah; Alsharif, Mohamed; Mhannayeh, Abdulaziz; Taftafa, Bader; Sibai, Dania; Elsalti, Abdulrahman; Alsharif, Raghad; Mir, Tanveer Ahmad; Khan, Mohammed Imran; Salma, Jahan; Yaqinuddin, Ahmed
abstract: Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) have emerged as an effective experimental platform for bridging the long-standing gap between traditional in vitro cancer models and the biological complexity of actual tumors. These three-dimensional cultures (3D), derived directly from patient tissues, preserve essential architectural, genomic, and phenotypic characteristics of their tumors of origin, enabling more accurate modeling of tumor heterogeneity and disease evolution. Over the last decade, rapid methodological advances in organoid culture systems, extracellular matrices (ECMs), and growth factor optimization have facilitated the establishment of organoid models for a wide range of malignancies and the development of large living biobanks representing diverse patient populations. These models are increasingly being utilized to study cancer biology, elucidate mechanisms of treatment resistance, and evaluate patient-specific therapeutic responses, highlighting their potential as tools for precision oncology. However, important challenges remain, including incomplete representation of the tumor microenvironment (TME), variability in culture conditions, and limited scalability, and the need for greater standardization and validation. Consequently, although PDOs show considerable promise for translational research and personalized medicine, their routine clinical implementation remains largely investigational, and their clinical utility has not yet been fully established. This review examines the technological foundations of PDO generation, assesses their role as experimental models of tumor biology, and discusses their expanding applications in translational cancer research and precision oncology while highlighting key challenges that must be addressed before their widespread clinical adoption.

title: Pandemic-Responsive Molecularly Imprinted Polymer-Based Electrochemical Sensor for Mpox Detection.
authors: Seo, Youngjun; Kim, Yonghwan; Kim, Jaeheung; Jang, Jae Won; Jung, Hyo Gi; Park, Dongsung; Shin, Yonghoon; Kim, Hongrae; Kim, Yeon Ho; Bang, Junho; Kim, Hyunji; Lee, Jeong Hoon; Lee, Dongtak; Hwang, Kyo Seon; Yoon, Dae Sung
abstract: In 2022, a global Mpox outbreak occurred, and the World Health Organization (WHO) declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC). Although the outbreak was quickly constrained, new cases of infection associated with mutated virions continue to be documented worldwide. In recent global health crises, there is an urgent need to develop rapid, cost-effective diagnostic assays. While nucleic acid assays (e.g., PCR and CRISPR-based methods) represent the current gold standard for Mpox virus (MPXV) detection, point-of-care (POC) assays for Mpox remain limited. Here, we developed a molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP)-based MPXV sensor targeting A29L, a surface protein involved in host cell binding. The MIP sensor exhibits a remarkable detection limit of 7.7 pg/mL (0.54 pM). Moreover, we demonstrated that the MIP sensor detected A29L in artificial interstitial fluid (AIF) with a detection limit of 12.4 pg/mL (0.86 pM), supporting sensitive detection in a lesion-relevant model matrix. The MIP sensor preferentially responded to A29L over MPXV B6R, vaccinia virus A27L, and biointerferents and retained its response after 30 days. The results indicate that the MIP-based MPXV sensor has strong potential for clinical Mpox detection and could serve as a valuable diagnostic platform in future pandemics.

title: Multiplexed Nucleic Acid Detection Using Sequence-Specific Cleavage Mediated by Repair Endonucleases.
authors: Garden, Padric M; Li, Yudan; Murugan, Vel; Green, Alexander A
abstract: Rapid, portable detection of multiple nucleic acid targets is essential for infectious disease surveillance and precision oncology. CRISPR-based diagnostics have set a high bar for sensitivity and single-base specificity, yet their reliance on collateral nuclease activity complicates multiplexing, integration with amplification, and point-of-care deployment. Here, we present TIMBER (templated incision mediated by endonucleases of repair), a non-CRISPR platform that achieves comparable performance without nonspecific nuclease activity. TIMBER uses a repair endonuclease to cleave probes containing abasic sites only when they are hybridized to a matched target. The system exhibits strong specificity, enabling single-nucleotide polymorphism discrimination. TIMBER provides an analytical limit of detection of 12 pM without preamplification or one copy per muL (1.6 aM) with preamplification through RT-PCR or RT-LAMP, with results observable by visual fluorescence or on lateral flow. We deploy TIMBER to detect SARS-CoV-2 in clinical saliva samples and further demonstrate multiplex detection of four targets, enabling identification of EGFR mutations in lung cancer samples. This approach offers a flexible, rapid, and low-instrument-ready solution for diverse nucleic acid diagnostics, from viral detection to cancer genotyping.

title: Wnt5a Is Critical for the Maintenance of Cell Proliferation and Differentiation in Xenopus Tadpole Tail Regeneration.
authors: Nakamura, Makoto; Nishijima, Ryutaro; Kyoda, Tatsuya; Moriyama, Yuka; Yoshida, Hitoshi; Koike, Ryota; Takebayashi-Suzuki, Kimiko; Horb, Marko E; Suzuki, Atsushi
abstract: Wnt signaling is essential for tissue and organ regeneration in animals such as amphibians, and several Wnt ligands are highly expressed in regenerating tissues. However, little is known about the specific role played by each ligand and their relative contribution to regeneration processes. Here, we show that Wnt5a plays critical roles in cell proliferation and differentiation during Xenopus tadpole tail regeneration. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out (KO) of the wnt5a gene in Xenopus tadpoles caused a delay in tail regeneration. Expression of wnt5a is induced after wound healing in regenerating tails and is positively regulated by the early injury response genes junb and inhba, which are required for the initiation of regenerative cell proliferation. Interestingly, in wnt5a KO tadpoles, cell proliferation initiated by JunB and InhibinbetaA was reduced at late stages of tail regeneration, suggesting an essential role of Wnt5a in the maintenance of regenerative cell proliferation. Moreover, differentiation of the notochord and neural tissue was also affected in the regenerating tails of wnt5a KO tadpoles. Our findings demonstrate that Wnt5a acts downstream of JunB and InhibinbetaA to maintain cell proliferation and that it also promotes differentiation in Xenopus tadpole tail regeneration.

title: A self-contained ternary probe assay integrating self-priming cascade amplification with CRISPR/Cas12a for ultrasensitive detection of infant UTI-related microRNA.
authors: Deng, Guoxian; Xia, Xiaowen; Li, Xianping; Guo, Jie; Wei, Guo
journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
abstract: Accurate quantification of infant urinary tract infection (UTI)-associated microRNAs remains challenging due to their short length, low abundance, and high sequence homology. Herein, we present a sensitive fluorescent biosensor that integrates a self-priming extension cascade with CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated signal amplification, with the core innovation being a rationally designed ternary sensing probe that consolidates all recognition and amplification elements into a single, self-contained architecture on magnetic beads. This integrated design eliminates the need for multiple exogenously added primers, offering three inherent advantages: fixed stoichiometric ratios ensure reproducible reaction initiation, the unified format simplifies the operational workflow, and stringent coupling of amplification to target recognition suppresses non-specific background. Upon target recognition, the probe undergoes programmed conformational rearrangements that trigger sequential self-priming extension events, simultaneously generating fragments that drive autocatalytic feedback and T7 promoter-containing products for downstream crRNA transcription. The transcribed crRNA activates Cas12a collateral cleavage, producing exponentially amplified fluorescence. Under optimized conditions, the assay achieves a detection limit of 0.48 fM, excellent single-base discrimination, and reliable performance in human serum. Quantification results correlate strongly with qRT-PCR. This exogenously primer-free, self-contained cascade uniquely unifies signal amplification, target regeneration, and crRNA synthesis in a single probe format, while the seamless coupling with CRISPR/Cas12a trans-cleavage ensures both ultrahigh sensitivity and exceptional specificity. The proposed strategy provides a promising platform for early diagnosis and screening of infant UTI.

title: An investigation of the dual mechanism of uORF-mediated regulation of GGP1 expression and the effects on drought stress in cotton.
authors: Liu, Menghan; Li, Chao; Zheng, Juyun; Cai, Yunpeng; Wang, Peng; Yuan, Jiachen; Wang, Ye; Yan, Mengyue; Li, Xueyuan; Bulley, Sean; Ge, Xiaoyang; Zhan, Jingjing
abstract: Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are intrinsic regulatory elements that fine-tune gene expression at the translational level without altering genomic sequences or protein structures. Here, we targeted the conserved uORF that resides in the 5'-untranslated region (5'-UTR) of a GDP-galactose phosphorylase gene (GhGGP1) in cotton (Gossypium hirsutum). Regulation of GGP1 is a key control point of plant L-ascorbic acid biosynthesis. Using a dual-luciferase reporter system, we demonstrate that this uORF represses translation of the downstream GGP1 coding sequence in a feedback manner in response to elevated ascorbate, confirming previous findings in other species. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the uORFGhGGP1 generated homozygous uorfGhGGP1 mutants with unchanged transcript levels but markedly increased protein abundance and L-ascorbic acid accumulation. Under drought stress, these mutants exhibit reduced malondialdehyde levels, enhanced total antioxidant capacity, and improved drought tolerance. Mechanistically, we further show that under drought conditions, the transcription factor GhBBM directly binds to the uORF-containing cis-regulatory element, enhancing (GhGGP1) transcription and drought resistance. Together, our findings establish the uORFGhGGP1 as a dual-layer regulatory module that integrates transcriptional activation by GhBBM with translational control of the downstream protein encoding open reading frame, thereby fine-tuning drought stress responses in cotton.

title: Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9: From Biology to Therapeutic Targeting in Cardiovascular Disease.
authors: Rizzo, Riccardo; Daraban, Bianca S; Tudorache, Irina F; Barbarossa, Davide; Protopapa, Francesca; Zeynali, Amirbahman; Esposito, Francesco M; Catapano, Alberico L
abstract: BACKGROUND: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a pivotal regulator of cholesterol homeostasis, primarily known for inducing the degradation of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). Beyond this classical pathway, PCSK9 exerts complex pleiotropic effects and interacts with various lipoproteins, contributing to cardiovascular and metabolic pathologies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on PCSK9 biology, its multi-organ implications and evolving therapeutic strategies. METHODS: This narrative review summarizes current evidence from experimental, translational and clinical studies on PCSK9 biology and therapeutics. The literature examined includes studies on PCSK9 transcriptional regulation, post-translational modifications, interactions with lipoproteins and the clinical development of established and emerging PCSK9-targeting therapies. RESULTS: PCSK9 activity is modulated by several transcription factors (e.g., SREBP2, HNF1alpha) and post-translational processes such as furin cleavage and sulfation. Clinically, elevated PCSK9 levels are linked to atherosclerosis progression, heart failure and adverse outcomes in infectious diseases and certain malignancies. Monoclonal antibodies (alirocumab, evolocumab) and siRNA (inclisiran) consistently reduce LDL-C by 50%-60%. Emerging approaches include oral inhibitors which may broaden access to PCSK9-targeting therapy, and CRISPR-based gene-editing strategies (e.g., VERVE-102), which aim to achieve sustained LDL-C lowering after a single treatment. CONCLUSIONS: PCSK9 is a multifaceted protein with roles extending far beyond LDL-C regulation. Understanding its diverse interactions is crucial for optimizing treatment in cardiovascular disease and potentially expanding its therapeutic application to metabolic and infectious conditions.

title: A novel protective role for SULF1 in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease through systemic compensation and binding to KRT15.
authors: Liu, Yu; Yi, Erkang; Xi, Yue; Zuo, Yujie; Wang, Hairong; Wang, Xiaoyu; Wen, Qianmei; Zhang, Jingwei; Mei, Xinyue; Li, Haiqing; Wu, Fan; Wang, Zihui; Wan, Qi; Tang, Gaoying; Zheng, Xiaoyang; Sun, Ruiting; Ran, Pixin; Zhou, Yumin
abstract: This study explores the role of Sulfatase 1 (SULF1) in the progression of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD). SULF1, a modifying enzyme involved in various biological processes, was quantified in human serum using ELISA, and its correlation with lung function was analyzed. The in vivo function of SULF1 was investigated through CRISPR-mediated gene knockout (KO) in mice, and SULF1 overexpression was induced via adeno-associated virus (AAV). A COPD model was established by exposing mice to cigarette smoke (CS). Our findings revealed that SULF1 levels were elevated in the serum of COPD patients, where they negatively correlated with the FEV(1)/FVC ratio and the FEV(1)/FVC ratio annual decline. In CS-exposed mice, SULF1 expression was downregulated in lung tissues but increased in serum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). SULF1 KO mice exhibited more pronounced emphysematous changes following CS exposure, whereas SULF1 overexpression partially mitigated these lung alterations. Additionally, SULF1 was found to play a protective role in COPD progression through stable binding with Keratin 15 (KRT15). In conclusion, this study elucidates the role of SULF1 in COPD progression, providing novel insights into its pathogenesis and identifying potential therapeutic targets.
